data.title: Half of homes selling at a real-terms loss
data.description:
Half of all property sellers are losing money on their home once inflation is taken into account, analysis shows.

A record 48pc of homeowners sold at a real-terms loss in England and Wales over the year to July – an even higher share than in the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis.

Flats were more likely to be loss-making than any other property type, Telegraph analysis of Land Registry transactions data found. Three quarters (76pc) of flat or maisonette sellers lost money, compared with 42pc of those selling detached houses.

Sluggish house price growth and high inflation since the pandemic have made it increasingly difficult for sellers to make a meaningful profit.

Between January 2021 to July 2026, cumulative inflation – including owner-occupier costs – came to 31pc, while house prices across Britain rose by just 17pc.

Someone buying an average home in January 2021 could expect an asking price of £245,000. This property would have needed to fetch at least £322,000 in July 2026 to have kept pace with the rising cost of living.

But the average house price increased to just £288,000. That would leave the seller £34,000 out of pocket in real terms, a figure that excludes stamp duty, estate agency, legal fees and any money spent on redecoration or renovation.

The analysis also revealed that 7pc of sellers made a nominal loss over the past 12 months, the highest rate for five years.

David Fell, of estate agency Hamptons, said: “Historically, property has been a reliable hedge against higher rates of inflation, but things have played out differently this time.

“Rapidly rising interest rates in a world of higher house prices have hit buyers’ purchasing power particularly hard.

“Today’s buyers typically spend a higher proportion of their income on living costs for longer than previous generations did.”

The property market boomed in the 1990s and early 2000s, as deregulation turbocharged an expansion in mortgage credit and buy-to-let investing.

But it all came crashing down after the global financial crisis: between September 2007 and March 2009, prices plunged by more than 18pc.

Despite the average buyer at the height of the bubble having to wait until 2014 to break even, inflation never topped 5pc throughout this period.

By contrast, inflation exceeded house price growth in 2022, and has been at least twice as high each year since 2023, according to the Office for National Statistics.

At the same time, property prices have stagnated after a pandemic-era surge. Persistently high mortgage rates, buoyed by the Bank of England raising the Bank Rate 14 times in less than two years, have prevented a significant recovery.

In London, house prices have fallen more than 15pc in real terms since 2021, according to UBS. The investment bank said “stronger employment growth and rising real income” were needed in order to reverse the downward trend.

data.title: City wins battle to build skyscrapers near Tower of London
data.description:
The City of London has won a battle with Historic England about skyscraper construction near the Tower of London, paving the way for a new generation of towers in the district.

Matthew Pennycook, the housing minister, has backed down on an intervention that delayed the City of London Corporation’s development plan for three months.

In a letter to planning inspectors, Mr Pennycook said the City plan’s policies would protect the 11th-century fortress’s status as a World Heritage Site.

He said the “City Plan’s heritage policies … provide substantial safeguards to protect the Tower of London World Heritage Site and mitigate the risk of harm to the Tower’s attributes of outstanding universal value”.

The Corporation had prepared to sign off its planning policies for the next 16 years this summer, but Mr Pennycook stepped in to demand more hearings amid concerns about the scheme’s potential effect on the landmark.

The withdrawal of the intervention comes after a row between the City of London Corporation, the governing body of the Square Mile and Historic England, the UK’s heritage watchdog, about the plans.

Historic England had called for a larger “uninterrupted gap of clear sky” between the Tower and the proposed buildings to preserve views of the landmark. It also argued that new buildings should “lean away” from the monument.

It warned that failing to act risked the Tower’s reputation and conservation status.

However, the Corporation warned such restrictions would kill one million sq ft of office tower projects.

Tom Sleigh, the chairman of the City’s planning committee, said: “This was never a choice between the Tower of London and jobs. The City was here first.

“William the Conqueror started his tower in 1078 in the corner of a city already a 1,000 years old, and the two have grown side by side ever since.”

The City of London argued that Historic England’s proposals on the heights of planned office towers would make it commercially impossible for property developers to build them.

This is because developers typically charge a premium for the sought-after upper floors of skyscrapers to make their projects financially viable.

The decision may reinforce conservationist fears that ministers will prioritise growth instead of heritage concerns.

In his letter, Mr Pennycook insisted the Government remained committed to protecting the historic environment.

He pointed to new “special regard” policies in Labour’s refreshed planning guidance, designed to give World Heritage Sites extra protection.

The City of London Corporation will now expect their development plan for the Square Mile to be adopted before the end of the year.

Mr Sleigh added: “Independent inspectors have now tested the plan and agreed: the Tower is protected and the City has room to grow.”

A Historic England spokesman said: “We acknowledge the minister’s decision and we remain committed to working constructively with all partners to achieve an appropriate balance between supporting economic growth and protecting London’s internationally significant historic environment.”

data.title: The Bank of England has been burned by past rate hike failures
data.description:
The Bank of England last week gave a pretty clear signal that it is likely to increase interest rates at its next meeting in November. But what is the interest rate outlook beyond that?

It feels as though we have been here before. There are some parallels with the period 2021-22.

The common factor is the upward pressure on inflation as the result of international energy prices, in both cases driven higher as the result of war. In the earlier case, it was Russia’s conflict with Ukraine which did the damage. In this case it is the US’s continued conflict with Iran.

In the 2021 episode, the Bank of England, in common with most other central banks, at first chose to “look through” the upsurge in inflation, arguing that it was caused by global events which the UK had no control. It took the view that the upsurge in inflation would prove to be “transitory” and comparatively minor.

In the event, however, inflation carried on rising, reaching a peak of 11.1pc in late 2022.

The Bank felt it had to take action and increased interest rates in stages from 0.1pc all the way to 5.25pc. It is now widely believed, and tacitly acknowledged by the Bank, that it made a major mistake in being so slow to raise interest rates.

In fact, the UK’s economic situation today is quite different. In 2021-22, the growth of the money supply was rapid. It peaked at 15.2pc in February 2021.

It was bolstered by quantitative easing (QE), the policy under which the Bank bought bonds in the market in exchange for newly issued Bank money.

More importantly, it was also bolstered by money arriving in the bank accounts of households and businesses as the result of the major fiscal loosening enacted by the Government as it tried to offset the depressive effects of Covid and the ensuing lockdowns. In addition, the labour market was then pretty tight.

Conditions now could hardly be more different.

There has been no substantial loosening of fiscal policy. Indeed, it is set to tighten. Meanwhile, QE has given way to quantitative tightening (QT). The growth of the money supply is not running away.

Indeed, it stands at 4.3pc, a rate that has barely budged in the last few years and which hardly seems to presage an inflationary upsurge. Meanwhile, the UK labour market is much weaker than it was in 2021.

So why does the Bank seem to be on the brink of increasing interest rates?

I suspect that the failure in 2021 to raise interest rates early and fast enough is a good part of the reason. The members of the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) are wary of being wrong yet again in the same direction as last time. Once bitten, twice shy.

Ironically, though, they risk being wrong in the opposite direction for the same reason. The variable that they ignored then, namely the money supply, is signalling that they should not raise rates now.

But it is not as though the Bank has a long period of anti-inflation success behind it. Indeed, in the last 61 months, the inflation rate has only been at or below the 2pc target for only two months.

Moreover, I suspect that the actions of other central banks have had a significant bearing on the MPC’s views. Admittedly, there is no reason why the Bank of England has to move in lockstep with either the ECB or the US Federal Reserve.

Yet, in general, interest rate movements by the world’s main central banks tend to be closely correlated, in trend if not in absolute magnitude.

This is especially relevant now because in both the eurozone and the US, inflation is being pushed up by the same global factors that are driving it higher in the UK, namely the effects of the Middle Eastern war on energy markets. But the economic situation there is different.

In the eurozone, the unemployment rate is close to an all-time low. In the US, it is the lowest since June 2025. In the UK, by contrast, apart from a few months ago when it briefly hit 5.2pc, at 4.9pc, the unemployment rate is the highest since 2021.

Yet if the Bank does not raise our interest rates while other major central banks increase theirs, then there is a danger that the sterling exchange rate would weaken. In the broader scheme of things, this may be no bad thing. But it would undoubtedly tend to increase the inflation rate here, if only temporarily.

The upshot is that John Healey, the Chancellor, is probably facing higher short-term interest rates, which will increase the Government’s interest costs, as well as hitting the economy.

As for the interest rates on new medium-term and long-term gilts that he needs to issue to finance the deficit, at the end of last week, longer yields initially fell a bit. They were helped by an easing in oil prices and by the announcement of a slowing in the QT programme and an end to the sales of long gilts from the Bank’s holdings.

Yet market sentiment can change at the drop of a hat. Either another rise in prospective inflation or a further splurge in government borrowing could see yields rise sharply.

My own hunch is that, even if UK official rates are driven a fair bit higher in the next few months, by the end of next year they will be headed lower again as the economy continues to be soft and the inflation impulse transmitted by higher energy prices passes through the system without igniting a second round of price inflation.

If I am right, then that would bring some relief to the economy next year. Mind you, by that stage, having been battered by yet higher taxes in the coming Budget, the economy may need rather a lot of relief.

Roger Bootle is senior independent adviser to Capital Economics and a senior fellow at Policy Exchange.

data.title: Railways at risk as weeks of record-breaking heat damages soil
data.description:
Around 20 per cent of England’s railways are vulnerable to derailment because of this year’s record-breaking heat, experts have warned.

About a fifth of railways in the country are built on clay soil, which can become very hard when dry, causing them to shrink and crack – and for anything built on top of them to move or subside.

Roughly 1,800 miles of rails lie on clay ground in areas classed as having a high or very high risk of drought, nature investment fund Rebalance Earth has said.

Rebalance Earth shared its findings after two train derailments took place less than 24 hours apart. Last week, a service came off the tracks just outside Lewes, East Sussex, injuring 30 people. A day later, another train derailed in Wickford, Essex.

Both incidents are under investigation by the Rail Accident Investigation Branch (RAIB), with experts looking into the effect of hot and dry weather on the railways.

Investigators are examining whether the East Sussex accident could have been caused by conditions making the ground shift, causing the rails above to buckle.

A picture released by the RAIB shows a visible buckle or kink in the rails that was visible 20 minutes before the derailment.

Prof Neil Entwhistle, of Rebalance Earth, warned that clay soils – including the ground under the tracks in Lewes – are especially vulnerable to shifting when they dry out after prolonged hot and dry conditions.

“The RAIB’s initial report notes that the railway at Lewes is built on clay and alluvium that are sensitive to changes in water content, with evidence that some ground movement had already occurred,” he said.

“Investigators also identified a track geometry irregularity on the approach to the derailment, meaning the rails had shifted or become uneven, with ground movement being one potential cause,” he added.

The British Geological Survey has described the clay shrink–swell cycle as “the most damaging geohazard in Britain today”, warning that it can cause subsidence in houses as well as tens of millions of pounds in insurance claims.

Prof Entwhistle and Gabrielle Edghill, a geospatial analyst, graded each area of clay across the country for its drought risk, assigning them ratings between “very low” and “very high”. They then cross-referenced this model with the locations of all 10,000 miles of railway lines in Great Britain.

Ms Edghill said: “Uneven shrinkage beneath a railway can alter the position and level of the track, potentially creating an irregularity that requires speed restrictions, tamping or other intervention.”

There are a number of places in Britain where clay is the dominant type of ground. Most notably, this includes London, which is where the name of the colour “London Clay” originates.

Other types of clay include Wealden, Wadhurst, Oxford and Mercia Mudstone and there are various railway lines laid on top of those soils across southern England. However, not every railway line laid in a clay area is necessarily built on a clay embankment.

The Victorian engineers responsible for building the railways favoured these flat, low-lying grounds because it kept construction costs down.

Heidi Alexander, the Transport Secretary, reportedly asked rail bosses whether anything “needed to be done across the network as a whole” after the incident in Wickford.

As reported by Rail magazine, Lord Hendy, a rail minister, said: “The Secretary of State asked on Friday afternoon [Aug 14] the most senior people in Network Rail, the operator, and the ORR [Office of Rail and Road] whether or not there was anything as a consequence of having two instances in a very short space of time that needed to be done across the network as a whole.”

Greater Thameslink Railway, which operates Southern-branded trains across the south of England, said earlier this week that the line between Lewes and Haywards Heath would not reopen until Sept 1.

A Network Rail spokesman said: “We have a range of techniques for managing drying clay around the railway.

“These include using technology to monitor our tracks and trackbed, maintaining the lineside to minimise water-hungry trees, and most importantly, preparing for summer with a programme of targeted track maintenance.

“With that work and the £2.6bn we are investing in climate resilience, our railway will be safe and reliable for years to come.”

data.title: Richard Branson’s plan to make the Eurostar feel like a second-class service
data.description:
Sir Richard Branson’s much touted plan to bring some of the glamour of Virgin Atlantic to his own version of the Eurostar has been derided as a pipe dream by critics.

Overcrowding at St Pancras, a chronic lack of suitable train-maintenance sites and the inevitable mountain of red tape have been viewed as almost insurmountable obstacles to anyone intent on ending Eurostar’s monopoly over services through the Channel tunnel.

But after securing permission to run 20 trains a day between London and the Continent from Britain’s rail regulator, the billionaire’s Virgin Trains is finally beginning to win over doubters.

Virgin must still negotiate access to the tunnel itself, as well as tracks in France, Belgium and the Netherlands. And it faces a nervous wait for a fleet of 12 as yet untested high-speed trains on order from manufacturer Alstom.

However, a ruling from regulators at the Office of Rail and Road (ORR) last week suggests Sir Richard may be about to make good on his ambition of returning to Britain’s railways after Virgin Trains lost the West Coast Main Line franchise in 2019.

Virgin Trains is not the only operator intent on challenging Eurostar’s 31-year monopoly.

Italy’s state-owned Trenitalia announced earlier this month a €2bn (£1.7bn) order for 19 new trains, around half of which it aims to deploy on Channel tunnel services, while a clutch of other would-be operators are also drawing up proposals.

If those plans come to fruition, competition on the route could explode within five years, which could have an impact matching that of the 1990s discount-airline boom.

Plunging fares may encourage an influx of new customers and further loosen the grip of airlines on routes such as London to Paris, where Eurostar already has 80pc of the market.

Train services from London are likely to reach further into Europe, with lower ticket prices making rail competitive as far as Germany, Switzerland and even Italy for travellers with time on their hands.

Mark Smith, a former ORR and Department for Transport executive who runs the Man in Seat 61 travel website, reckons ticket prices could drop by close to a third.

“You’d be looking at more capacity, higher service standards and fares that could be 30pc lower based on what we have seen with the advent of competition in Italy and Spain,” he says.

“That will in turn drive further market share gains for rail compared with the airlines and make it feasible to travel further into Europe on a single ticket.”

Customer service front and centre

Virgin has so far been tight-lipped on what the Channel tunnel service might look like, with Phil Whittingham, its project lead, saying only that the route is “ripe for change” and that Sir Richard intended to build a “premium customer experience on board”.

A spokesman adds: “We don’t want to ruin the element of surprise, but just as we’ve done with Virgin Atlantic and our holidays and hotels offering, you can expect bold ideas with the customer experience front and centre.”

On Virgin Atlantic, that experience has included in-flight bar and massages, with a shift to focusing on tech innovation in recent years, including free Wi-Fi from Elon Musk’s Starlink and an AI-powered virtual concierge.

Virgin has specified single-decker trains for its purchase from Alstom, with one insider suggesting that they were more compatible with providing a full at-seat meal service than the double-deckers with which Eurostar is renewing its fleet.

Virgin has said it intends to operate an initial six return trains a day between London and Paris starting in October 2030, later increasing to 13, followed by four to Brussels and three to Amsterdam.

That would represent a substantial increase on the current timetable, with Eurostar offering 14 daily services to Paris, eight or nine to Brussels and five to Amsterdam.

The company, owned by French state railway SNCF, said Virgin’s plan confirmed “the huge potential for growth in international rail” and that it intended to “play a full part in that growth”.

Jon Worth, an expert in European railways, says Virgin had impressed with its work to secure access to St Pancras, the line to the tunnel and the last remaining space at Temple Mills maintenance shed near Stratford before Trenitalia.

“Seeing this project through has been like threading the eye of a needle,” he adds. “Forget the rhetoric from Branson about transforming travel. They’ve been very methodical and very clear headed in devising a project that will just about fit with all these restrictions.”

No room for slippage

However, he says Virgin had taken a risk in choosing a bespoke version of a train built by Alstom in Italy which has not yet been approved in France, introducing the “nightmare” scenario of the trains not being ready for 2030.

Any slippage could open the door to Trenitalia, which is viewed as among the most aggressive of European high-speed operators.

Trenitalia’s train order, from Hitachi Rail, adds to an existing commitment with the Japanese manufacturer and will provide guaranteed delivery times, potentially beating Virgin to the market by a year.

Worth says Trenitalia is likely to expand on routes such as Paris to Lyon and Marseilles and Milan, rather than focusing on London.

Eurostar’s switch to double-deckers for an order of up to 50 new trains may also be problematic, he adds, since the Celestia model is not currently compliant with evacuation requirements within the tunnel in the event of fire.

It is likely that a significant number of the new trains will instead be used on the Paris-Brussels route that Eurostar took over in 2022, easing the pressure on Virgin.

Waiting in the wings are Evolyn, backed by Spanish industrialist Jorge Cosmen, an investor in the owner of National Express, the Dutch startup Heuro, and UK-based Gemini, which has proposed running trains from Stratford and Ebbsfleet to avoid the St Pancras bottleneck.

According to Smith, of the Man in Seat 61 website, Virgin’s best bet will be to play to its strengths by offering upmarket food and wine, exploring initiatives such as allowing carriage of bicycles and dogs, which is currently banned from most Eurostar services.

He says: “It’s that hard-to-define Virgin pizazz that people most want to see and they’ll need to bring that to these trains.”

data.title: Reform drums up business support at conference
data.description:
Large firms are flocking to Reform UK’s national conference as the party prepares to host its inaugural business day.

First Bus, BT, Vodafone, Google, Heathrow, JCB, Dubai Ports and TikTok are among the businesses sponsoring or running events at the three-day summit which starts on Thursday in Birmingham.

The party’s decision to host a business day forms part of a wider Reform UK strategy to replace the Conservatives as the main opposition party to Andy Burnham’s government by fighting Labour on economic grounds.

In recent weeks, the party has unveiled plans for the biggest welfare shake-up “in a generation” by scrapping key benefits to save £50bn a year, more than double what the Tories plan to save, as well as pledging a £30 rebate for taxpayers stuck on hold to His Majesty’s Revenue and Customs (HMRC).

To appeal to wealthy backers, they are also offering conference packages worth up to £3,000, which include a champagne breakfast with Nigel Farage, an opportunity to meet and network with senior Reform leaders and a three-course meal in the Platinum hospitality area.

‘Increased engagement’

The party has toned down its offerings from last year in an attempt to professionalise, scrapping offers of custom cocktail naming rights and the delivery of bottles of sparkling wine to business stands.

A Reform UK spokesman told The Telegraph: “Engagement from British business has increased significantly. Companies across the country recognise they need to understand Reform and what a future Reform government could mean for them.

“Businesses now realise that the possibility of a Reform government is very real and are acting accordingly.”

Until 2025, Reform had a relatively low attendance from big business compared with similar events organised by Labour and the Tories.

But the influx of big business to this year’s annual event signals that the corporate world is taking the possibility of a Reform government seriously, as the party continues to outperform rivals in voter intention polling.

Crypto sidelined

Reform, which topped polls for almost 16 consecutive months between March 2025 and July 2026 and won hundreds of councillors in May, is now in second place trailing the Labour Party following a so-called Burnham bounce.

Meanwhile, Mr Farage is also believed to be sidelining crypto companies in favour of mainstream corporates following a backlash over the Reform leader’s £5m gift from Christopher Harborne, the Bitcoin billionaire.

Crypto companies are not among the businesses sponsoring the 2026 conference, which last year included donations from crypto payments firm Zebec.

The party has also scrapped perks it had previously offered to crypto industry leaders, including free tickets and access to senior figures, according to City AM, in a notable departure from previous years.

Conferences and the sponsorship fees that come in from big businesses are one of the ways that political parties raise revenue for their campaigning efforts.

A Heathrow spokesman said the airport had “a long history of constructive engagement across the political spectrum”.

He said: “Like many businesses – from airlines to pubs and banks to supermarkets – it is common practice to sponsor events at party conferences to engage policymakers and ensure they better understand the needs of consumers and the economy.”

data.title: Burnham warned warehouse tax would drive up cost of weekly shop
data.description:
Andy Burnham risks worsening the cost of living crisis if he mounts a tax raid on warehouses, retailers have warned.

The prime minister has signalled that Labour will ramp up a so-called “Amazon tax” to help fund a tax cut for “businesses that bring social benefit” such as pubs, bars and other high street stores.

However, supermarket executives and retail groups warned that the plan would push up the cost of living because high street retailers occupy the majority of warehouse space. Higher taxes are likely to be passed on in the form of higher prices for shoppers at the tills.

James Bielby, the chief executive of Food and Drink Wholesale UK, said: “It’s very simple. If they put it on, it’s going to be passed on.”

A senior executive at one of Britain’s biggest supermarkets said: “A warehouse tax on its own, without corresponding action to cut the rates burden on shops – of all sizes – would be a disaster for job creation and put further pressure on prices.”

The British Retail Consortium (BRC), which represents more than 200 major retailers, said a warehouse tax risked “driving up prices and adding pressure to family budgets”.

John Healey is finalising plans to hand a tax break to small high street stores in his maiden Budget. The Chancellor is looking at raising the minimum threshold for business rates for the first time in a decade.

Mr Healey also needs to find around £10bn in increases to ensure he balances the books “with a buffer”.

Retailers fear that the Chancellor will target warehouses with higher property taxes to help fund his Budget, arguing that many are tied to online businesses that should be paying more.

However, analysis by Savills shows high street retailers occupied 97 million sq ft of warehouse space in 2024, while online retailers took up only 69 million sq ft.

Analysis by consultants Ryan shows that the 10 warehouses with the biggest business rates bills in the country are owned by Lidl, Tesco, John Lewis, Sainsbury’s and Marks & Spencer.

‘Fuel to the fire’

Retailers that own big warehouses have already seen their business rates bills rise under Labour following reforms announced by Rachel Reeves, the former chancellor. The Treasury claimed that the change targeted online giants like Amazon.

Helen Dickinson, the chief executive of the BRC, said: “Retail already pays far more than its fair share of tax. The industry makes up just 5pc of the economy, yet pays 20pc of the total business rates bill, on top of significant increases in employer NICs and packaging taxes.

“A warehouse tax would add fuel to the fire, hitting the distribution hubs that keep our shops stocked, driving up prices and adding pressure to family budgets.”

The BRC has been campaigning to exempt large supermarkets from higher business rates, arguing that doing so would help address the cost of living crisis as the war in the Middle East triggers a fresh wave of food price rises.

In a submission to the Chancellor ahead of the Oct 28 Budget, the BRC called on Mr Healey to freeze business rates, cut net zero levies and cut National Insurance for businesses.

A separate BRC survey showed that consumer confidence was waning ahead of the Budget, with families now more worried about their personal finances and the wider economy.

Many of Britain’s biggest retailers have backed a government drive to help get more young people into a job by giving them more work experience.

However, the BRC’s submission warned that the sector, which already contributes £41bn in business taxes each year, was struggling under a slew of levies.

Ms Dickinson said: “Retailers want to invest in jobs and high streets across the country, but this is being choked off by a smorgasbord of taxes and levies. Government should support shoppers and avoid piling further taxes onto an already overtaxed industry.”

A Treasury spokesman said: “As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the Chancellor to set out at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals.”

data.title: Guardian offices infested with bedbugs
data.description:
The Guardian’s offices are infested with bedbugs, in a fresh setback to the newspaper’s efforts to get journalists back into the newsroom.

Pest controllers have been called in to fight the outbreak at the media group’s headquarters in King’s Cross, prompting some staff members to work from home.

An initial deep clean was carried out on the second floor of the building earlier this month. However, the treatment will be extended this week after staff reported a number of further bug sightings.

In an email to staff, Guardian bosses said journalists would be allowed to work from home if they felt uncomfortable coming into the office.

They added: “We appreciate this might be unsettling for some staff.”

The National Union of Journalists (NUJ) said any employees who felt pressured to work in the office should report this to a union representative.

It also encouraged members to learn about bedbugs and linked to a Guardian story about the parasites.

The outbreak threatens to undermine the Guardian’s efforts to encourage more journalists to come back into the office.

Katharine Viner, the editor, introduced a compulsory minimum of three days per week in the office at the start of 2024 after many failed to return following the pandemic.

But the mandate has been met with resistance from the NUJ, which argued that staff were not consulted on the new rules.

In a survey canvassing opinion on the policy at the time, members were asked about the impact of returning to the office on a number of factors, including the financial and environmental cost of commuting and how much time they would have to spend with their pets.

The bedbug infestation follows repeated issues with the air conditioning in Kings Place, which stopped functioning during the summer’s heatwaves.

Staff have raised repeated complaints about the building’s eco-friendly design, which automatically shuts down the air conditioning when it gets too hot. Insiders said the issues had been fixed.

Journalists are also staging a revolt over pay despite the newspaper’s offer of an above-inflation increase.

The NUJ said the offer of a 3.85pc pay rise did not “meaningfully” address concerns about the cost of living crisis and ballooning workloads.

In an indicative vote last week, 86pc of members said they would support a strike over the issue, while 96pc were in favour of action short of a strike.

The Guardian has said its pay offer is fair and compares “very favourably” to other employers in the sector.

data.title: Sir Andrew Nicol, co-author of the standard text on media law who presided over the Johnny Depp libel trial
data.description:
​Sir Andrew Nicol, who has died aged 75, was a highly regarded media and civil liberties barrister but came to wider attention as the judge at Johnny Depp’s libel trial in 2020, which earned Nicol both professional acclaim and online vilification from the so-called “Deppheads”.

The case arose from an article written by Dan Wootton in the Sun newspaper headlined “GONE POTTY: How Can J K Rowling be ‘genuinely happy’ casting wife beater Johnny Depp in the new Fantastic Beasts film?”

Depp contended that the term “wife beater” was untrue and had caused him serious harm – professional and personal. In its defence, The Sun referred to 16 incidents in which Depp had allegedly been physically violent toward his ex-wife, Amber Heard, who gave evidence ​on the newspaper’s behalf.

A leading media practitioner and co-author of the standard textbook on the subject while at the Bar, Nicol was well qualified to preside over one of the most high-profile libel cases since the passing of the Defamation Act in 2013, and he demonstrated his usual meticulous analysis and calm, careful reasoning.

In his judgment he held that The Sun had proved that the statement was “substantially true”, finding on 12 of a possible 14 occasions that Depp had been physically violent towards Amber Heard. “I accept that Mr Depp put her in fear of her life,” Nicol added.

Nicol was subsequently subjected to a wave of online attacks, harassment and conspiracy theories by the actor’s ardent fans, known as “Deppheads”. Nicol and his wife Camilla Palmer – whose feminism (she founded the Women’s Equality Network Forum) Depp fans suggested had influenced the judge in Amber Heard’s favour – briefly left London to escape the press attention.

Nicol’s ruling was later upheld, however, by the Court of Appeal, which said that it was “clear from a reading of the judgment as a whole that the judge [Nicol] based his conclusions on each of the incidents on his extremely detailed review of the evidence specific to each incident” and that therefore Depp’s proposed appeal had “no real prospect of success”.

Nicol came in for further online attacks from the actor’s fans in 2022, after Depp won a subsequent libel case against Amber Heard in the US over an article in the Washington Post, but the consensus among Nicol’s colleagues in Britain was that the American decision in no way undermined his 2020 judgment on what had been a separate matter.

Andrew George Lindsay Nicol was born at Ashtead, Surrey, on May 9 1951, the elder child of Margaret, née Mason, a physiotherapist, and Duncan Nicol, a gas engineer. After City of London Freemen’s School, he read Law at Selwyn, Cambridge, where he also rowed for his college.

After graduating, he spent two years as a Harkness Fellow at Harvard Law School (1973-75), followed by a year in California helping the director of housing and community development draft legislation to provide state funding for low-income homes.

After a further year in Sydney with the commercial​ law firm Allen Allen & Hemsley, Nicol returned to London, where for the next 10 years he lectured part-time at the LSE in commercial law, although he soon became more interested in social justice and human rights.

After being called to the Bar by Middle Temple in 1978, he was taken on that year by Geoffrey Robertson as his first pupil at No 1 Dr Johnson’s Buildings, then the pre-eminent liberal/civil liberties set, headed by Emlyn Hooson (who had defended the Moors murderer Ian Brady) and John Mortimer.

Robertson’s fellow members of chambers had turned down his previous suggested recruit, the comedian Clive Anderson, but Robertson recalled Nicol as “a great boon to have at my side”.

Among those he taught at the LSE, meanwhile, Nicol was able to talent-spot Robertson’s next pupils, Heather Rogers and Heather (later Mrs Justice) Williams, both of whom went on to become successful silks.

When Nicol began his pupillage, Robertson was acting as junior to Jeremy Hutchinson QC in the ABC secrets trial (so-called after the first letter of each of the defendants’ names), which had arisen from an article written by their client Duncan Campbell for Time Out magazine in 1976.

Nicol impressed everyone by coming up with an authority to challenge the Attorney General’s secret order that the jury be vetted for “extremist opinions”, finding in the LSE library a rare copy of Jeremy Bentham’s 1821 treatise denouncing jury-vetting, which was then extensively cited by Hutchinson in his impassioned opening attack on the unconstitutionality of the practice.

After qualifying, Nicol began taking cases in immigration law, which became an area of expertise – he co-wrote the book Subjects, Citizens, Aliens and Others (1990) and chaired the Immigration Law Practitioners’ Association from 1997 to 2000.

He also shared Robertson’s interest in media law and in 1984 they co-authored Media Law, initially a slim volume which they dubbed “The Journalist’s Toothbrush”, as reporters would stuff a copy in their suitcase when summoned to court in case they were sent to prison. By 2008 it was into its fifth edition and ran to more than 1,000 pages.

In 1986 Nicol acted for the investigative reporter David Leigh and The Observer in the case that brought an end to the practice in lower courts of withholding the names of magistrates from the press. In another case, he was junior to Robertson in his successful defence of the New Statesman on a charge of contempt of court for interviewing jurors in the Jeremy Thorpe trial of 1979. The opposing Treasury Counsel on that occasion reported Nicol to the Bar Council for wearing brown shoes, which in those days were forbidden by Bar etiquette ​and never to be seen below a black gown.

Nicol was Robertson’s junior for the 1992 appeal of Kiranjit Ahluwalia, who had been convicted of murdering her husband after suffering 10 years of abuse following their arranged marriage.

It was Nicol who devised the argument that she had been suffering from diminished responsibility and persuaded the Lord Chief Justice Peter Taylor to order a retrial, at which she was instead convicted of manslaughter and sentenced to the time she had already served – three years and four months – so released immediately.

In 1990 Nicol was among those (including a young Keir Starmer) who broke away with Robertson to found Doughty Street Chambers, where for many years he acted as the set’s treasurer. With his academic background, quiet, modest nature and infectious sense of humour, he was very persuasive on paper and when appearing before a judge, if less well suited to jury advocacy. He was also noted for his kindness and generosity to junior barristers making their way.

He took Silk in 1995 and served as a Recorder from 2000 until he was appointed a High Court Judge in 2009, assigned to the Queen’s Bench Division.

Punctilious and firm but far from pompous on the bench, Nicol could seem embarrassed when his textbook on media law was referred to in his court. In the terrorist case of R v Incedal (2014), Nicol was persuaded to impose a blanket secrecy order, only to have his textbook – albeit a section written by his co-author – cited by counsel on appeal as authority for the proposition that a trial held in secret is no trial at all.

This was one of very few of his judgments that were overturned. Another one in 2016 involved the consultant surgeon David Sellu, who was convicted of gross negligence manslaughter but released after serving 15 months in prison. His conviction overturned on the grounds that Nicol’s jury directions on what amounted to “gross negligence” had been insufficient.

Away from the law, Nicol enjoyed sailing and walking near the holiday home in north Norfolk he shared with his wife Camilla Palmer, a solicitor and now mediator specialising in employment and discrimination, whom he married in 2005. She survives him with their two sons.

​​Sir Andrew Nicol, born May 9 1951, died August 22 2026

data.title: Odeon value slashed by £230m as cinema visits slump
data.description:
Odeon has cut the value of its movie theatres by more than £230m after a slump in the number of people going to the cinema.

The group, which has more than 100 sites across the UK, lowered its expectations for future attendance as theatres struggle to persuade customers to return to their old cinema-going habits.

Annual accounts for Odeon Cinemas Group show the company booked a one-off £232.7m impairment for the year ending December 2025 because of a “downward revision of market attendance volume”.

The write-down follows a bruising period for cinema chains as audiences fail to return to their pre-pandemic habits, despite a string of blockbuster releases.

British cinemas sold 123.5 million tickets last year – 2pc fewer than in 2024 and 30pc below 2019, according to the British Film Institute.

Odeon, which is now owned by US giant AMC Entertainment (AMC), was Britain’s first cinema chain, having been founded by Oscar Deutsch, an entrepreneur, in 1928.

Its flagship site, the Art Deco-inspired Odeon in Leicester Square, opened in 1937 and remains a key venue for the business.

Odeon was later owned by private equity group Terra Firma and merged with European counterpart United Cinemas International (UCI). AMC bought the group in 2016.

Cinema attendance has been heavily hit by the availability of major blockbusters.

Hollywood’s writers’ and actors’ strikes in 2023 delayed a number of releases, leaving cinemas with a thin slate of releases during the first half of 2024.

Cinemas struggled to maintain momentum last year, with A Minecraft Movie, Bridget Jones: Mad About the Boy and Wicked: For Good being the year’s three biggest films.

The UK Cinema Association said the industry had entered the second half of 2025 with admissions 20pc higher than a year earlier, only for a weaker final-quarter line-up to gradually wipe out the gains. It described the year as “stop-start”.

A parliamentary inquiry recently found the frequency with which people visited cinemas was down 40pc since before the pandemic, from six times pre-Covid to three or four times afterwards.

Shorter periods of cinema exclusivity have also made it easier for audiences to wait for films to appear on streaming sites.

Before Covid, films typically remained exclusive to cinemas for around four months, but studios subsequently experimented with much shorter windows and simultaneous streaming releases.

AMC has backed longer theatrical windows and said studios were increasingly committing to at least 45 days.

There are signs of recovery in 2026. Odeon attendance rose 8pc in the first two months of the year to 11.9 million, according to AMC, although the wider European market was up 12pc.

AMC expects European cinema attendance in its markets to increase by as many as 40 million visits this year.

An Odeon spokesman said: “The impairment is historical, related to our 2025 financial results and reflecting a short-term decrease in attendance seen across the wider cinema market.

“In 2026, we have seen attendance continue to improve, leading to a record-breaking box office in the UK and Ireland over the summer, with Odeon welcoming almost 10 million guests between June and August.”

data.title: The Bank of England is being far too timid
data.description:
The Bank of England last week cemented its growing reputation as an international outlier. 

While other major central banks have lately raised their main policy interest rates, responding to the growing threat of a renewed inflation spike, the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) voted to keep rates on hold.

The Bank has also been alone in recent years in aggressively selling sovereign bonds back into the market, so pushing up the cost of borrowing, compounding the UK Government’s increasingly serious funding difficulties.

Our central bank did finally address that matter last week – but in an unconvincing manner.

The UK is significantly more inflation-prone than the rest of the G7. Headline inflation averaged 3.4pc in 2025, but just 2.8pc across other comparable nations. So far this year, monthly figures show the consumer price index (CPI) rising by 3pc on average per annum, while the same G7 measure has stabilised at just 2.2pc during 2026.

In the last three months, Brent crude has soared from $72 to around $103 a barrel – a 43pc rise – mainly because of ongoing hostilities between the US and Iran.

The Strait of Hormuz remains largely unnavigable, with southern tanker routes out of the Red Sea now also controlled by Iran-backed rebels – which is why oil prices have spent most of September in triple-digit territory.

High energy costs push up inflation, of course. And while rate rises don’t solve diplomatic impasses, or otherwise help lower oil prices, they do show central banks are serious about fighting inflation, helping to prevent the effect of high energy prices becoming embedded in supply chains and the broader economy.

At a crucial moment, the MPC is collectively conveying the impression that it is more interested in doing the Government short-term favours – interest rate increases are rarely popular – than it is in bearing down on price pressures.

The UK’s public finances are on a knife-edge, with 10-year gilts now firmly above 5pc, compared with 4.6pc at the peak of the October 2022 “mini-budget crisis” – which saw our political and media class suffer a collective nervous breakdown and oust the then-prime minister.

Yields touched 5.4pc last week, close to a 19-year high.

The difference is that back in 2007, Britain’s national debt was below 40pc of GDP. That same figure is close to 100pc today – which is why the UK’s annual debt service bill, now more than the state spends on education, is also uniquely high among G7 nations.

Bond yields, the cost of government borrowing, are driven in part by the fiscal outlook. And with Andy Burnham’s Labour government looking even more wedded to high-spending, trade-union-appeasing policies than its predecessor, the fiscal outlook is alarming.

But yields are also hugely affected by inflation, with creditors demanding compensation for the loss in real-terms value of the money they lend.

That’s why it’s of cardinal importance that the MPC presents itself as ultra-hawkish – so estimates of future inflation are kept as low as possible. And by voting 6-3 to keep the Bank’s main policy rate at 3.75pc last Thursday, the MPC collectively failed.

The eurozone faces the same external, energy-driven inflation pressure as the UK. The European Central Bank, having already put rates up a quarter of one percent in June, raised eurozone borrowing costs another 25 basis points (bps) earlier this month.

The day before the MPC’s decision was announced, the Federal Reserve increased its policy rate from 3.5pc to 3.75pc, the US central bank’s first rate increase in three years. And then on Friday, the Bank of Japan implemented its second 25 bps interest rate increase of 2026.

Headline UK inflation hit 3.1pc in August, up from 2.9pc in July and 2.6pc the previous month. CPI inflation has been above the Bank’s 2pc target for the last 23 months and is now widely expected to breach 4pc early next year. The retail price index, which includes some housing costs, is already at 3.4pc.

By leaving interest rates on hold, while other central banks increased theirs, including the mighty Fed signalling the start of a new global interest rate cycle, the MPC looks as if it’s kicking the can down the road. Raising rates last week would have helped rebuild the Bank’s credibility – which is sorely needed – while reducing the chances of steeper and more damaging rate increases further down the road.

The MPC was far too slow to raise rates in the aftermath of the Covid pandemic – consistently ignoring those of us who correctly warned of a post-lockdown inflation jump. Headline inflation has been above target for most of the last five years.

It seems highly likely the MPC will raise rates when it next meets in early November, after John Healey’s, the Chancellor, first Budget. So why not just raise them now?

No one is saying monetary policy is easy – I’m not criticising individual MPC members. But when it comes to central banking, credibility is everything – and, under current circumstances, arguments to “look through” what are described as “temporary” or “transitory” inflation pressure simply don’t stack up.

What also doesn’t stack up is the MPC’s approach to quantitative tightening (QT). The Bank of England has been the only major central bank actively selling bonds bought during earlier quantitative easing back into the market – rather than passively letting them mature.

This has driven up long-term borrowing costs while crystallising losses, which the Treasury is forced to cover, piling even more pressure on the public finances.

The MPC has agreed to reduce the Bank’s gilt holdings at an annual average pace of £46bn, down from £70bn, until QT is set to end in 2034, while pausing active sales until next April.

This is far too timid. Active QT should be cancelled entirely – with policymakers doing everything possible to pull Britain away from fiscal oblivion.

data.title: I travelled the ‘border’ between North and South. Here’s what I learnt
data.description:
A sign by the estuary warns of danger, but it’s hard to see much to be afraid of here apart from the nettles and a fairly ominous sky. Under the Severn Bridge, on a spit of land on the river’s west side, it seems peaceful enough. Traffic roars overhead, but you can’t see the cars from below. There’s birdsong and the smell of wet foliage, glimmering water fringed by sodden sand and then cracked earth. It doesn’t feel like a border, but I’m standing at the far western end of England’s North-South divide.

There is, of course, no official line across England’s midriff. No razor-wire fences or passport checks mark where the South ends and the North begins. But nor is the boundary a figment of our imagination. We’ve heard enough jokes about the Watford Gap to know that Southerners see the North – the people, the places, the culture – as somehow different. And we Northerners, admittedly, can be bloody-minded about our Northern identity.

But how entrenched does the North-South divide remain today, after years of political talk of levelling up, Northern powerhouses and ill-fated high-speed rail connections? How much does our geography still shape how we see those from elsewhere in the country? And where, actually, does the notional dividing line start and end?

Apparently, not where you might expect. Recent YouGov data from almost 46,000 adults in England revealed that many people along the borders of the areas classified as North, South and Midlands don’t place themselves in the same regions government maps would suggest. Feelings of “Northernness” extended south of the regional borders, the pollsters found, while in the parts of East Anglia that supposedly sit in the South, people don’t all feel Southern. In short, like many types of identity, it’s complicated.

With that in mind, I have set out to travel along an unofficial boundary line between the North and South of England – one commonly used in academic research – to interrogate these feelings and explore what the divide means today. My editor has suggested I walk the entire 340 miles from Beachley Point on the Severn estuary to the Wash, between Lincolnshire and Norfolk, possibly in one go. I have counter-suggested the use of a motor vehicle.

The journey is a personal one. Having grown up in Leeds, my Northern identity is one I have insisted on throughout my adult life (which I’ve spent mostly in the South). When I started writing my debut crime thriller novel, The House on Otley Road, I knew it had to be set in West Yorkshire. Home.

The tug of the North has never left me, and I spend much of my time on the East Coast Main Line, travelling to and from where I spent my youth. But I’m surprised to find that it supposedly begins more or less where I’m standing by the Severn. The first (and only) person I encounter on the footpath here is Justin Charnock, 37. He identifies as Southern (this is fair – he comes from near Bristol) and thinks “people in the North are a lot nicer than people in the South” (also fair). “More welcoming,” he says.

It’s a commonly held perception, mentioned frequently by those I meet on my journey – almost all of whom have strong ideas about how Northerners differ from Southerners.

Charnock thinks being Southern traditionally means being “wealthier; a lot more aloof; snobby; much less hospitable, welcoming, friendly or helpful”. Working in the South West (he won’t divulge his job), he never gets tipped and “often people are a bit snooty”.

‘It’s become very middle class here’

Behind the popular images of Northerners lie some dispiriting numbers. The North East remains the region with the lowest healthy life expectancy at birth (HLE), at 57 years, according to the most recent figures from the Office for National Statistics (ONS). It has had the lowest HLE in every period since the ONS began measuring it. The South East remains the region with the highest HLE (63 years for men, 64.3 years for women).

A similar disparity can be seen in economic activity. In 2023, London had the highest gross domestic product per capita, at £69,077, while the North East had the lowest, at £28,583. It is worth noting, though, that the poverty rate is higher in London (26 per cent) than anywhere else in the country, according to figures from the charity Joseph Rowntree Foundation.

Meanwhile, perceptions of Northerners and Southerners that seem to stem from our economic histories – the North as industrial, the South as the country’s financial engine – have stubbornly persisted.

The first stop on my journey is Brockweir, a scenic Gloucestershire village on the river Wye. Old stone houses are painted in creamy yellow, pale blue and white, while green hills rise behind them. All the villagers seem to know each other. They all have dogs, and their dogs know each other too. The community owns its pub, the 16th-century Brockweir Inn.

“We tried to sell our bodies [to raise the money for it], but we’re all too old,” says Carol Knight, 76. (I think she’s joking.)

Her family has lived here for centuries. “It’s become very middle class,” says the suntanned, denim-dungaree-clad former English teacher, while clutching a bunch of Whitsuntide boss flowers and the leads of her two labradors. “Property prices have skyrocketed.”

Does this mean Brockweir must be Southern? House prices are, after all, a stark divider between North and South. Prices may be rising more steeply in the North at present, but the gap remains vast, even after removing London from the equation: in March 2026, the average house price across the South East and South West was £340,000, compared with £188,500 across the North East and North West.

‘We need more Northern leaders’

I travel onwards, trying to keep close to the Wye, down winding lanes bordered by verdant hedgerows and cow parsley. I stop at Upper Redbrook, where I can’t find a pub, or a shop, or a human, then Staunton, where the 18th-century pub isn’t open yet (it’s still too early). Traffic rattles through the village of silent modern houses.

In the Herefordshire village of Lea, I encounter a friendly pair of Scousers who decamped here long ago. Mike Tyson, a 46-year-old roofer and carpenter (“Yes, it’s my real name,” he says, for probably the millionth time), talks of his daughter’s “Northern attitude”.

What is it? “Friendlier, more easy-come, easy-go. ‘Chippy’ is the right phrase.”

The men are not the only ones to claim Northerners have a different (better?) sense of humour. But there’s uncertainty about whether we’re in the North or the South here – the consensus seems to be the middle – but Tyson believes there’s more money to be made down here than up in Liverpool.

Tied up with the question of economic activity and affluence is that of political power. Devolution to England’s cities and regions has given some control to communities far from Westminster. Whether it has helped those communities feel less overlooked is uncertain. Phil Henesey, 71, who is drinking in a beer garden with Tyson in the late-afternoon sunshine, says the North still feels farther (figuratively) from Westminster decision making.

“That’s why we need more Northern leaders,” he says.

He is speaking not long before the enthroning of a Northern leader in Downing Street. Andy Burnham, the Liverpool-born former Mayor of Greater Manchester, has made much of his links to, and concern for, the North of England. The new PM has created a No 10 North. In doing so, he has set himself up to be judged on how successfully he makes Northerners feel more connected to the centre of power. Also on how he does this without alienating the South.

‘There’s more chivalry in the North’

It’s raining when I reach Ledbury, the sky a grey-white sheet. The Tudor buildings are picture-perfect and well preserved. “It’s very much Middle England,” says a shopkeeper on the high street who doesn’t want to be named. “Did you ever see Keeping up Appearances? It’s full of Hyacinth Buckets [here].”

He identifies as a Southerner. “When you go up North, it’s dark,” he says. “It’s a funny old thing, that divide.”

Declan Butler, a 68-year-old Irishman who moved to Britain in the 1970s and now runs a gift shop down the road, thinks Ledbury is “probably more Southern”, judging by its disposable income.

“I had a couple in here from North Yorkshire at the weekend and they spoke to me as if we were old friends, whereas people from the South East are much more reserved,” he says. “If I was to choose a Southerner or a Northerner to be friends with, I’d choose a Northerner, because they’re friendlier. They’re probably harder workers. They’re grafters.”

He concedes that Cockneys and people from Essex can be friendly, too. Has he been to the North much? “I’ve been to Birmingham,” he offers.

Crossing into Worcestershire, I see the grey-blue shadow of the hills rise up ahead. I pass an old roadside chapel and an abandoned filling station, and arrive at Bredon, where the local Spar sells cider on tap.

“I thought the North started at Crewe,” muses Steve Fowler, an ex-Army man, inside the still-quiet Royal Oak pub, where there’s horse racing on the TV. He’s surprised to hear that by some definitions he is in the North right now. A Southerner by birth (Surrey), he awards the North another point for humour. “The funniest comedians are Northerners,” he says.

“I think [people] are more materialistic in the South,” says David Gray, a semi-retired gardener from Scotland. “There’s a lot more chivalry in the North.”

“It’s all about survival in the North,” chips in Paul Sefton, a retired butcher. He came here from North Wales 30 years ago “purely because someone said to me my kids would never get a proper job up North”.

‘The Cotswolds is becoming the Home Counties’

The North-South divide has been with us for a long time, chronicled and perpetuated by our art and culture. Elizabeth Gaskell’s North and South (published 1855) contrasts England’s tranquil, idyllic South with a grimy industrial North plagued by poverty and suffering. Almost 150 years later, David Peace evoked a dark and lawless North in his fictional Red Riding quartet. There was always something harder and edgier about the most famous Northern bands than their Southern counterparts. Contrast the Beatles with the Kinks, Oasis with Blur.

Yet in today’s hyperconnected society, how long can such differences last?

“It’s flattened out quite a bit by sheer mobility,” says Steve Fowler. And, he says, by exposure to the internet. “You would have to go very deep into the countryside, to very isolated communities, to find residual differences.”

In the Plough Inn in Stretton-on-Fosse, Warwickshire, Gordon Everett, 59, says, with both sadness and pride, “This is one of the last old-fashioned drinking pubs.” Local accents are waning a lot, he says, touching on the most overt marker of Northern or Southern identity. When he was a boy, you could tell the difference in accents between people from two local villages that lay just three miles apart. “Now, everyone’s got this flat English accent.”

Non-locals, he says, have come to the area and changed it. “The Cotswolds is becoming the Home Counties.”

Still, tracing this line across the country is a lesson in the extent to which our villages and small towns either cling to their past or else are haunted by it. Between Bredon and Stretton-on-Fosse, I pass houses with names such as the Old Bakehouse, the Old Stoves. A croquet club and a country clothing store. Less picturesque: a dead badger on the A44.

In Brackley, Northamptonshire, there’s a similar nostalgia in evidence. On the high street, there’s the Old Bakery and the Old Hall Bookshop. The sign for Brackley Community Shops is painted in old-fashioned fairground colours. One of these shops offers tattoos, but still.

In the Courtyard Shops farther along, I’m reminded of one of those mock-Victorian streets you find in museums, except there’s a vape shop here. Browsers are welcome, says a sticker in the window, and they’re also on CCTV.

A 75-year-old woman I meet in the town, when I ask what Northerners are like, suggests they’re either industrious farmers or else they work in “industrial places”. I don’t have the heart to tell her that no one I know in West Yorkshire does any such thing.

Did you know Brackley is in fact north of the North-South divide, I ask Anne Mellor, a volunteer in a local charity shop? “No,” she says, “we thought we were in the middle, surrounded by HS2.”

Depending on where you are in the North, transport links can be a sore point – and another marker of difference from the South. Burnham might be proud of his re-regulated Bee Network buses in Manchester, but raise the subject of the still-non-existent tram service in Leeds and that fabled Northern grit might give way to heavy sighs of Northern frustration.

In the North East, poor transport links were said last year to put more than 30 per cent of the region at risk of poverty. In 2022, lack of transport connectivity was found by the Centre for Cities to cost the North £16bn a year in productivity losses. Against this backdrop, HS2 has become a punchline, not an answer.

‘They’re parochial and territorial’

I’m travelling to Silverstone, Northamptonshire, which is famous for a different sort of transport. Pictures of motor-racing heroes adorn the walls of the village pub, the White Horse. I pass through a familiar landscape of roundabouts and roadworks before arriving. A poster on the village noticeboard invites me to become the best version of myself. (I decline.)

Gary Baird, 38, who runs the pub, thinks the North is more working class, while the South attracts more tourism. No one, he argues, goes to Hull on holiday.

Onwards to Rushden, Northants, a “historic boot and shoe town”, passing en route an American diner, a Starbucks, a Travelodge, a McDonald’s, a Toby Carvery and a new-build housing estate. I could be anywhere now. I don’t know whether I’m North or South, my senses are scrambled, or numbed by the dreary uniformity of our in-between spaces.

But in Rushden, for the first time, I feel I could be in the North. Behind the bar in the town’s Working Men’s Club, 30-year-old Tomethia Bartley confirms, “They’re Northerners here.” (She’s not – she’s from London.) “They’re all in a community together. Everyone knows everyone.”

She’s wearing a T-shirt saying, “Don’t like me? F--- off. Problem solved.” I don’t know how Northern or Southern this sentiment is.

Howard, 67, a former helicopter pilot enjoying a pint in the club with his partner, Lynette Keirnan, says: “I was married to a woman from Lancashire. She was bloody weird, actually. They seem to see things differently up there. They’re very parochial and territorial.

“They eat food like barm cakes [a bread roll from the North West] and black peas,” he adds. “They feel disenfranchised, I think.”

But out on the high street, it doesn’t feel so different here from many post-industrial towns further North, with grand old Victorian buildings and the sense of better days being behind it. There’s a kebab shop and an amusement arcade now. A nail bar, a Poundstretcher and, curiously, a large reptile specialist called House of Venom.

Deeply ingrained perceptions

The land flattens out as I enter Lincolnshire, stopping briefly in Market Deeping for a scalding portion of battered fish. “Sunny days are here at last,” it says on a small blackboard inside the Market Gate Deli. Outside, a fine rain falls. An unseasonable chill hangs in the early June air.

My odyssey ends in Norfolk, where I meet arable farmer Richard Ward, 55. “Where am I?” I ask.

“You’re probably North more than anything, because that’s the North Sea,” he says, pointing to the horizon, where I can’t see anything but farmland. A few years ago, a bomb squad came to remove a load of Second World War ordnance found in the fields. “It was quite a hairy experience,” says Ward.

Do people fish out there? I ask, pointing vaguely to where the sea should be. No, he says. “It’s dead vegetation and horrible black, boggy clay soil.”

I finish my journey not far from this, by a soggy field overlooking some marshland. The sun has finally emerged. Some desultory wasps buzz above the glistening wet grass. A crow caws, a cockerel crows and my feet are becoming very wet.

The conversations I’ve had along my journey have shown that, despite our increasingly homogenised culture, perceptions of differences between Northerners and Southerners remain deeply ingrained. Perhaps we will always retain these in some form.

As Richard Collett writes in his book Along the Borders, “We carve landscapes apart to define our very sense of self and identity.”

I recognise this impulse. And I’m not going to claim it’s all grim down South, but I’ll always be Northern and proud.

data.title: National security alert as TalkTalk risks insolvency within days
data.description:
Whitehall is on high alert because of the threat that TalkTalk, the broadband provider, may go into administration within days and open up a national security vulnerability.

Security officials responsible for Britain’s most critical infrastructure are in close daily contact with senior civil servants and telecoms regulators as they seek to ensure that TalkTalk is able to keep operating in the event of an insolvency.

It is feared that disruption to services could hit the Ministry of Defence and weaken Britain’s security at an unstable moment in international affairs.

Networks on which national security depends were partly dependent on TalkTalk systems, telecoms sources said. The company operates as a provider of both consumer broadband and secure services for large organisations.

The discussions have been accelerating on the belief that the company, Britain’s fourth-biggest broadband provider with around 1.5 million customers, could appoint administrators early next week.

The company and its advisers on Thursday night were still hoping to complete a complex plan to sell off the two arms of TalkTalk as going concerns. However, The Telegraph earlier this week revealed that talks to offload its wholesale business, PXC, to Octopus Investments for around £300m had faltered.

It is also possible that shareholders, including Sir Charles Dunstone and lender Ares Management, could inject yet more money into the stricken company, having already provided £350m in emergency funding in the last two years.

Taxpayers risk footing the bill

The sale was required to secure a buyer for the consumer business, as it is dependent on the infrastructure controlled by PXC. Now both TalkTalk businesses are threatened with what would be the biggest insolvency in the UK telecoms industry for decades.

Opus Broadband this week cut its offer for the consumer business in half to £100m after it was proposed that the division of TalkTalk should be more generous to PXC.

Meanwhile, officials are racing to understand whether keeping TalkTalk, which employs around 900 workers, online during an administration might trigger significant costs to the taxpayer, and how the business might be transferred to a new owner without disruption.

The talks are grappling with the fact that there is no special administration regime in telecoms comparable to that in the water industry. Ministers would be able to oversee and use public money to underwrite the operations of an insolvent water supplier to guarantee supplies.

The situation threatens to bring close scrutiny to Sir Charles, TalkTalk’s billionaire founder, who remains a major shareholder. In 2020, he orchestrated a debt-fuelled buyout of the company alongside the private equity and credit funds, which ended its disappointing run on the stock market and saddled it with costly debt.

The burden has since climbed further, to £1.4bn, while TalkTalk’s business has deteriorated, as the market has left it behind without the financial firepower to compete. Although Sir Charles remains chairman, it has been effectively under the control of its lenders, led by the private credit giant Ares, for some time.

Even if solvent sales of TalkTalk’s businesses can be salvaged, its lenders are expected to lose hundreds of millions on their exposure.

The company is understood to be in significant arrears with BT’s network arm, Openreach, which leases its access to broadband lines into homes. Many other bills are also due at the end of the month.

Openreach is viewed as unlikely to trigger an insolvency, given the potential disruption for customers, who are said to include more than 250,000 vulnerable households. They include people with chronic kidney disease who are dependent on connected dialysis machines and elderly people with personal alarms.

Ofcom regulators have sought guarantees from potential bidders for the consumer business that vulnerable customers will be protected in a solvent rescue deal, industry sources said.

BT takeover discussions

It is understood that the option of transferring control of TalkTalk to BT as quasi-“supplier of last resort” in an insolvency is also under discussion. The troubled company has its own ageing equipment installed in telephone exchanges, which would make a takeover more costly for Sky or Vodafone, for instance.

However, there are questions about whether BT would want the business and how its rivals would react to a takeover of millions of broadband lines by the dominant player in the market. It is possible such competition concerns and legislation could be overruled by the potential national security threat of an insolvency.

Such a scenario would mark a dramatic end for TalkTalk, which began as part of Sir Charles’s retail empire Carphone Warehouse and went on a series of acquisitions in the early broadband market of the 2000s. The legacy of that dealmaking was poor customer service, which left TalkTalk with limited ability to challenge the likes of BT and Sky outside the budget segment of the market.

The rollout of faster and more expensive full-fibre broadband in recent years has eroded the company’s customer base and left a business unattractive as an acquisition target.

A Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport spokesman said: “This is a commercial matter, and we do not comment on speculation.”

An Ofcom spokesman said: “While we have no formal role in this process, we’re closely monitoring developments.”

TalkTalk declined to comment.

data.title: Kremlin seizes Nestlé’s Russian assets in new crackdown
data.description:
Nestlé said it is assessing its options after Vladimir Putin ordered the seizure of its Russian business.

The KitKat maker suggested it would take action to protect its rights after the Kremlin announced a presidential decree taking control of the Swiss company’s assets on Thursday.

It told shareholders: “The company is assessing the situation and its options.

“Nestlé is committed to taking all necessary steps to protect its rights and ensure continuity of business operations in the interests of all stakeholders, particularly its employees.”

Russia has tightened control over foreign-owned assets since the start of the Ukraine war in 2022.

A 2023 decree signed by Putin gives Moscow the power to place ‌assets from countries it deems “unfriendly” ‌under temporary administration.

The mechanism has been used to take control ​of the Russian subsidiaries of Danone and Carlsberg.

Nestlé shares fell 1.7pc on Friday in the wake of the Kremlin’s order, which also put the Russian business of French ​supermarket group ‌Auchan into a temporary administration.

The decree also covers the Russian subsidiaries of French logistics group FM Logistic and the former Leroy Merlin DIY chain, now known as Lemana Pro.

Each company’s assets have been transferred to a company called LEV Management.

Nestlé has six factories in Russia producing coffee, pet care and infant formula.

⁠It generated sales of about 2bn Swiss francs (£1.8bn) in Russia in 2021, the last year it released figures, and has about 7,000 employees there.

Warren Ackerman, an analyst at Barclays, said the Kremlin’s order means the “risk of Nestlé losing the business looks materially higher”.

However, Jean-Philippe Bertschy of the Swiss investment bank Vontobel said he expected the financial impact to Nestlé would be small “given Russia’s limited contribution to group sales”.

He said Russia now accounted for just over 1pc of the group’s sales, down from around 2pc before the Ukraine war.

It has suspended “the vast majority of sales, non-essential imports, advertising and capital investment”, he said, while continuing to supply essential food items.

Moscow took control of French dairy company Danone’s Russian business ‌and beer company Carlsberg’s stake in a local brewer in 2023.

Danone ​was removed from the list of assets under temporary Russian state ​management in March 2024 amid reports that a Russian businessman ⁠known for his pro-war ⁠credentials planned to buy the business at a steep discount.

In December 2024, Carlsberg sold its shares in Baltika Breweries in a management buyout.

Jon Cox, a Kepler Cheuvreux analyst, said such experiences did not bode well for Nestlé.

He said: “Ultimately, Nestlé may end up losing those assets – around 2pc of its sales and cash tied up in Russia – for the foreseeable future and any compensation is unlikely to be ​an offset.”
