data.title: Tories pledge to restore tax-free shopping for tourists
data.description:
Kemi Badenoch will bring back tax-free shopping for overseas visitors as part of an effort to boost Britain’s struggling high streets.

The Tory leader will unveil plans on Sunday to restore VAT refunds for non-EU visitors, a move expected to generate £4.1bn in extra spending.

The tax break will be funded by a crackdown on NHS tourism, under which foreign visitors receive free hospital care to which they are not entitled.

Last week, Labour announced a tourist tax across mayoral authorities under its control, which the Tories said would add to the price of the family holiday and drive people to travel overseas instead.

Before 2021, overseas visitors were able to claim back the VAT they paid on goods in high street shops.

Under Boris Johnson, the Tories scrapped tax-free shopping, a move that businesses said made them less competitive than their European counterparts.

Mrs Badenoch said a future Conservative government would restore VAT refunds for eligible visitors from outside the EU.

If the evidence confirms the scheme pays its way, it would be extended to visitors from the EU by the end of the next parliament.

‘We have so much to offer’

“Britain should be the place where the whole world comes to shop,” the Conservative leader said.

“We have iconic retailers, inventive designers and brilliant manufacturers, but they are being let down by a tax policy that is chasing their customers away. Holidaymakers are choosing rival cities in other countries for the simple reason that it saves them money.

“British retailers are closing down shops with the knock-on effects damaging small manufacturers, suppliers and jobs across the UK. I want them to know I’m on their side and Conservatives will sort out taxes so companies can create jobs and grow our economy.

“That is why we will restore tax-free shopping for overseas visitors, helping British firms compete and encouraging more people to choose Britain. Why should we send shoppers away to France or Italy?

“This attitude that we’re just helping wealthy tourists is ignorant of the reality that they bring much-needed income. We have so much to offer – we should not be giving visitors a reason to go anywhere else.”

The Centre for Economics and Business Research estimates that the move could attract up to 2.35 million additional visitors annually, generating billions of extra revenue for retail, hospitality and tourism.

They also estimate that for every £1 of VAT refunded to tourists, another £1.56 could be generated in other taxes.

The Conservatives say the abolition of tax-free shopping in 2021 left the UK less competitive than major European destinations just as the country left the EU.

Although visitor numbers have recovered to near pre-pandemic levels, real-terms spending remains 8 per cent lower.

The annual £540m cost of the tax cut will be partly offset by a crackdown on unpaid or unidentified NHS tourism, including more consistent charging of patients ineligible for free treatment.

The Conservatives would also impose targets for the amount of debt that NHS trusts are expected to recoup, for which chief executives will be held accountable.

In addition, visitors will have to repay in full their NHS debts when they apply for a visa.

The balance will be funded from a package of savings the Tories set out at their conference last year.

The policy has received the support of a number of high-profile businessmen, including Sir Rocco Forte, the chairman of Rocco Forte Hotels; and Tom Athron, chief executive of Fortnum & Mason.

Sir Rocco said: “Kemi Badenoch is absolutely right to commit to restoring tax-free shopping for international visitors.

“This is a policy that has been crying out to be reversed. Britain is the only major shopping destination in Europe that denies international visitors a tax refund, and the consequences have been entirely predictable: tourists are choosing to spend their money in Paris, Milan and elsewhere rather than UK tourist centres.”

It is also supported by the bosses of Charles Tyrwhitt shirts and Watches of Switzerland, as well as the chief executives of the British Retail Consortium, the British Fashion Council and UKHospitality.

Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, said: “Winning is about showing up with a determination to compete. That mindset for Britain is what today’s announcement is all about, with the restoration of tax-free shopping for tourists benefitting the economy in all parts of the UK.

“Whilst Labour talks about a tourism tax, Conservatives get on with our plans for growth.”

Following Mrs Badenoch’s announcement, Labour and Reform UK sought to criticise her over the pledge. Reform claimed that she had been responsible for abolishing tax-free shopping in the first place.

Mrs Badenoch was a Treasury minister when the Tories scrapped the policy, when Mr Johnson was prime minister and Rishi Sunak was the chancellor.

Robert Jenrick, Reform’s Treasury spokesman, said: “In 2020, she defended scrapping VAT relief for overseas visitors, calling it a ‘costly relief’.

“Now, after years of damage to British retailers and high streets, she wants to reverse course when she is no longer in a position to do anything about it. I warned at the time that this would harm British businesses, as did Nigel Farage.”

Speaking for the government in the Commons in 2021, Mrs Badenoch said that proposals to reinstate tax-free shopping in its original form “would be subsidising the shopping of EU visitors”.

She went on to argue that such a move “would be an unwise use of taxpayers’ hard-earned cash”, adding that it “disproportionately benefited London and the south-east of England”.

A Labour spokesman said: “The Tories have pulled off a spectacular U-turn. Kemi Badenoch used to say tax-free shopping was a costly giveaway and now she’s trying to sell it as an economic miracle.

“If they really think it’s such a great idea, they should explain why they scrapped it in the first place and how they’d pay for bringing it back. Labour is getting on with delivering good growth in every postcode and backing businesses across Britain.”

data.title: At 71, Donatella Versace is proving she’s nobody’s pensioner
data.description:
Milan Fashion Week commences on Tuesday, and while Versace is absent from the official schedule, that doesn’t mean it won’t be talked about. In fashion, timing is everything – and with impeccable timing, less than 24 hours before the Milan shows are set to kick off, Donatella Versace has just revealed her next move.

After stepping down as Versace’s chief creative officer in March 2025, Donatella, 71, has announced a new joint venture with Revolve Group, the Los Angeles-based online fashion retailer. While the venture is yet to have a name, what we do know is that she will serve as its chief creative officer and that it will cover beauty as well as fashion. This could be excellent news for those of us who’ve had a lipstick-shaped hole in our make-up bags ever since her much-loved cosmetics were discontinued in 2007.

Admittedly, Revolve isn’t as well known in the UK as it is in its native US, meaning that some Britons might be left scratching their heads at the news. After all, Donatella is a fashion legend, one of only a handful of living designers with true cross-generational appeal. She’s loved as much by Gen Z (who buy up vintage Versace on eBay and Vinted) as by their parents and grandparents, along with everyone else who remembers the glory days of Versace, the house founded in 1978 by her brother, Gianni Versace, for whom “little sister” Donatella functioned as a muse.

Granted, Revolve isn’t a blue-chip luxury brand in the manner of Prada Group, which acquired Versace from Capri Holdings in December 2025. There are still fans who would love to see Donatella back at the helm of Versace, a position she held for 30 years. Given that she and Miuccia Prada are, by all accounts, friends, many fashion lovers felt disappointed at Prada Group’s decision to appoint Dario Vitale as Versace’s chief creative officer in March 2025, not least because he only lasted a season. His successor, ex-Alaïa head Pieter Mulier, is set to show his debut collection in early 2027.

In fact, Donatella’s latest move is far savvier than any return to Versace would be, as well as being exponentially more ambitious. Revolve sells a curated mix of third-party and in-house clothing brands designed to appeal to millennials and Gen Z, featuring a dizzying array of names from the well-known (Birkenstock, Coach, Levi’s) to the niche (Coperni, Magda Butrym) to the frankly never heard of. In 2025, it reported revenues of $1.23bn (£910m) and profits of $61.1m (£45m). In short, it has deep pockets, as well as the infrastructure and digital know-how to manage and extend Donatella’s brand on a global scale.

Revolve’s 29 “in-house” brands currently account for 20 per cent of sales, and while it has previously forged long-term and short-term partnerships with actress Jennifer Lopez, designer Peter Dundas and influencer Nicole Richie, Donatella is by far its most high-profile joint venture to date. Given its expertise in marketing, operations and e-commerce, the sky’s the limit. Donatella must be rubbing her hands in glee.

“I believe creativity should be fearless, inclusive and alive in the world. I have always been inspired by the next generation, in music, film, art and, of course, fashion,” she said in a statement. “This partnership gives me the freedom to speak to that generation in a completely new and personal way, through beauty and fashion.”

“Freedom” is surely what it’s all about. While it’s impossible to overestimate Donatella’s creative input at Versace, the fact that it was founded by her brother inevitably meant that she was duty-bound to honour and uphold his legacy, possibly to the detriment of ever cementing her own. The pressure must have been immense. This new partnership with Revolve means that she can finally step out of Gianni’s shadow and into a brave new dawn.

At 71, it feels particularly brave to be entering such uncharted territory. But that’s what makes it so exciting. At a time when women older than 45 are struggling to find gainful employment, a septuagenarian launching a new business venture feels rarer than a hen’s tooth. But Donatella, like Anna Wintour, 76, is of that redoubtable generation that isn’t stopping any time soon. Like Wintour, she’s a household name who has helped define the public’s perception of what fashion is.

Which is precisely her appeal to Revolve. With 12.2 million followers, Donatella is one of the most popular fashion designers on Instagram. But she’s also part of the culture: case in point, her cameo in The Devil Wears Prada 2. Every time another A-lister wears one of her vintage designs on the red carpet, as Zendaya, Miley Cyrus and Jennifer Lopez have done, interest in Donatella spikes anew. Even her look – the flaxen hair, the “molto sexy” bodycon clothing – is perfectly calibrated to cut through the noise, making her instantly recognisable in the highly visual social-media age.

In a world where the word “icon” is too frequently overused, Donatella is one of the few who deserve the descriptor. For a certain vintage of fan, her win feels like a win for all of us. Let’s hope Revolve allows her the freedom she has earned and, in doing so, earns them both a fortune.

data.title: Minister who privatised Thames Water blames Ofwat for crisis
data.description:
The man who launched Britain’s water privatisation has blamed the regulator, Ofwat, for the crisis engulfing Thames Water.

Lord Baker of Dorking, the former environment secretary under Margaret Thatcher, said the watchdog failed to let companies raise bills quickly enough to fund investment.

The 91-year-old, who oversaw the privatisation of Britain’s water industry in the 1980s, said he had not foreseen water companies becoming so heavily indebted or ending up in the hands of overseas infrastructure investors.

“I think it was the regulation. I think Ofwat has quite a lot to answer for,” he told Bloomberg.

Asked whether he had envisaged a company such as Thames ending up with almost £19bn of debt, Lord Baker said: “No, I certainly did not.”

His intervention comes as Labour considers whether to take control of Thames, Britain’s biggest water company, after rescue talks between its creditors and Ofwat stalled.

Thames’s lenders have proposed a £10bn restructuring that would see them inject billions of pounds to fund upgrades. The consortium, known as London & Valley Water, has also pledged not to take dividends until 2035.

MPs have urged Andy Burnham to block the deal and put Thames into special administration instead, which would give the Government control while it finds a long-term solution.

Lord Baker rejected calls to renationalise the water industry, saying privatisation was designed to free investment from the constraints of government spending.

He said there was “great sadness” that too little had been invested in water infrastructure in recent decades, and that private ownership had ultimately delivered more investment than the industry would have received under state control.

The water industry was privatised in 1989 after the Thatcher government argued that private capital was needed to modernise the country’s ageing network.

Lord Baker said the Government had backed privatisation because the department responsible for water “was always the first to have its budget cut”.

But the system is facing its biggest overhaul since privatisation. Ministers plan to scrap Ofwat and replace it with a single regulator overseeing the industry’s financial, environmental and drinking-water standards.

The Government is also considering plans for regional water boards that would give mayors and other local leaders greater influence over companies.

Thames has warned it could run out of cash by the end of the year, leaving the Government to choose between a taxpayer-backed rescue and a restructuring led by its lenders.

data.title: Boots in £7.5bn sale talks with billionaire family behind Primark
data.description:
Boots is in talks to sell itself for £7.5bn to the family behind Primark and an Australian pharmacy chain.

The billionaire Weston family, which owns Primark, is weighing up a bid that would see the chemist scrap plans for a London listing, according to the Financial Times.

The retail giant is understood to be in talks alongside Sigma Healthcare, an Australian pharmacy group, about a possible takeover of the 177-year-old chemist from Sycamore Partners, its private equity owner.

A takeover of Boots would derail plans for a stock market listing. The recent appointment of Alex Baldock – the former Currys boss credited with turning around the electronics retailer – as chief executive had fuelled speculation that Boots was being prepared to join the London Stock Market. 

Insiders had previously suggested that a flotation valuing the chain at up to £7bn was “always the plan”.

News of the talks came as Boots revealed that profits jumped by a quarter to £337m last year, as demand for weight-loss jabs, vaccinations and beauty products helped drive sales growth.

The Westons are one of the world’s richest retail families. Through their sprawling business empire they already control Primark-owner Associated British Foods (ABF), as well as Fortnum & Mason and major supermarket and pharmacy chains in Canada.

A deal would also deepen the family’s ties to British retail just months after it unveiled plans to split Primark from ABF, ending a six-decade partnership between the fashion chain and the conglomerate’s food operations.

Sigma, meanwhile, is a fast-growing Australian healthcare group best known for its links to Chemist Warehouse, Australia’s largest pharmacy retailer.

It has recently signalled ambitions to expand internationally and only last month entered the UK market through a pharmacy joint venture in and around London.

Hundreds of stores closed

A sale of Boots has been talked about for years. Walgreens first tried to offload it in 2022, before abandoning the effort when bids failed to meet expectations.

Sycamore Partners revived expectations of a breakup when it bought Walgreens Boots Alliance last year and carved out Boots as a standalone unit.

Boots has spent the past two years trying to improve its attractiveness to potential bidders. 

It has closed hundreds of under-performing UK stores as part of a broader cost-cutting drive, including a programme to shut branches, trimming its footprint from about 2,200 stores to roughly 1,900 in 2024.

At the same time, the chain has benefited from a boom in private healthcare services and a push into premium beauty brands, with online sales also rising sharply as more shoppers turned to its app and delivery partnerships.

The Weston family already has a presence in the pharmacy sector through Shoppers Drug Mart, a Canadian chain with more than 1,300 locations that it acquired in a multibillion-pound deal more than a decade ago.

Boots declined to comment.

data.title: Paramount settles US states’ lawsuit to unlock $110bn Warner deal
data.description:
Paramount is poised to close its $111bn (£83bn) takeover of Warner Bros after settling a legal challenge to block the deal.

The US media giant, controlled by Larry Ellison, Oracle co-founder and billionaire, has struck an agreement with a dozen US states that will clear the way for the biggest shake-up of Hollywood in decades.

As part of the deal, Paramount has agreed to maintain independent editorial boards for CBS and CNN.

It has also agreed to pay a $30m penalty per film if it falls short of its promise to release 30 films in cinemas each year, Bloomberg reported.

The merger has effectively been on hold since July after a group of Democratic-run states, led by Rob Bonta, the California attorney general, launched legal action to derail it.

The case warned that the tie-up, which would hand Paramount control of the film studio behind Harry Potter as well as CNN, would cause “substantial harm” to cinemas, cable TV operators and audiences.

It cited the impact of reducing the number of major Hollywood studios from five to four, as well as combining two of the largest US news networks.

But the challenge also underlined the merger’s political nature, as critics raised concerns about the Ellison family’s close ties to Donald Trump.

Scores of Hollywood stars have spoken out against the deal, while Christiane Amanpour, former CNN host, warned it could lead to “improper political meddling” and pose a threat to democracy.

The companies had agreed to pause the transaction until a judge ruled on the case, with a trial date set for March next year.

However, the two sides have reached an agreement after Paramount threatened to pull out of California unless the case was dropped.

The warnings put pressure on Mr Bonta, who accused the company’s executives of blackmailing him to reach a settlement.

The settlement was reached after four of the states dropped their opposition to the takeover amid fears of soaring legal costs.

Paramount has been racing to reach an agreement to avoid incurring its own substantial bill.

It agreed to pay a “ticking fee” of $650m to Warner Bros shareholders for every quarter the transaction is delayed beyond the end of September, equivalent to $7m a day.

The merger has already been cleared in dozens of countries, including the UK, where Paramount owns Channel 5.

David Ellison, Paramount’s chief executive and son of Larry, pledged to boost investment in British programmes to ease concerns raised by Lisa Nandy, the Culture Secretary, about competition and media plurality.

David Ellison thanked Mr Bonta, his fellow attorneys general and the Writers Guild of America “for engaging in good faith to find a path forward to a resolution that serves all parties”, and Gavin Newsom, the California Governor, “for his support throughout this process”.

He added: “Our goal has always been to build a stronger Hollywood – one with more stories told, greater choice for consumers and stronger competition ... We have complete clearance for this merger and look forward to putting these commitments into action.”

data.title: Firms fined £1.3m after man killed by window that fell from penthouse
data.description:
The widow of a man killed by a window that fell 300ft from a riverside penthouse said in a statement it “could have happened to anybody”, a court heard.

Mick Ferris, 53, was crushed when a window fell 26 storeys from The Corniche, a luxury development in Vauxhall, south London, on Oct 2, 2018.

St James, a property developer owned by the Berkeley Group, was fined £1m and Lindner Prater, a specialist façade contractor, was fined £300,000 at a sentencing hearing at Inner London Crown Court on Thursday.

Mr Ferris, a father of two who was a driver for Clarkes of London, had been returning to his coach when the window pane, which weighed 130kg and was about 85cm wide and 190cm tall, fell at 10.40am.

The Corniche, located on the River Thames’s Albert Embankment, features “panoramic views” over the Houses of Parliament. Flats in the building – which has a gym, pool and spa – have been listed for sale at £3m.

St James and Lindner Prater were found guilty of ignoring “foreseeable risks” at a trial. Both firms were convicted of “failing to discharge a duty” under the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974.

A window panel fell from the same development in August 2017, but the design had not been substantially changed as a result, the trial heard.

Mr Ferris’s widow, Rachel Ferris, said his death had been “so sudden” and “out of the blue”, adding that it “could have been prevented”.

In a statement read out in court, Mrs Ferris said: “I know it wasn’t just one person, but one person could have changed this. One person could have asked ‘can’t we do this better?’. What those companies did killed my husband.”

She added: “The thought this could have happened to anybody is always with me. It could have been a child.”

Jurors had been told the design of the window in the Corniche was “not safe” because it opened outwards and was held in place by a single metal “restrictor”, so could be prised off by the wind.

Judge Matthew Boyle said he was not sentencing the firms on the basis that the design itself was unsafe because it was “common within the industry” and there was no Health and Safety Executive guidance prohibiting their use.

He added that the “restrictor, if present and connected, would have prevented detachment”.

Judge Boyle said St James should have been more “robust” in “ensuring the critical safety component was present and engaged”. He added that Lindner Prater “should have done more to complete and document the risk assessment process”.

In addition to the fine, Judge Boyle ordered the two firms to pay costs of £125,000 each.

Mitigating for St James, Prashant Popat KC said it had been a “horrific tragedy and preventable incident”, adding that Mr Ferris’s death “should not have happened”.

He added that the company was “deeply remorseful and regretful”, and the incident was “taken incredibly seriously by the company”.

Death ‘should not have happened’

Mr Popat said the firm’s failure was “secondly to Lindner’s failure” and “occurred even though St James did carry out a considerable amount of monitoring activity on this site”.

Mitigating for Lindner Prater, James Leonard KC said the incident “should not have happened”, adding that the “fatal accident was almost certainly a consequence of a failure of reinstatement” by a contractor the firm had hired to work on the site.

James Goldfinch, principal inspector of the Health and Safety Executive, said Mr Ferris was a “hardworking man just going about his day”.

Speaking outside court, Mr Goldfinch added: “He lost his life due to the failings of two leading companies in their field. The fact lessons had not been learnt from a near miss the year before makes what happened on that day all the more galling.

“For a window to fall once was quite extraordinary, for it to fall again was simply criminal.”

data.title: Octopus adds further block on withdrawals from inheritance tax scheme
data.description:
Thousands of pensioners have been hit with a further block on withdrawing their cash from Octopus’s inheritance tax scheme.

The fund, which has 18,000 customers and is known as the Octopus Inheritance Tax Service (OITS), has been frozen to redemptions since early July, meaning savers have been banned from getting their money back.

Octopus was supposed to have reopened the fund either this week or next. However, it said on Thursday that the closure would “need to remain in place for a short additional period”.

OITS, a subsidiary of Octopus Group, had raised money from thousands of pensioners with the promise of lowering their inheritance tax bills by investing in businesses to qualify for relief.

However, the scheme has been plagued by uncertainty in recent weeks after it told savers no withdrawals could take place until it finalised a takeover which risked changing the value of their investments.

Octopus Investments, which administers the scheme, warned customers that while significant progress had been made on the transaction, it still needed to reach a final agreement and the outcome was not “certain”.

The note, authored by Kristy Barr, head of retail investments at Octopus Investments, said: “I know this continued uncertainty is frustrating, particularly for investors who are currently looking to buy or sell shares.

“However, our priorities are to make sure that the outcome of this process and its terms are as favourable as possible for investors and that we maintain our fair and robust valuation and governance process.”

The timeline for the suspension has repeatedly slipped. Financial advisers were told the scheme would be paused for “approximately one week” on July 9.

Later that month, on July 28, investors were told it would be paused for a further six to eight weeks.

Octopus has also faced growing scrutiny about its transparency after The Telegraph revealed that savers had been bankrolling failed hospitals and care homes.

This raised questions about whether pensioners had been given adequate information about the performance of their investments.

Octopus froze the fund over a plan to acquire PlatformX Communications, the wholesale arm of TalkTalk. The deal would trigger a revaluation of the fund, changing the value of customers’ investments.

The deadline for the TalkTalk deal to complete was Friday but this has been extended.

Octopus Investments and TalkTalk said in a joint statement on Thursday that both sides had conducted advanced due diligence and funding was in place.

“As a result, they are optimistic of delivering the proposed transaction and will update stakeholders with further news in due course,” they said. “There can be no certainty of any transaction completing.”

Some investors have become increasingly concerned about the extent of the suspension and the inability to get their money out of the scheme.

Octopus Investments has communicated extensively with customers that have outstanding withdrawal requests, including offering direct phone calls with affected individuals.

Alongside the delay, Octopus Investments also told customers that it was undergoing another valuation of the businesses that make up the investment scheme.

It has completed the process on the part of the portfolio unaffected by the TalkTalk deal, representing about two thirds of the business, with the remaining one third outstanding.

In response to the suspension, Octopus Investments said: “Our priority during this process is securing the best possible outcome for investors and ensuring that all customers are treated fairly.

“We completely understand investors’ frustrations with the ongoing uncertainty but we wouldn’t be pursuing a transaction of this significance if we did not believe it was in the long-term interests of OITS and its shareholders.

“Once we have certainty over how this process will impact valuations, we will communicate with investors and re-open trading as soon as possible. To be clear, the current pause has nothing to do with liquidity: this is currently within historical and expected levels.”

data.title: Fund tied to controversy over India’s richest man lent millions to failed shadow bank
data.description:
An offshore fund linked to a controversy involving India’s richest man also lent to the collapsed UK shadow bank Market Financial Solutions (MFS), it has emerged.

MFS, which collapsed this year amid accusations of fraud and a £1.3bn black hole in its accounts, was lent tens of millions by Oyster Bay Fund, which is managed by London investment firm Elara Capital.

Elara Capital was previously linked to claims surrounding Gautam Adani, the Indian billionaire, whose business empire was accused three years ago of “brazen stock manipulation” by a short seller, which he denies.

MFS collapsed into administration in February, prompting allegations that at least £1.3bn had been “misappropriated” from the business. Its founder and chief executive, Paresh Raja, has denied the allegations.

Since MFS imploded, it has been unclear how it turned itself into a property lender which boasted a reported loan book of around £2.5bn, raising money from some of the City’s most important institutions.

The shadow bank, which provided buy-to-let mortgages and bridging finance, had funded its loans by borrowing from lenders including Barclays, Santander, Wells Fargo and Jefferies.

Yet in 2020, well before it secured hundreds of millions of pounds from major lenders, Oyster Bay lent to MFS through Mrida Solutions, an intermediary vehicle whose sole director was Mr Raja.

Accounts show that Oyster Bay’s exposure to Mrida peaked at £16.5m in 2022 and stood at £14.8m in its last filed accounts. In turn, Mrida lent that money to at least one part of MFS.

At the same time, Oyster Bay was also lending to companies tied to Mr Adani, court filings reveal.

Court records show that the fund had made a series of bets on India’s Adani Group. These were funded by borrowing from Nomura, the Japanese bank, which is now in a dispute with Oyster Bay.

These bets unravelled after Hindenburg Research, a short-selling firm, claimed in a 2023 report that a number of funds, including some managed by Elara Capital, were fronts for Adani, investing exclusively in shares in his companies to manipulate their stock prices.

The collapse of the bets prompted the dispute between Oyster Bay and Nomura, where the accusations from the controversial report reemerged.

Lawyers for Nomura cited the report in legal filings claiming that some of Elara Capital’s other funds “appeared to be supported by the Adani Group”.

Oyster Bay was not among the funds originally named in Hindenburg’s report.

Mr Adani has rejected the allegations by Hindenburg as “baseless” and “nothing short of a calculated securities fraud”.

In a 413-page rebuttal to Hindenburg’s allegations, he described “innuendos” about the Elara funds as “incorrect”.

Mrida is listed as a creditor to at least two MFS entities, one of which provided debt in a £300m funding deal with Barclays. Barclays declined to comment.

Oyster Bay’s dispute with Nomura centres on allegations that, following the Hindenburg report, senior bankers had become “concerned about its exposure to Adani”.

It alleges that Nomura breached a deal to keep the fund’s bets open, selling the underlying Adani shares at a significant loss for Oyster Bay.

A Nomura spokesman said: “Nomura disagrees with Oyster Bay’s claim and will vigorously defend it.” Elara Capital did not respond to requests for comment.

In September last year, India’s capital markets regulator ruled that the evidence relating to the Adani Group was insufficient to support fraud claims.

A spokesman for Mr Raja declined to comment.

data.title: One in eight Britons to take weight loss drugs by 2027
data.description:
One in eight Britons will be taking weight loss drugs by 2027, a new report has predicted.

The number of UK adults taking glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) weight loss medication will more than double from three million to seven million by next year, according to analysis by consulting firm PwC Strategy&, accounting for 13pc of the population.

This uptick will be fuelled by the approval of a new Wegovy pill, which will make weight loss treatment easier and more accessible.

This is expected to trigger a sharp drop in the sale of sweets and crisps, according to PwC, as the rollout dramatically changes consumer spending patterns.

Those already taking the medication cut their spending on snacks and sweet treats by 70pc and spent 60pc less on sugary drinks, PwC Strategy& found in a survey of more than 2,300 adults.

The latest findings have been released just weeks after the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) approved a tablet version of the blockbuster weight loss drug Wegovy.

This is the UK’s first GLP-1 pill for weight loss and can now be prescribed to adults with obesity.

It means that millions of Britons can access GLP-1 drugs, which mimic gut hormones to regulate people’s appetites, without needing to administer them by a weekly injection.

The pills will soon be rolled out across major retailers including Boots, Morrisons and Superdrug.

However, they are not yet available on the NHS. Before this can happen, the pill will need to be evaluated by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence.

While businesses selling confectionery or fast food will suffer from a drop-off in spending on unhealthy foods, those selling healthy products are likely to see a surge in sales.

GLP-1 users spent 60pc more on fresh food, 54pc more on high-protein options and 40pc more on vitamins and supplements, PwC Strategy& found.

They also spent 30pc more on fitness and an additional 40pc on clothing.

These spending patterns are likely to continue even after they have lost weight and stopped taking the drugs.

More than 80pc of those who had stopped treatment said they maintained at least some of the dietary changes they had made while taking the GLP-1s.

Jacqueline Windsor, head of retail at PwC UK, said: “GLP-1 is the most consumerised medication today. Who your GLP-1 customers are, and how your category changes, will dictate how brands and retailers compete.

“We’ll see consumer businesses reshape their portfolios to manage near-term risk.”

More than a quarter (28pc) of GLP-1 users said they would maintain their current levels of spending on the drugs even if the cost of living rose.

The drugs, which are only prescribed on the NHS for those with severe obesity, have predominantly been purchased by wealthier households, but are becoming increasingly mainstream.

Of current users, 6pc came from lower-income households, compared to 20pc for wealthier households.

Adoption of weight loss drugs has so far been highest among women, who account for 60pc of current users.

data.title: Burnham to cut energy bills by up to £200 for benefits claimants
data.description:
Andy Burnham is to cut up to £200 off benefits claimants’ energy bills this winter as the Iran war sends gas and fuel prices surging.

The Prime Minister is exploring providing targeted subsidies to millions of households living in fuel poverty including those who do not currently qualify for existing support.

Whitehall officials are understood to have started drawing up the scheme after the outbreak of the US-Iran war put a squeeze on global oil and gas supplies coming out of the Strait of Hormuz trade choke point.

The energy price cap is poised to jump from £1,663 to £1,723 in October, with analysts forecasting that it will rise again to £1,872 in January – a total increase of about £200 across the winter.

The support scheme, called the Energy Price Protection Payment (EPPP), is “ready” to be implemented in January, according to industry insiders. It would aim to mitigate some or all of the impact of the rise in energy prices.

It could be announced as soon as the Budget on Oct 28, or potentially in late November when the next energy price cap adjustment is confirmed.

There are also discussions about whether a wider package of support could be provided to all households but this would be more expensive and could clash with the vow by John Healey, the Chancellor, to protect the public finances.

No final decision has been made yet on whether to proceed with the EPPP or how much the support will be worth.

It would apply to people who already receive the Warm Homes Discount as well as some others deemed in need of support.

To receive the discount, a claimant must be in receipt of benefits. But sources said the support was poorly targeted and did not cover another estimated 2.5 million extra households who were still classed as being in fuel poverty.

It is unclear whether the EPPP would seek to target only some or all of those households.

One person familiar with the plan said it could be part of a wider energy bills intervention that could “layer” support to benefits claimants on top of more universal measures.

However, they stressed the final shape of any package would be determined by the strength of the public finances and how energy prices evolve.

The Iran crisis has sent European gas prices to their highest point since 2022, prompting fresh concerns about the cost of living at a time when Mr Burnham has pledged to put “more money in people’s pockets”.

He has already cut VAT to zero on electricity bills, saving a typical household about £45 per year.

However, the cut has already been wiped out by rising energy costs and is scheduled to expire at the end of March.

Industry sources suggested that the Government was looking at other ways to bring down bills in the long term such as reducing or eliminating network charges and green levies.

Ministers cut bills by £150 for households last year by removing the energy company obligation and 75pc of the renewable obligation in the last Budget.

However, a letter on Friday from more than 120 businesses, trade groups and charities including Nationwide, Octopus Energy and British Gas urged Labour to go further and cut levies by an additional £100 a year.

They said: “Moving electricity levies from both business and household bills to government spending would immediately make energy costs more affordable and competitive, providing a greatly needed boost for our manufacturing industries and tackling cost of living challenges.”

Miatta Fahnbulleh, the Energy Secretary, is also thought to be championing proposals inside the Government for a so-called block tariff. This would grant all households a discounted “block” of electricity and gas, with anything used above that threshold charged at the normal rate.

A government spokesman said: “The Chancellor is fully focused on giving families and businesses breathing space and helping ease cost pressures.”

data.title: Dragons’ Den star’s retailer rescued by fridge magnate
data.description:
Dragons’ Den star Peter Jones has sold struggling camera retailer Jessops to AO World, more than a decade after he first saved the chain from administration.

Jessops has collapsed three times since 2013, when Mr Jones initially bailed out the camera chain, and has since shrunk to just eight shops, compared with more than 300 at its peak.

AO, the online white-goods store led by entrepreneur John Roberts, said it would use its scale to grow the business, while taking control of its specialist expertise in cameras and photography.

The deal, announced on Thursday, also includes Camera Jungle, Jessops’ second-hand business. It will sit alongside musicMagpie, which sells used phones and other consumer electronics that AO bought in 2024.

Mr Roberts said: “I am delighted to welcome Jessops into the AO family and look forward to growing the existing business as well as integrating the category into the wider AO business.”

Jessops was founded in Leicester in 1935 by Frank Jessop and grew into one of Britain’s best-known photography retailers. It eventually became a national chain with hundreds of shops, but was hit by the shift towards online shopping and the growing quality of smartphone cameras.

Mr Jones stepped in after Jessops fell into administration in January 2013, buying the brand and some of its assets and putting in £5m of his own money to relaunch business.

At the time, he said Jessops was an “iconic British brand” that could “lead the retail resurgence on Britain’s high streets”. He reopened 30 shops and re-employed hundreds of former staff.

The rescue ultimately failed to revive Jessops and the current business is a fraction of its former size. The retailer entered administration again in 2019 and a third time in 2021, after which Mr Jones agreed a company voluntary arrangement with creditors.

Its latest accounts show sales of about £19.9m in the year to September 2025, up 6.5pc, but a £1.1m loss. The business has increasingly moved its sales online and shifted towards second-hand photography equipment.

The sale brings an end to Mr Jones’s 13-year ownership of the brand. The entrepreneur made his fortune in mobile phones before becoming one of the investors on Dragons’ Den, the BBC One show that he has appeared in since it debuted in 2005.

The deal gives AO another foothold in the second-hand market after it bought musicMagpie in 2024 and turned the loss-making business profitable.

AO said the Jessops deal was funded from its existing cash and did not disclose the price. It had more than £200m of headroom at the end of September.

The acquisition comes as AO reported a 5.5pc rise in first-half revenue and said pre-tax profit was up more than 20pc to about £21.5m.

data.title: France draws up emergency measures as petrol panic-buying sweeps country
data.description:
France has rushed out emergency measures to tackle a looming fuel crisis, with diesel prices at record highs and forecourts running dry.

The cash-strapped French government announced €450m (£386m) of handouts and subsidies to households and businesses to deal with what Roland Lescure, the finance minister, called “a very difficult and unchosen situation”.

The measures include cash handouts to people who use a car for work, energy vouchers for low-income households, and zero-interest loans for fishermen, who blockaded ports last week in protest at rising fuel prices.

“We must continue to help our fellow citizens who are on the front line, who are working and whose fuel prices have increased sharply,” Mr Lescure told reporters.

Attacks by Iranian proxy forces on Saudi Arabia’s pipelines and coastline have disrupted oil supplies to Europe, driving petrol and diesel prices to the highest level since Donald Trump attacked Iran on Feb 28.

France’s diesel price averaged €2.42 a litre on Monday, up more than 10 cents in the past week. Unleaded petrol has jumped to €2.19 a litre.

Panic-buying has swept the country, leaving one fifth of French petrol stations short of at least one fuel type.

TotalEnergies forecourts, which cap prices at €2.25 a litre for diesel and €1.99 for petrol, are bearing the brunt of the shortages. Independent petrol stations have seen customer traffic drop between 20pc and 40pc, as motorists turn to Total.

Mr Lescure insisted there were “no supply problems”, but added: “We must prepare for a possible deterioration of the situation. ... Uncertainties remain high.”

The French government had already allowed fuel distributors to top up supplies to forecourts by selling “summer-blend diesel”, which is less cold-resistant, for two weeks beyond the usual Nov 1 cut-off.

Ministers have also extended previous support measures introduced in April until the end of the year. These subsidies, ranging from 15 to 35 cents a litre, target diesel-intensive sectors, such as agriculture, fisheries and construction.

That followed a wave of strikes and protests last week against rising fuel prices, including a blockade of French ports by irate French fishermen.

The government on Tuesday expanded its €100 grant to “high-mileage” drivers, those who commute more than nine miles each way between home and work or drive more than 5,000 miles a year for work.

Only half of eligible French motorists have claimed the cash so far, but the pool of eligible drivers has been widened from three million to 5.5 million.

The energy vouchers for low-income households will range from €48 to €277. Employers will be able to offer a fuel bonus of up to €1,000 to their workers, and rural nurses will be entitled to a separate €80 bonus.

The promise of yet more support comes amid France’s ongoing battle to get public spending under control.

Mr Lescure said he would not be cutting excise duties on petrol, adding that a 20-cent cut would cost the public purse almost €10bn.

He has already admitted that the budget deficit will remain stuck above 5pc this year, and the government’s debt-to-GDP ratio will swell to a record 119pc.

An election to choose a successor to Emmanuel Macron, the president, in April 2027 is pressuring politicians to spend more to shore up the economy and ease voters’ pain.

Germany has demanded an EU-wide windfall tax on oil companies’ profits to help pay for national governments’ cuts to fuel duties.

Mr Macron wrote to Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, on Friday demanding that Brussels also take action to support business and motorists.

In a letter reported in the French media on Tuesday, he said the EU should relax fuel standards on kerosene and diesel, which would help oil refineries turn crude into fuel more quickly.

He also called for more biofuel blending into diesel, and said Brussels should postpone new methane-emission rules on oil and gas importers.

data.title: Lime withdraws bikes from London borough after complaints from blind residents
data.description:
Lime has removed its electric bikes from a London borough after the company’s vehicles were accused of endangering blind residents.

The company said it had stopped users from being able to hire e-bikes in Bromley, south-east London, where it was operating without an agreement.

It came after Jason Beal, a resident, said he had had to force his guide dog into a busy road because of the company’s lime green bikes being strewn over the pavement.

Councillors had also threatened to pull Lime’s bikes off the streets and charge the company for the hassle.

Liam Conlon, the area’s MP, raised the matter with Bromley council after Mr Beal contacted him to complain.

Lime’s e-bikes have become ubiquitous in London and a popular way of getting around, but the hundreds of them parked on pavements have been seen by critics as a nuisance.

The company had started offering e-bike hire in the Bromley suburb of Penge in recent weeks, despite not having local approval. 

Lime put this down to a technical issue in which the map for neighbouring Lewisham mistakenly covered parts of Bromley. Councillors said they had “blighted” local areas and caused hazards on pavements.

Simon Fawthrop, of Bromley council, said: “We have already raised concerns with Lime that they appear to be operating without our consent in part of our borough.

“Bromley council have long had misgivings about Lime Bikes and other similar bikes that are quite frankly blighting some areas, where they are strewn across pavements causing multiple hazards.

“The council has not agreed anything with Lime and we call upon them to remove their bikes from our borough forthwith.”

Mr Beal, 53, told the London Standard that bikes parked on the pavement meant he had to walk on the road and listen out for traffic, frightening Caine, his guide dog.

“There have been a number of times the Lime bikes have been parked up or propped up against the tree or left over the pavement,” he said.

“So I’ve got to make a decision to try to take him into the main road. That’s a very frightening experience for myself.”

Lime was recently valued at $1.7bn (£1.3bn) in a US initial public offering.

The company operates bikes and scooters in more than a dozen London boroughs.

It has been blighted by claims of personal injuries caused by the bikes, and said recently that it had set aside $56m for personal injury claims.

Lime apologised to Mr Beal and said that it had suspended bike hiring in the borough until it could agree an approach “with appropriate parking locations”.

data.title: Julia Braybrook, Sunday Telegraph lawyer and ‘voice of sanity’ who kept campaigning journalists out of trouble
data.description:
Julia Braybrook, the media and immigration lawyer who has died aged 80, met the world with an expression of wry amusement, but her career placed her behind the scenes of some of the most consequential newspaper litigation of the late 20th century, ultimately winning her The Lawyer magazine’s “In-house Lawyer of the Year”.

Buccaneering journalists often see in-house lawyers as obstacles, but Julia Braybrook took any barracking in her stride and remained on cordial terms with even the most seditious diarists and investigative reporters. One colleague saw her as “a lone voice of sanity, trying to hold back a tsunami of crazy ideas”.

She was born in W​andsworth on November 17 1945. Her middle name, Militza, came from her Russian godmother, a friend of her father, Frederick “Freddy” Haughton Braybrook, and gave a hint of her cosmopolitan background.

Her mother, Sylvia Mavis Braybrook, née Lightoller, was the daughter of Charles Lightoller, the most senior surviving officer of the Titanic, and, like Julia, fiercely independent.

Julia was four when her family moved from Ham in west London to Vaucresson, a suburb of Paris, where her father was a senior executive in Shell’s growing international chemicals business. She was sent to the École Suger armed, she said, with only one sentence of French: “Ma tante a une plume bleue”.

Her progress in the jardin d’enfants was consequently not effortless, but she acquired French, and later Italian, with such fluency that as an adult, she was as likely to read Le Figaro as any English newspaper and would devour massive tomes – often political biographies – in all three languages.

When she was eight, the family returned to England, settling in Woldingham, and Julia went to Parkfield prep before the all-girls Wycombe Abbey, a school she described as “brutal”, even though it gave her a rich cultural education. Like her father Julia loved opera and, when the family moved abroad again to Genoa when Julia was 15, it became the mainstay of their outings together.

Living in the relative splendour of Villa Pontini, Julia went skiing in the Alps, played tennis and enjoyed an early education in the finer things in life, including wine taken from her father’s enormous cellar.

After receiving offers from both Oxford and Cambridge, she went to Newnham College, Cambridge, to read French and Italian. and in anticipation of her future career was an eager contributor to Varsity magazine. Donning a green velvet baker-boy cap that she rarely took off, she cut a raffish figure in the still overwhelmingly male common rooms of the day and embarked on a life spent largely in men’s worlds.

After Cambridge, she had a short stint as a junior analyst at The Economist before returning to Newnham to read Law. She then qualified at Allen & Overy and was among the first women to work in its litigation department, and was posted to Brussels.

In one small tribunal case, she instructed a young barrister whom she rated highly but the firm barely knew – Jonathan Sumption, later one of Britain’s most distinguished judges.

Julia’s first job was on the short-lived newspaper Today from where she moved to The Observer. In 1986 she found herself confronting the government over their attempts to prevent publication of material from Peter Wright’s memoir of his time in MI5, Spycatcher – one of the most important press-freedom battles of that decade.

Her work also brought her into the extraordinary aftermath of the Jeffrey Archer affair which led to Archer being convicted of perjury and sent to prison.

Later, she moved to The Sunday Telegraph, where she was closely involved in the newspaper’s defence of libel proceedings brought by Saif al-Islam Gaddafi, son of the Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi, while also expending much energy keeping the controversial columnist Christopher Booker out of trouble.

But it was her defence of The Sunday Telegraph against Adam Musa King that brought one of her most important victories. King, who was represented on a no-win, no-fee basis, had sued over articles concerning his alleged links to al-Qaeda, and although the Telegraph did not win the case, it reached the Court of Appeal, which ruled that newspapers should not face ruinous costs in defending libel actions.

In naming her “In-house Lawyer of the Year” in 2004, The Lawyer magazine praised Miss Braybrook for her role in this episode, with the editor Catrin Griffiths hailing the victory was “an outstanding achievement that will ensure media organisations can continue to publish controversial issues”. Julia Braybrook, with typical generosity and modesty, accepted the award as “a recognition of the tremendous efforts of the whole legal team involved in the case”.

At 58, increasingly afraid that she would be deemed too old to work in newspapers for much longer, she began sitting in immigration appeals. Eventually she became a Tribunal Judge, handling cases such as that of a Jamaican boy who had arrived in Britain aged 10, where she helped uphold his appeal after the Home Office failed properly to apply its “under 12” policy.

As time went on, she became increasingly frustrated with the Home Office’s system, yet she kept working until she was no longer allowed to, aged 75.

Although she lived in London all her working life, much of Julia Braybrook’s work was scheduled around visits to Menton on the French Riviera, where she owned a flat on the piano nobile of the Clos du Peyronnet, a fin-de-siècle villa she shared with friends, which had once hosted Clive and Vanessa Bell and Ford Madox Ford, who wrote in its exotic garden.

The place became a kind of open house, with revolving drinks and dinner parties, and Julia Braybrook added her own improbable assortment of local friends to the mix – a grower of exotic vegetables, a tax inspector – as well as old friends from London.

From Menton she regularly walked in the Alps, crossing into Ventimiglia to see Italian friends, and swam in the sea.

Described by one friend as Macavity the Mystery Cat on account of the legion of boyfriends she kept discreetly under wraps, Julia Braybrook never married and had no children of her own. Yet throughout her life she was a devoted aunt and godmother and in her later years became an honorary grandmother to a host of small children. She died at the Hospital of St John & St Elizabeth in St John’s Wood surrounded by many of these young people.

​Julia Braybrook had the great lawyer’s virtue of being unflappable, but her greater gift to the people around her was as a genial, generous friend and ally.

Julia Braybrook, born November 17 1945, died August 26 2026

data.title: Gary Lineker shares in £5m payout from Goalhanger podcast empire
data.description:
Gary Lineker has shared in a £5m payday as he benefits from the success of booming podcast empire Goalhanger.

The company, which produces the “The Rest Is” podcast series, made the dividend payout last year as revenues and profits more than doubled. It marked a sharp increase on the £36,000 dividend distributed in 2024.

Mr Lineker held a 33pc stake in Goalhanger last year alongside Tony Pastor and Jack Davenport, co-founders, suggesting his personal share was around £1.6m.

The founders’ shares were diluted in January this year after the company sold a minority stake to a media firm founded by Peter Chernin, a Hollywood mogul.

The stake’s value was not disclosed, but analysts have estimated the company could be worth around £100m.

Mr Lineker, a former England footballer, stepped down from his £1.3m job presenting the BBC’s Match of the Day last year in the wake of an anti-Semitism controversy and run-ins with the broadcaster over sharing his political views on social media.

The 65-year-old, who made a presenting cameo on ITV at this year’s World Cup, has said he does not miss “treading on eggshells” while working at the BBC.

Mr Lineker was one of 120 millionaires who wrote to Andy Burnham in July asking for higher taxes on Britain’s wealthy.

The letter, signed by the musician Brian Eno and film director Richard Curtis, called for a 2pc wealth tax on assets worth more than £10m.

It also backed calls to equalise capital gains tax with income tax in a move estimated to raise at least £12bn for the Treasury.

The millionaires wrote: “We want you to tax us. We can afford it.”

data.title: We are finally discovering the true cost of ‘free’
data.description:
Banking is a funny business. Millions of people regularly deposit money with institutions in the belief that their liabilities, or IOUs, can reliably be used as a means of payment. The more people do this, the more power such institutions accrue.

In Britain, this information-based confidence trick is especially strange.

Because of the country’s highly financialised nature, competition to attract such deposits has led to a weird phenomenon: most people do not pay anything at all for core banking services.

The economics of the resulting “free banking” model instead depend on banks capturing large numbers of customers within their walled gardens to upsell them higher-margin products – mortgages, overdrafts, foreign exchange and so on.

The arrangement is made even more lucrative thanks to the information advantage this engineers for banks.

Ultimately, banks know far more about their customers’ financial circumstances than either rival providers or, in some respects, the customers themselves know about the relative value of the products being sold to them.

British banking is, consequently, the archetypal “if it’s free, you’re the product” industry, and has been since long before the internet economy normalised data capture as a business model.

But something remarkable may now be happening. And it may even be having a bearing on the economy in ways statisticians are yet to account for.

For years, when customers complained they were being ripped off elsewhere in the banking relationship, banks defended their models by saying unwinding the “freemium” effect would be impossible.

No single institution had an incentive to unbundle services because doing so would immediately cost it market share.

The surprising thing is that this assertion may finally be proving false.

The surging popularity of neobanks, such as Revolut and Monzo, shows that customers are willing to pay monthly fees for better banking services if they think they can receive a better deal elsewhere in the bundle.

Moreover, now that the process has begun, it is revealing something pretty important.

People don’t necessarily like being the product after all. They may even be prepared to pay the going price for institutions to work for them rather than accept hidden cross-subsidies whose real costs are difficult to see.

More importantly still, the phenomenon doesn’t look to be restricted to banking.

Across the economy, a great unbundling is slowly unwinding services that we have long come to think of as free with significant consequences for inflation measures.

The news economy is an obvious example, with advertising-funded content increasingly giving way to paywalls.

The streaming economy has, meanwhile, normalised the idea of paying directly for digital content to avoid ads.

Nearly four in five UK consumers now have access to paid video platforms, with households holding an average of 2.86 TV and film subscriptions, according to Deloitte – almost double the 1.45 recorded in 2018.

Most pertinently, there is AI itself. Subscription models arrived almost immediately, with clearly segmented free and paid offerings.

This matters not just because it all feels rather inflationary, but because the digital economy was assumed by many economists to be a powerful deflationary force, built as it was around zero marginal costs.

Not all agreed. Some warned that the proliferation of apparently free services was obscuring where – and how – their costs were really being borne.

The crude analogue is the old nightclub model, where women can enter in free because their presence attracts higher-spending male customers. The price is zero because the customer is partly the product. The negative externalities of that arrangement are rather harder to capture economically.

So what happens when people decide they don’t want to be the product any more?

Economists would do well to distinguish the various inflation effects.

One is the explicit pricing of goods and services that were previously free. Another is consumers switching towards higher-quality alternatives, creating price pressure while supply adjusts.

AI itself is an industry touched by this.

But it is its capacity to accelerate the great unbundling that economists especially need to take note of.

Companies are already building systems specifically to keep sensitive workloads and data away from conventional public-cloud AI infrastructure.

There is a reason for this: the economics of cloud AI is becoming much more visible.

Take for example the recent controversy about OpenAI’s claimed breakthrough on the Navier-Stokes maths problem.

Tristan Buckmaster, a mathematician, alleged that information about work he and a colleague had been doing with OpenAI’s Codex reached the company before OpenAI launched its own assault on the problem.

OpenAI said it did not access their user data or see their work before publication, though it acknowledged it could not rule out de-identified usage data having contributed to improvements in its models.

Whatever the rights and wrongs of that particular case, the economic issue is obvious.

If customers believe that handing valuable information to an AI service could ultimately help improve a product available to competitors – or otherwise erode their informational advantage – they will put a price on preventing that from happening.

And increasingly, it looks like customers are deciding those costs are worth paying.

Furthermore, the same logic could soon encompass consumers too. Membership-based retailers, such as Costco, already show that people will pay an intermediary to deploy its concentrated buying expertise on their behalf, shielding them from poor-quality goods before they ever reach the shelves.

Now technologists think AI shopping agents operating on private datasets could do much the same thing online – potentially revolutionising the economics of shopping altogether.

Tellingly, Amazon is fighting attempts by third-party agents to shop its marketplace on behalf of customers, even as it develops its own agentic shopping tools.

If that’s right, something that initially looked deflationary could begin producing an inflationary effect as users start paying to reclaim control of the value they were previously giving away.

Fascinatingly, there is a faint echo here of the great unbundling that followed the collapse of the Soviet planned economy. That episode demonstrated particularly starkly what happens when a vast system of hidden subsidies is unwound: artificially low prices have to rebalance at much higher levels.

As British banking relationships are beginning to show, you receive only what you pay for. And people want more.

data.title: Wind farms accused of pushing up bills by exploiting loophole
data.description:
Wind farm owners have been accused of pushing up household bills by exploiting a “loophole” in green energy subsidies.

The loophole involves contracts for difference (CfDs), the 15- or 20-year fixed-price deals that are handed to wind farms to give developers certainty about their future income.

These are used to underpin the finances of most renewable energy schemes and are ultimately funded through consumer bills.

Ministers have repeatedly described CfDs as good value because they lock in relatively low-priced supplies of power for consumers that can shield them from price increases during crises.

But some developers have repeatedly exploited a rule allowing them to delay the start of their contracts so they can sell power at higher market rates instead. This has allowed some to reap huge windfalls.

Ministers closed the loophole in 2023, but projects awarded CfDs before then can still use it.

One energy executive claimed the situation was an “absolute p---take”.

They accused some developers of “making out like bandits” from the arrangement at the expense of millions of households and businesses, at a time when the US-Iran war has sent power prices surging.

One wind farm, Seagreen, off the coast of Angus, Scotland, is thought to have made about £27m extra by exploiting the loophole in the past two years, according to an analysis of market data by The Telegraph.

The scheme’s first phase secured a CfD in 2019 and construction finished in 2023.

Its CfD had a target start date of March 2025, but this has been repeatedly pushed back, with owners SSE, TotalEnergies and PTTEP now saying that they expect to activate it in March 2027.

There is no suggestion of wrongdoing by the companies, which must activate the CfD by a “hard stop” deadline of September 2028.

Spot power prices in Britain have jumped about £75 per megawatt-hour (MWh) during 2026 and are currently sitting at around £156 per MWh.

This means a wind farm, such as Seagreen, which was awarded a fixed CfD price of about £55 per MWh in today’s prices, can currently reap substantial profits by selling electricity at market rates.

David Turver, an independent energy analyst, argued this went against the spirit of CfDs, which are meant to help support the business cases of wind farms.

He said: “The ability to delay the start of CfDs was originally intended to help developers manage the risk of construction delays.

“But in some cases, the wind farms have been built already and they are simply choosing not to activate the contracts so they can get higher merchant power prices. They are benefitting in that way from higher gas prices.”

The energy executive added: “The CfD bid they made was predicated on what they [would] earn over the period covering construction, plus operations, plus the cost of capital – so the extra earnings now are pure windfall.

“In these times of high energy prices, they make out like bandits before activating it at their discretion.”

The Government previously urged wind farms to “act fairly on this matter, recognising the public support they have received for development”, before closing the loophole in 2023.

A spokesman for Seagreen Wind Energy Limited said on Friday: “In August 2026, we updated the Low Carbon Contracts Company regarding the expected start date for the CfD for Seagreen Phase 1.

“This has been done in accordance with the terms and conditions of the contract.”

data.title: Britain spends £84bn on energy imports
data.description:
The UK spent £84bn on buying oil, gas and electricity from abroad last year, amid warnings that high taxes are killing jobs in the North Sea and risking energy security.

The figure is the highest since 2022, when Vladimir Putin’s invasion of Ukraine plunged Europe into the most severe energy crisis in decades.

A report by Offshore Energies UK (OEUK), which represents the oil, gas, hydrogen, carbon capture and offshore wind industries, also said imports accounted for more than 40pc of the country’s energy needs. It warned that this leaves families and firms more vulnerable to global disruption.

Energy prices have come under immense pressure from Donald Trump’s war with Iran. Last week, Labour delayed a decision on whether to approve the Jackdaw gas field and Rosebank oil project in the North Sea, which its backers say will boost energy security.

Gas prices in the UK have in recent days spiked to a four-year high, while oil prices surged as high as $108.50 a barrel.

The report warned that successive governments have undermined the UK’s domestic oil and gas sector, accelerating a decline in domestic production.

The UK will need 561 billion cubic metres (bcm) of gas in the decade to 2035, it noted. The UK is expected to produce only 176bcm over this period. However, OEUK said this figure could be as high as 288bcm if the Government adopted “an investable fiscal regime and a pragmatic approach to licencing”.

If it does not, liquefied natural gas (LNG) imports could make up 46pc of supply by 2035, as opposed to only 6pc in a scenario where domestic production is prioritised.

The report warned: “LNG should be treated as a complement to domestic production, not a substitute. Future Norwegian piped imports also cannot be taken for granted.”

Norwegian officials have warned that supplies from the North Sea are in decline, threatening supplies to Britain, which relies on the Scandinavian country for around half of its gas.

LNG imports from the US rose by more than a third last year, increasing “exposure to global market volatility, geopolitical risk and higher lifecycle emissions”, the report said.

Three quarters of the LNG bought by the UK comes from the US, according to separate government figures.

The UK’s industrial energy consumption has meanwhile slumped to more than a 50-year low, amid industrial decline and greater power efficiency.

Enrique Cornejo, from OEUK, said: “It is concerning that we are importing more LNG, when we could produce half of our demand of gas for the coming years domestically with domestic resources. From the perspective of climate and emissions as well, LNG imports are more than three times more carbon-intensive compared to the average footprint of emissions in domestic [production]”.

The trade body urged Andy Burnham to scrap the Energy Profits Levy next year rather than in 2030, when the Government is planning to replace it with a 35pc tax on oil and gas sales.

Bringing in the oil and gas revenue levy three years early would help boost receipts by £14.9bn over the next decade, OEUK estimates.

The levy would have a less damaging effect on driving away investment, with £12.6bn of the boost to receipts coming from additional payroll taxes.

The report said: “The existing energy profits levy was introduced in response to a short-term price shock that has since ceased. The levy no longer reflects the market conditions and is constraining long-term investment in the UK continental shelf.”

data.title: We must use the remaining fossil fuels to build nuclear. Time is perilously short
data.description:
Britain is trying to replace fossil fuels with weather-dependent energy generation. It is not going well. According to the Government’s own figures, British industry now pays more for electricity than any other International Energy Agency country – a quarter more than Germany and over 60 per cent more than France.

Output of basic iron and steel is down 37 per cent since the start of 2021. Industrial electricity use has fallen in four of the last five years, and is now 13 per cent below its 2021 level – the lowest since 1983. We got rich by making things. We are making fewer of them every year.

In the prevailing narrative, this transition is necessary – to alter the earth’s climate, and to secure our energy supply. The high prices are temporary, an unfortunate combination of badly designed pricing and immature technology.

The remedy is more money, the abandonment of our sovereign oil and gas, and faster deployment of wind and solar. Do that, and we will eventually enjoy abundant, secure, cheap, high-quality energy. We will also lead the world by our example.

Let us grant the concerns about the climate are legitimate. And grant that a supply of inexpensive, reliable, high-quality energy can be scavenged from the wind and sun. The narrative still fails.

It fails because energy is only one of two things fossil fuels give us. The other is raw material. Hydrocarbon is the reducing agent that strips oxygen from iron ore to make steel – a chemical reaction, not a source of heat. It is restructured, molecule by molecule, into plastics. It is the source of the hydrogen in ammonia fertiliser, which feeds about half the world. Every component of a wind turbine – the steel, the plastics, the electronics – is made by burning and consuming hydrocarbons.

As is every component of the equipment that makes the turbine. And when the turbine goes to landfill in 20 years, all of it is required again. There are no affordable industrial-scale processes that replace hydrocarbons with electricity in these applications. Renewable technology is not a substitute for our hydrocarbon system. It is an additional burden on it.

Which brings us to the real problem. That raw material is running out.

“Peak oil” – the prediction that oil supply would rise to a peak in the early 2000s and then fall – goes back to M. King Hubbert in the 1950s. It has been written off ever since, not least because global oil production has kept rising. The dismissal rests on a historical misunderstanding.

The theory is simple. Oil that has not been discovered cannot be produced. So the historical pattern of oil discovery limits the available patterns of future production – “more now, less later” or “less now, more later”, but never “more now, more later”. Global oil discovery peaked in the 1960s and has trended down ever since.

By 2024, new discoveries had fallen to 6 per cent of annual production. From that, simple statistics allow the total discoverable volume to be estimated from that falling discovery curve. And then simple maths allows the shape and timing of production from that volume to be predicted. That shape is a peak.

The maths holds until the economics change. In 2008, they did. Peak oil always meant peak economic oil, the oil worth the cost of lifting it; nobody at the time thought the qualification necessary. Peaking economic oil drove its price to $147 a barrel, and that broke the financial system at its weakest point.

The crisis was answered with credit. Central banks created $28tn, global debt nearly doubled to $348tn and a significant quantity found its way into the petroleum system. Drilling at a loss and refinancing pulled economic oil forward and mobilised volumes that had never been economic, most notably US tight oil. The mechanism held.

What has kept oil volumes rising since has been the uneconomic kind, while the economic stock dwindled underneath it. We do need an energy transition, but not because of the weather – because the supply of economic oil is contracting.

Every successful energy transition in history has met two conditions. The new source was better than the old one – more energy from less material and less land. And there was a large surplus of the old fuel still available, enough to build the new system and keep everyone alive while it was built.

Wood to coal and coal to oil met both. This transition fails both. Wind and sun are diffuse, and they arrive when the weather decides. Everything that follows comes from those two facts. The land, the steel, the concrete and the copper all scale with how thinly the energy is spread; the cost and engineering scale with how much of the time it is absent.

To make a weather-dependent system behave like a dispatchable one, you must build additional capacity to store energy and fill the gaps. That makes the system more complex because wind and solar cannot provide reliable power on demand.

And our hydrocarbon system is contracting, so the second condition fails too: there is no surplus, and we are spending what remains on a system that cannot do the job. Every barrel that goes into it is a barrel unavailable to build something that can.

A time will come when there is not enough energy left to build the replacement – like being 60 miles from a petrol station with 50 miles in the tank.

We have been there before. Transitions have failed, and when they have, people have died – of hunger, of cold, and of the disorder that follows.

The alternative is not complicated. Maximise and conserve what fossil fuel is left and reserve it for manufacturing. Abandon the uses that produce nothing. Electrify everything that sensibly can be electrified now. Work out how to electrify the rest.

Nuclear is the only source dense enough to replace fossil fuel, and the only one we could build with what hydrocarbon remains. Strip away the regulation designed to strangle it, settle the waste question, and build at speed. We must spend what is left on the thing that works.

Richard Lyon is a petroleum engineer, electrical engineer and energy economist. His book The Energy Trap is published by Swift Press on Sept 24
