data.title: Labour’s race to net zero is driving up bills, warns IFS
data.description:
Labour’s race to net zero is driving up household bills unnecessarily, a think tank has warned.

A goal set by Ed Miliband, the former energy secretary, to decarbonise the electricity grid by 2030 risks “exacerbating” rises in energy bills, according to the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS).

In a report on electricity prices, the think tank called on the Government to water down this target to ease pressure on household bills as net zero costs enter a “crunch period” of steep increases.

Peter Levell, the IFS deputy research director, said: “That target is not necessary to reach net zero, but it does require you to push renewables and make these grid upgrades at pace, and doing it at speed is one of the things that pushes up costs.”

The IFS warned that the speed at which Labour was seeking to ditch fossil fuels meant the costs of getting to net zero carbon emissions by 2050 would be more expensive than it needed to be.

“It’s about the pace of doing this,” Mr Levell said.

The report casts further doubt on Labour’s general election campaign promise to bring down household energy bills by 2030.

Since Labour came to power, the energy price cap has instead climbed by £155, rising from £1,568 to £1,723.

This has been driven by soaring oil and gas prices in the wake of the Iran war, but analysts have warned that a swathe of UK government policies mean bills are higher than they need to be.

Taxes and levies on energy bills, excluding VAT, surged by 59pc in real terms between 2017 and 2025, the IFS calculated.

By 2025, these charges made up 23pc of an average household’s electricity bill. The Government has since reduced this share to 17pc by shifting some net zero costs to general taxation.

Mr Levell said that racing towards a totally net zero grid by the end of the decade was an inefficient and expensive way to lower emissions.

He said: “Squeezing that extra drop of carbon out of the electricity system is quite expensive at this point because it involves replacing the gas generation that is there on standby to ensure the grid is stable and running when you don’t have enough renewable power.

“Meeting that involves a lot of upgrades to the grid and it involves adding a lot of renewable capacity very quickly, even relative to the last few years. There’s a risk that that is going to push up costs fairly significantly.

“The carbon savings that you make by doing that could be more cheaply achieved in other sectors.”

In one of his first acts as energy secretary in July 2024, Mr Miliband announced a mission to “turbocharge” Britain’s net zero drive and decarbonise the UK electricity grid by 2030, five years earlier than the 2035 goal set by the Conservative government.

This has necessitated massive increases in investment to increase Britain’s capacity to generate and store renewable power, as well as to make the necessary upgrades to the electricity grid so that the power can be transported around the country. Both of these costs flow through to household bills.

The cost of network upgrades – driven mainly by new pylons carrying wind power from where it is generated in the North to where it is consumed primarily in the South – is on track to more than double from £5.1bn in 2025-26 to £12.3bn by 2030-31.

On top of this, the cost of balancing supply and demand for power on the grid is about to surge from £3bn to £7bn over the same period. Much of the cost comes from paying wind farms to switch off because the grid cannot handle their power.

Earlier this month the National Audit Office (NAO) warned that Labour’s 2030 goal was adding £1.9bn per year to bills.

It found that constraint costs, as payments for wasted wind power are officially known, would add up to £100 to annual household bills by 2030.

The IFS urged the Government to limit increases to bills by making “time of use” tariffs the default across the country. These deals mean households are charged different prices for electricity at different times, depending on supply and demand.

The IFS said this would provide stronger incentives to encourage consumers to do things like charging electric vehicles or running washing machines at times when it is cheapest to do so.

Bobbie Upton, at the IFS, said this could help to lower bills “with minimal cost to the Government”.

However, critics say these tariffs punish those who do not have the luxury of shifting the time of when they use electricity, such as people who require electrical medical devices. Households would be charged higher rates to use power at times of high demand.

A Department for Energy Security and Net Zero spokesman said: “We inherited a broken system. Breaking the link with fossil fuels, upgrading our network and transitioning to clean power is the only way to bring down bills for good.

“Alongside this, we have cut VAT on electricity bills from October, on top £150 we removed earlier this year, and we will keep looking at what more we can do to protect families from unaffordable bills.”

data.title: Volkswagen to slash up to 50,000 jobs
data.description:
Volkswagen’s shares have surged after the German giant confirmed plans to cut 50,000 jobs as it battles competition from China.

The carmaker’s Frankfurt-listed shares jumped by more than 8pc on Friday after it unveiled the sweeping job cuts, which are the biggest in Volkswagen’s 89-year history.

Volkswagen said on Thursday it would cut tens of thousands more roles as it faces fierce competition from Chinese rivals that are flooding into Europe.

The German carmaker said that the restructuring would be in addition to 50,000 reductions that it has already made since 2024 and could lead to plant closures.

It is racing to cut costs as it grapples with fierce competition from Chinese rivals such as BYD and slowing demand in Europe. It has also struggled under US tariffs and Volkswagen vehicle sales fell by 8.4pc in the first half of the year, while its operating profit dropped by 11.6pc.

News of the restructuring plans emerged earlier this year, but had yet to be approved by Volkswagen’s supervisory board, which represents the labour force and shareholders.

The carmaker said its European capacity “currently exceeds demand by more than 500,000 units”. The new plan will pave the way for Volkswagen to slim its vehicle line-up by as much as 50pc by 2035.

“Given intensifying global competition, shifting demand and technological change in the automotive industry, a consistent alignment of workforce capacity with economic reality is essential,” the company said in a statement.

Last September, Porsche, which is owned by Volkswagen, blamed a decision to delay the launch of its new electric SUV in September on weak demand for electric cars as it warned of a €5.1bn (£4.4bn) hit to profits.

Volkswagen added that it could not guarantee that a number of its plants would be used from 2030 onwards. It said it was considering alternative uses for the four affected factories. Some could potentially be converted into use by Germany’s defence industry.

Oliver Blume, the Volkswagen chief executive, said last month that the company was in talks with defence companies to use its site in Osnabrück.

The new cuts represent about 8pc of the company’s global workforce of roughly 650,000 across brands such as Škoda, Seat, Porsche and Lamborghini.

It comes after lengthy talks between the company, its unions and Lower Saxony, the German state where the company is headquartered. The state is also a large minority shareholder in Volkswagen.

Mr Blume has previously said that Volkswagen needed to rein in costs, which were roughly 30pc higher than its competitors. The company said it was seeking to lift its margin to 9pc by 2030, up from just 3.8pc in the first half of this year.

In a statement, he said that the new cost-cutting plans were “a strong signal for the future of the Volkswagen Group”.

“We are taking responsibility for our entire workforce, for our partners and for industrial jobs worldwide,” he added.

data.title: Revolut eyes stock market listings in London and New York
data.description:
Revolut is plotting a dual stock market listing in London and New York.

The digital bank, valued at $115bn (£85bn), has previously shied away from committing to a UK float. However, Nik Storonsky, its founder, said it was considering the London Stock Exchange (LSE) for the first time on Thursday.

Such a move would be a major boost for the UK market, which has been hit by an exodus of companies and a drought of new listings.

Vue, the cinema chain, is also exploring plans to list on the LSE, its chief executive Tim Richards told the Financial Times. He said there was “too much gloom” around the London market and hoped to debut its shares in the UK.

A London float of Revolut would make it one of Britain’s largest listed companies, putting it on a par with FTSE 100 giants including Barclays, BP and GSK.

Mr Storonsky said that although Revolut would list in London, he still wanted it to have a presence on Wall Street “because it’s a larger market”.

He said: “We have the choice between selling in a small market with few buyers, or in a gigantic market with a huge number of buyers who will compete fiercely for our shares. Therefore, yes, we prefer the United States.

“In reality, we are currently planning a dual listing, on the London Stock Exchange and the Nasdaq.

“If you truly have a strong brand in the United States, with a popular and accessible product, your customers will also participate in the [initial public offering], which will have a positive effect on our market capitalisation.”

UK ‘less liquid’

Mr Storonsky has previously dismissed the possibility of a London float, arguing that it was “not rational” to list in Britain because of the 0.5pc stamp duty charged on purchases of shares.

Two years ago, he said: “The UK is less liquid so it’s much worse compared to the US plus it’s much more expensive because you pay stamp duty – it’s just not rational.”

Earlier this year, Mr Storonsky said any listing of Revolut would only happen by 2028 at the earliest. A source close to Revolut said a float would be subject to market conditions.

Mr Storonsky, who was born in Russia, started Revolut in London in 2013. The company has since grown to become one of Europe’s largest and most valuable online banks.

He later renounced his Russian citizenship in 2022 in the wake of Vladimir Putin’s invasion of Ukraine.

Mr Storonsky has previously criticised Britain’s “extremely bureaucratic” regulators, while claiming “it’s hard to do business in the UK”.

Revolut was awarded a full UK banking licence in March this year, having first applied to become a full bank in 2021.

They will be used in the three Rolls-designed SMRs that are being built in Anglesey, as well as further reactors set to be built in the Czech Republic and Sweden.

It will be the first time large steam turbines have been made domestically in more than 20 years.

The expansion will follow an investment in the Newcastle factory understood to be worth tens of millions of pounds. It is expected to create 550 jobs.

It follows concerns raised by MPs that SMR components were set to be built abroad.

Rolls-Royce SMR said the decision by German engineering giant Siemens demonstrated how the company was “delivering its commitment to localisation, driving investment and re-shoring work that would have taken place overseas”.

Rolls-Royce SMR is an independent company, majority owned by Rolls-Royce but with investors including Qatar and France’s Perrodo family.

Chris Cholerton, the company’s chief executive, said: “We are building on a remarkable industrial legacy while creating and sustaining the skills and supply chain needed to deliver clean, secure and affordable energy for decades to come.”

Darren Davidson, of Siemens Energy, added: “We’re preparing to manufacture the next generation of steam turbines for small modular reactors, supporting energy security, creating skilled jobs and helping power the UK’s future energy mix.”

The Government awarded Rolls a contract to design and develop Britain’s first three SMRs last year.

They will be built in Anglesey, North Wales, in a project aimed at proving the commercial viability of the still-nascent technology by the mid-2030s. Each one will generate 470 megawatts of power.

Rolls selected Siemens Energy as its supplier of steam turbines last year, but there had been uncertainty about where the key components would be manufactured until now.

The British company faced a backlash earlier this year after it emerged that some other parts would be made overseas, including reactor pressure vessels that will be imported from either South Korea or the Czech Republic.

Labour ministers have set a target for 70pc of components to be made in Britain, and on Thursday they hailed the announcement by Siemens as proof their plan to “reindustrialise Britain” was working.

Miatta Fahnbulleh, the Energy Secretary, said: “Producing these components here in the UK will help strengthen our energy security, reduce our exposure to volatile international gas markets, create new export opportunities for British industry, and reindustrialise the UK.”

Jonathan Reynolds, the Business Secretary, added: “Building small modular reactors here in the UK presents huge benefits for us, from more export opportunities to more jobs on the ground at home.”

The Newcastle factory is expected to make both high-pressure turbines and valve casings.

It will also become the service hub for the turbines in the Rolls SMR fleet, ensuring a pipeline of work for the site that is expected to last decades.

The historic Parsons Works is the site once run by Sir Charles Parsons, the revered British engineer who helped to revolutionise marine propulsion with his invention of the multi-stage steam turbine.

It was established in 1889 and was where the steam turbine for Calder Hall – the world’s first commercial nuclear power station, in Cumbria – was built.

Grid-scale steam turbines have not been manufactured in the UK since the early 2000s, when Siemens scaled back its operations in Newcastle.

A steam turbine for a nuclear power plant has not been built in Britain since the early 1990s when one was supplied for the Sizewell B plant in Suffolk.

Tom Greatrex, of the Nuclear Industry Association, said: “This is what reindustrialisation looks like: a vital clean energy project reviving our old manufacturing capabilities to provide good, skilled jobs where we need them.

“The announcement is a real vote of confidence in industrial Britain and shows what SMRs and nuclear projects can deliver for this country.”

data.title: Ofcom accused of covering up data showing GB News more trusted than BBC
data.description:
Media regulator Ofcom has been accused of covering up data showing that GB News is more trusted by its viewers than the BBC.

The watchdog’s latest news consumption survey found that GB News viewers score the channel more highly for trustworthiness than viewers of the BBC, Sky News, ITV and Channel 4 score those channels.

GB News was also ranked by its viewers above all other British broadcasters for the range of viewpoints on offer and scored first equal with Sky for impartiality.

Ofcom has in previous years published these figures alongside a press release summarising its main findings.

However, the regulator omitted the figures from this year’s publication, which was released last week.

The oversight has prompted accusations that Ofcom deliberately sought to suppress the true scale of GB News’s popularity among viewers.

A GB News spokesman said: “These figures prove why GB News is Britain’s undisputed number one news channel.

“Our viewers and listeners trust us to provide them with news, and our bold and fearless journalism is connecting with communities everywhere.”

An Ofcom spokesman said: “An administrative error led to a short delay in publishing the underlying data for this year’s report, which we corrected as soon as we became aware.

“More broadly, not all of the vast amounts of data we produce can be included in the main report, which focused on our key findings.”

It comes at a critical time for broadcasters as they grapple with the shift to streaming and a tidal wave of often unreliable information circulating online.

In June, the Government set out proposals to require social media apps such as YouTube, Facebook and X to prominently feature material from “trusted” news providers.

But ministers have failed to explain how broadcasters or newspapers would qualify as a trusted news source, triggering concerns that the Government could ultimately influence where people get their news from.

In its green paper, the Government said public service broadcasters – the BBC, ITV and Channel 4 – “remain among the most trusted news sources”.

But GB News insiders argue that Ofcom’s data fundamentally undermines this claim, raising concerns that the fledgling channel is being intentionally overlooked in discussions over the future of British TV.

GB News has previously argued that it should be counted as public service media, alongside other commercial broadcasters such as Sky.

In a submission to ministers earlier this year, GB News said it should be allowed to compete for public funding alongside its rivals, rather than taxpayer money automatically being channelled to the BBC.

Figures from official ratings agency Barb show GB News has been the most-watched non-public service broadcaster in the year to date, with an average daily audience of just under 90,000.

According to Ofcom’s latest research, 74pc of GB News viewers consider the channel to be trustworthy. That compares with 71pc for Sky News and 66pc for the BBC.

Both GB News and Sky News scored 63pc for impartiality, eclipsing the BBC’s 53pc, while 72pc said GB News presented a broad range of views.

Sky viewers narrowly edged out GB News for impartiality, though both ranked ahead of the BBC in this category.

Ofcom’s decision to omit these findings risks stoking long-running tensions between the regulator and GB News.

The two sides have repeatedly clashed over impartiality rules, in particular its use of politicians such as Nigel Farage and Sir Jacob Rees-Mogg as presenters.

In 2024, Ofcom fined GB News £100,000 over a programme featuring Rishi Sunak, who was prime minister at the time. It has also censured the broadcaster for airing conspiracy theories and is currently investigating comments by a guest who linked Pride with paedophilia and bestiality.

However, GB News scored a major victory over the regulator last year, when the High Court overturned a ruling that the channel had breached the broadcasting code in a programme presented by Sir Jacob.

Bosses have previously insisted that GB News is the victim of a coordinated political attack by opponents, including the Good Law Project, a campaign group founded by Jolyon Maugham, an activist lawyer.

data.title: UBS considers quitting Switzerland
data.description:
UBS is considering leaving Switzerland as executives at the lender revolt against stringent financial rules intended to prevent another banking crisis.

The 164-year-old Swiss bank has been exploring options to leave its home nation, including through a potential merger with an overseas rival.

It comes after politicians in Bern voted to increase the bank’s capital buffers to protect against financial shocks as part of reforms to the country’s “too big to fail” rules.

Swiss officials have been seeking to increase the amount of capital the bank needs in the wake of the near-collapse of Credit Suisse three years ago.

UBS was forced to bail out its biggest rival to avert a European banking crisis. That deal dramatically increased UBS’s balance sheet, which is now nearly double the size of the entire Swiss economy.

The Swiss parliament this week advanced a law that would require UBS to bolster its reserves of capital by up to $16bn (£12bn), which executives warned would erode the bank’s international competitiveness and profitability.

Semafor reported on Friday that the bank’s leadership had “revived discussions” about quitting its home nation, including potentially through a combination with a rival. The report named Morgan Stanley as a potential suitor.

The loss of its biggest bank would threaten Switzerland’s status as an international banking and private wealth hub.

It comes amid fears in the City that British lenders could face a fresh bank tax raid in Labour’s upcoming Budget.

The potential windfall tax has prompted warnings that major banks could shift away from London.

In a statement this week, UBS called the tighter capital requirements “extreme regulatory proposals” that would be “damaging to the Swiss economy”. It called the additional capital call “excessive” and said Switzerland’s current rules were “already among the most stringent globally”.

The bank added: “As the parliamentary process continues, UBS will focus on protecting its long-term interests.”

‘We can live with a black eye’

Sergio Ermotti, the chief executive of UBS, said: “We can live with a black eye, but two black eyes and a broken nose is too much.”

It comes after the Swiss upper house, the Council of States, voted to require UBS to back its foreign branches with 90pc of high-tier common equity.

Executives at UBS have reportedly privately warned that failure to ease the rules could force it to move its headquarters. UBS shares climbed 3.5pc on Friday after news it was considering quitting Switzerland.

The near-collapse of Credit Suisse three years ago triggered a scramble to bail out the bank and a shotgun merger with UBS, which was forced through by the Swiss government and banking regulators.

UBS declined to comment.

data.title: Nationalise Thames Water to block hedge fund takeover, MPs urge
data.description:
Andy Burnham should immediately take control of Thames Water to prevent hedge funds from seizing it, MPs have urged.

The embattled utility company faces takeover by its lenders under a £10bn rescue deal, but MPs have urged the Government to act before that happens.

Alistair Carmichael, the Liberal Democrat MP who chairs the environment select committee, said: “Thames Water’s 16 million customers have largely lost faith.

“We do not believe this opaque consortium of 100 hedge funds has the interests of the public, the company or the environment at heart.”

The committee has called on the Government to push ahead with a so-called “special administration regime”. This form of nationalisation would see officials and the water regulator, Ofwat, appoint an administrator to manage the business.

The company could then be restructured, and the Government could find a new approved buyer.

The MPs called on the Government to bring in emergency legislation to push through the administration “to draw a line under this debacle and restore stability to the sector”.

Thames is struggling under a debt pile of almost £20bn and has admitted that it faces running out of cash by the end of the year.

A group of more than 100 lenders, known as London & Valley Water, includes US hedge funds Elliott Investment Management, Silver Point and Apollo.

As part of the £10bn deal, London & Valley Water has said it will inject billions of pounds into the business to fund upgrades to Britain’s ageing water network.

It has also committed to paying out no dividends until 2035 and offered the Government a “golden share” in the business.

Mr Burnham indicated that he would explore bringing Thames into public ownership. However, Thames’s advisers have suggested that this could cost £4bn and officials have raised concerns about the cost of the process.

Mr Carmichael said the cost of placing the company into special administration would be “neutral to the taxpayer” if the investors, whom he alleged had lent money to Thames “at payday-lender rates”, were not compensated.

He called on the Government to reject any further offers from the company’s current creditors.

The MPs added that Ofwat’s current special administration rules were too vague and appeared to trigger only if the business collapsed.

They called for the public takeover to be “triggered earlier” or for “fresh legislation” to push the company into special administration.

The committee also criticised Thames’s current environmental performance and customer service.

A Thames Water spokesman said: “Turning Thames Water around will take a decade and require significant and sustained investment, but we are already making progress, and this is a different business from the one it was two years ago.

“We are delivering the biggest upgrade of our infrastructure in 150 years, and we are seeing the benefits of that investment.”

A spokesman for the lenders said: “All profits will be reinvested, and no dividends will be taken until the company is turned around and returned to the public markets. There will be no cost to the Government or taxpayers, and customers will be protected from the costs of Thames Water’s restructuring.”

data.title: Johnson & Johnson offers £4.1bn to settle talcum powder cancer claims
data.description:
Johnson & Johnson (J&J) has agreed to pay an estimated $5.5bn (£4.1bn) to resolve tens of thousands of claims that its baby powder caused ovarian cancer.

The pharmaceutical giant’s offer of a settlement could end a decade-long legal battle that has dogged the company.

Erik Haas, vice-president of litigation at J&J, said the claims that its talcum powder products caused cancer were “meritless” ‌but said the company was willing ⁠to settle to get closure.

The settlement covers around 76,000 claims and must be accepted by 95pc of the ovarian cancer claimants in state or federal court before it becomes final.

J&J previously settled the majority of cases alleging that its talc contained asbestos and caused mesothelioma, a rare but aggressive cancer affected the lungs, abdomen or heart.

Mr Haas said: “While we are confident the company would have ultimately prevailed with further litigation, as it has in the vast majority of cases tried to date, this resolution allows the company to put this matter behind it and remain focused on its mission to develop medicines and devices that save ⁠lives.”

J&J expects to pay $3bn in 2027, and it will make further payments in 2028.

More than 3,000 people filed lawsuits at Britain’s High Court last year alleging that either they or a family member developed ovarian cancer or mesothelioma as a result of using Johnson’s Baby Powder between 1965 and 2023.

The settlements announced on Monday included groups who filed claims in federal and state courts.

J&J ended global sales of baby powder containing the mineral talc in 2023, switching to a formulation based on corn starch.

The settlements come after cases were put on hold for more than three years after a series of bankruptcy filings by J&J.

It filed three bankruptcies through a shell-company subsidiary in an ‌effort to settle the cases. Each bankruptcy ended in dismissal and the litigation resumed in March 2025.

Chris Seeger, an attorney who represents about 2,500 clients with talc claims and helped negotiate the agreement, said J&J could ultimately pay $7bn or more.

The settlement assigns specific values to qualifying ovarian cancer claims but does not cap J&J’s total payout.

He said: “We got ‌a fair settlement, and our clients are going to be happy with it.”

data.title: Embattled housebuilder slumps to record £660m loss
data.description:
Struggling housebuilder Vistry has plunged to its biggest-ever loss of £661m as Britain’s property crisis deepens.

The business said it planned to build fewer homes and pull back from the South East as it recorded £475m in write-downs and a further £73m hit from rising building safety costs.

Vistry said it would cut annual housebuilding from more than 15,000 homes to 12,000 and reduce the number of its regional businesses from 25 to 12, while seeking £50m of annual cost savings.

It marks a dramatic reversal from a previous target set by former chief executive Greg Fitzgerald, who aimed to build 20,000 homes a year.

The company – one of only two private sector providers eligible to become a “strategic partner plus” for Labour’s affordable housing scheme – reported an adjusted loss before tax of £83.3m in the six months to June, compared with an £80.6m profit a year earlier.

The £661m pre-tax loss eclipses a £79m loss recorded by its Bovis Homes predecessor during the 2008 financial crisis.

Britain’s housebuilders are grappling with a slump in property sales as mortgage rates rise and buyers hold off on purchases amid soaring living costs. Sellers have been forced to cut prices, which have dropped around 0.4pc over the past 12 months.

Vistry’s plans to scale back its housebuilding – which follow a review by Adam Daniels, the new chief executive – come despite the business securing £350m from the Government to help build new social and affordable homes.

Labour has launched a drive to build 1.5 million new homes during this parliament but the number of new homes being built is currently far short of this target.

England added an estimated 199,500 homes in the year to March 2026, according to the latest government figures, down from 208,600 the previous year.

Vistry said it has been cutting the prices of some homes to raise cash, selling assets and slowing construction on sites where sales had been weaker.

The housebuilder added that it would stop selling homes on the open market in the South East to individual buyers, instead selling them to investors or housing associations prior to construction.

It said it has made £25m of savings through a voluntary staff exit scheme and recruitment freeze, on top of the £50m annual savings targeted through its restructuring.

Mr Daniels’ plans mark a climbdown from the vision previously set out by Mr Fitzgerald, his charismatic predecessor.

The new chief executive is rowing back on Mr Fitzgerald’s stated aim to switch “fully” to a “partnerships” housing model, through which Vistry would focus completely on joining forces with housing associations, councils and the Government to build affordable homes using taxpayer-backed funds.

Mr Daniels is now aiming to restore the quantum of its housing back to 60pc partner-funded and 40pc to be sold on the open market.

He was also forced to cut £475m from the amount of profit that Vistry hoped to earn from Mr Fitzgerald’s billion-pound acquisitions of Countryside and Galliford Try in 2020 and 2022, contributing to its huge writedowns.

Mr Daniels told analysts on Thursday: “The rapid M&A caused us some challenges, but things here are absolutely fixable.

“We acknowledge that the execution of our model since 2023 [hasn’t] all gone as we planned, but there is very good reassurance in the work we’ve done that the models worked excellently in some areas, despite the difficult market conditions we’ve had.”

On top of its losses, Vistry reported its net debt had climbed to £468.8m, up from £293.1m in the same period last year. Vistry’s stock is down 58pc so far this year.

Mr Daniels said: “Vistry has strong fundamentals: a differentiated mixed-tenure model, deep partner relationships, a quality product, exposure to structurally attractive affordable and partner-backed housing markets and highly motivated people.”

He added: “The business will therefore be resized, simplified and repositioned to deliver lower leverage, stronger cash conversion and more sustainable returns.”

Vistry shares fell 7pc on Thursday morning after the announcement.

data.title: Jaguar Land Rover to axe 4,000 jobs
data.description:
Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) has confirmed plans to cut 4,000 jobs as its battles against competition from low-cost Chinese rivals and the shift to electric vehicles.

The company said on Monday that it would make the cuts over the next two years amid “intense competition and ongoing geopolitical uncertainty”.

Bosses insisted the move was necessary “to build a stronger, more competitive JLR”, as they targeted £1.7bn of savings from a wider overhaul of the business.

PB Balaji, the carmaker’s chief executive, added: “We recognise this will be difficult news for colleagues affected, and are committed to supporting everyone with care, fairness and respect.”

The cuts represent a major setback to Andy Burnham’s pledge to reindustrialise Britain.

It is understood they will largely fall on white-collar, salaried workers across JLR’s UK business and will not affect employees working in car production.

Some staff working in the manufacturer’s overseas divisions are also expected to be given the opportunity to take voluntary redundancy, which could reduce the effect on the British business.

Around 30,000 of the company’s 44,000 employees are based in the UK.

JLR’s global headquarters are in Coventry, while it operates major factories in manufacturing sites in Solihull, Wolverhampton and Merseyside.

No state bailout

MPs have warned that the cuts will have a “devastating” effect, with Mr Balaji set to hold a meeting with ministers and union officials on Tuesday.

He will sit down with Sharon Graham, the general secretary of Unite the Union, and Jonathan Reynolds, the Business Secretary, who has already made clear that there will be no money for a bailout of the company to protect jobs.

However, Mr Reynolds appeared to leave the door open for the Government to offer other forms of support.

“If it’s about long-term investment in the future, we do invest alongside industry on that,” he told Laura Kuenssberg’s Sunday morning BBC TV show.

At Tuesday’s meeting, Mr Balaji is expected to bring up the Government’s electric vehicle mandate – which could be watered down under changes being considered by ministers – as well as general pressures on the business, such as high energy costs and taxes on employment.

However, a source close to the company acknowledged that although improving conditions in the UK would help, JLR’s troubles were global in nature and echoed those of European giants, such as Volkswagen and Stellantis.

JLR, owned by Indian conglomerate Tata, is under pressure to shore up its finances amid rising costs and a slump in sales.

Revenues fell by almost 10pc in the first quarter, while pre-tax profits dropped by two thirds to £109m.

The carmaker, whose largest market is North America, has been rocked by Donald Trump’s 10pc tariff on vehicle imports to the US.

It is also still reeling from a crippling cyber attack that shut down production for more than a month and is estimated to have cost the company £1.9bn.

Further supply chain disruption and tough competition from cut-price Chinese rivals have also taken a toll.

Mr Balaji said the company was investing at least £15bn in electrification overall while it also seeks to make £1.7bn of savings.

Union officials are pushing for those who are losing their jobs to be retrained, potentially with support from the Government.

Unite’s Ms Graham said: “While the cuts planned are not expected to impact the UK manufacturing footprint, we need to ensure that the company is doing all it can to avoid unnecessary job losses amongst its highly skilled white collar workers.

“JLR’s vague statement today was not helpful and has only created increased uncertainty.

“Once again Unite will leave no stone unturned to support JLR workers. It cannot be acceptable that workers again are made to pay the price.”

She added that the union supported changes to the zero-emission vehicle mandate, which along with high energy costs had been “crippling the industry”.

A spokesman for Andy Burnham said on Monday that the Government remained “in close contact” with JLR.

They added: “We understand that this will be an uncertain and concerning time for affected workers, their families and the wider communities.”

data.title: Luxury British homeware brand collapses into administration
data.description:
A leading British luxury home decor brand has collapsed into administration after more than 50 years of trading, triggering dozens of redundancies.

Designers Guild, founded in 1970 by Tricia Guild, an English textile and interior designer, has appointed administrators from Interpath following a downturn in trading.

Of the workforce, 93 employees were made redundant immediately, while a small group will remain temporarily to help wind down operations.

The firm built a reputation for bold patterns from its flagship store on London’s King’s Road.

Clients over the years have included high-profile stars such as Sir Mick Jagger, The Good Life’s Felicity Kendal and Dame Joan Collins.

Designers Guild created collections influenced by royal properties, such as Buckingham Palace and Windsor Castle.

Its high-end price points included vintage overdyed rugs selling for around £2,500 and sofas priced up to £6,250.

A notice in the window of its flagship store in on Thursday said the “store is closed... very many thanks and much love to our many customers and friends for your support over the decades”.

The business was heavily affected by Brexit-related bureaucracy, which increased costs for its largely European customer base.

The company sold its brand name and design archive in April 2025 to Dunelm, continuing its operational trade under a licencing deal.

Interpath reportedly oversaw a months-long sales process leading up to September, with interest from at least one prospective buyer. However, a deal failed to materialise.

Ms Guild and Simon Jeffreys, her brother and the company’s chief executive, said they were sad at the decision to close.

Ms Guild said: “Designers Guild Ltd has been so much more than a business to me. It is my passion and my life’s work.

“The brand was built over decades with an unswerving belief in the power of creative design and a constant striving to achieve only the very best.”

Rick Harrison, a joint administrator and managing director at Interpath, said his focus lay in helping the affected staff while assessing options to liquidate or sell the remaining assets, including leftover stock.

On Friday, Dunelm announced that a 10-year licence to design and sell fabrics, wallpapers and paint under the Designers Guild name had been agreed with upmarket furnishings company Sanderson.

data.title: GSK plots £400m Cambridge research hub in push for cancer breakthrough
data.description:
GlaxoSmithKline (GSK) will invest £400m in a major new science hub in Cambridge as part of plans to pour more money into developing new cancer drugs.

The pharmaceuticals giant said it planned to acquire a new 300,000 sq ft site on the Cambridge Biomedical Campus, which will house most of its research and development (R&D).

The new centre of excellence will employ more than 1,000 scientists, GSK said, with its researchers developing new vaccines, HIV treatments and cancer drugs.

However, the move will also end the FTSE 100 company’s 50-year relationship with Stevenage, Hertfordshire, which was previously its main UK research base. Some Stevenage staff will be asked to relocate to another lab in nearby Ware.

The investment in Cambridge comes as GSK seeks to ramp up its pipeline of medicines under Luke Miels, its new chief executive, who took on the role from Dame Emma Walmsley at the start of the year.

The company has been accelerating investment in cancer drugs after it acquired US-based Nuvalent in June for nearly £8bn.

GSK won approval from US medical regulators last week for Jideytro, a lung cancer treatment secured as part of the takeover of Nuvalent.

The decision to open a new Cambridge campus will bolster the Government’s efforts to turn the 100-mile corridor between Oxford and Cambridge into an economic powerhouse.

GSK said the investment would build its presence “in the heart of the UK’s life sciences ‘Golden Triangle’” – made up of Oxford, Cambridge and London.

Earlier this year, Rachel Reeves, the former chancellor, set out Labour’s ambition to turn the area into a hub for science businesses, building new homes and transport links to create Europe’s “Silicon Valley”.

The Cambridge Biomedical Campus already employs more than 22,000 people and hosts treatments for one million patients each year. GSK hopes to build its links with research hospitals in Cambridge and benefit from proximity to the University of Cambridge.

Mr Miels said: “This investment will accelerate our R&D and help us deliver new, competitive products.”

On Tuesday, GSK also announced plans for a major cost-cutting drive aimed at saving £1.9bn by 2029 to fund the development of new drugs. The savings are expected to include job cuts around the world, including reducing some back-office roles.

Alongside the plans for a new Cambridge site, GSK said it had launched 20 phase three trials as part of its plans to expand its pipeline of treatments.

These trials are the final stage of clinical testing before a drug is submitted to the Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency for approval.

Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, said the £400m investment was “a vote of confidence in British business”.

Life science is one of eight sectors that form part of the Government’s modern industrial strategy.

The investment from GSK comes after its rival AstraZeneca announced that it would pour £200m into its Cambridge site, along with £100m for a project in Macclesfield, Cheshire.

GSK’s relocation to the Cambridge Biomedical Campus means Britain’s two largest pharmaceutical companies will neighbour each other in the city. GSK said it would keep its global headquarters in London.

data.title: AstraZeneca dumped by investors over £300bn US merger talks
data.description:
AstraZeneca shares have taken an £18bn hit after investors baulked at reports it was plotting a mega-merger with a US rival.

Shares in Britain’s second-most valuable company slumped on Monday after it emerged that AstraZeneca had held talks about a potential $400bn (£300bn) tie-up with Bristol Myers Squibb.

If completed, the merger would create one of the world’s largest pharmaceutical businesses. The potential deal would also raise fears that AstraZeneca could shift its business to the US in a blow to Britain.

However, analysts said it was a high-risk deal that risked destroying more value than it created. It would be one of the biggest mergers of all time, meaning any missteps could prove hugely costly, and would be likely to draw the attention of competition regulators and politicians.

News of the talks, first reported by the Financial Times, sent AstraZeneca’s shares plunging 9pc on Monday to their lowest level since September 2025.

Markus Manns, a portfolio manager at Union Investment and an ‌AstraZeneca ⁠shareholder, told Reuters: “A combination with Bristol ​does not make strategic or financial sense.

“Many past mega-mergers have destroyed value and there is no apparent need for Astra to do it.”

Jefferies analysts said in a note: “If there is ​one company that doesn’t need financial engineering, it’s AstraZeneca.”

Michael Leuchten, an analyst at Jefferies, said he was “perplexed” by the potential takeover. He said investors backed the company because of its consistent sales growth, not because management “go out and do big deals”.

AstraZeneca is worth around £184bn on the London Stock Exchange, while New York-listed Bristol Myers Squibb has a market value of $133bn.

Bristol Myers Squibb shares surged as much as 3.8pc on Wall Street on Monday.

Analysts said competition concerns would be the biggest hurdle to a deal as both companies have large cancer treatment businesses.

The potential deal could also trigger a political backlash from Donald Trump’s administration, Jefferies warned.

Mr Leuchten added: “AstraZeneca would effectively be a UK-based acquirer of one of America’s large Pharmas, at a time when US policymakers are focused on domestic manufacturing and strategic industries.”

The deal would raise questions about AstraZeneca’s continued links to Britain as Sir Pascal Soriot, its chief executive, pushes ahead with a pivot towards the US.

AstraZeneca upgraded its listing on the New York Stock Exchange last September to let American investors buy its shares directly, while keeping its listing in London.

The move put AstraZeneca’s New York listing on a par with that of London, in what was seen as a blow to the UK’s struggling stock market.

AstraZeneca subsequently struck a $50bn deal with the Trump administration to invest in US manufacturing and transatlantic research facilities.

At the time, Sir Pascal described the drugmaker as a “very American company”.

The business subsequently agreed to sell some medicines at a discount to the US Medicaid programme to avoid being hit with tariffs.

Despite this, Britain’s biggest drugmaker has insisted that it intends to remain headquartered in Cambridge and retain its listing on the London Stock Exchange.

Mr Leuchten said buying Bristol Myers Squibb as a way to shift permanently to the US would be “a fairly drastic way to go about it”.

However, Neil Birrell, the chief investment officer at Premier Miton, an AstraZeneca shareholder, said the likelihood of the pharmaceutical business shifting its shares to the US would increase if the Bristol Myers Squibb deal went ahead.

Mr Birrell added: “There hasn’t been a huge amount that I’ve seen coming out from any of the authorities – whether it be the Government or the London Stock Exchange – of any great substance to try and keep these sort of companies here.”

The Prime Minister said the talks were “a private matter for the companies involved”.

A No 10 spokesman said: “More broadly, the UK life sciences sector is one of our greatest national assets, driving innovation, skilled employment and investment across the country while developing medicines that improve health outcomes and save lives.”

AstraZeneca has around 10,000 staff at five UK sites, including 4,000 at its main facilities in Cambridge and Macclesfield and another 2,000 in London and Luton.

Steve Boden, a regional organiser at GMB Union, said he was seeking urgent assurances from AstraZeneca that jobs would be protected.

“These reports of a merger are causing great concern amongst AstraZeneca’s loyal workers. While no deal has been formally announced, mergers can create pressure to cut costs, so staff are understandably worrying about what this could mean for them.”

The proposed mega-merger will evoke memories of Pfizer’s attempts to take over AstraZeneca a decade ago.

The US company’s acquisition ultimately collapsed after a wave of resistance from the board and politicians alike.

Ed Miliband, then Labour leader, said at the time that Pfizer’s assurances about protecting research and saving jobs were “worthless”.

Bristol Myers Squibb is headquartered in Princeton, New Jersey, and was started in 1858, making it one of the US’s oldest pharmaceutical companies.

data.title: Factories slash hiring ahead of Budget
data.description:
British manufacturers have cut back on hiring as they await greater certainty from John Healey’s Budget.

The balance of factories expecting to ramp up recruitment has dropped to just 3pc in the third quarter of this year, compared with 15pc in the previous three-month period.

While this indicates growth in hiring overall, the figures suggest it has slowed almost to a standstill.

As well as fears around the Budget, manufacturing trade body Make UK suggests factories are reluctant to recruit because of high taxes and inflated energy costs.

Manufacturing’s recruitment slowdown is compounded by a 6.2pc drop in the number of vacancies across the sector last quarter, according to the Office for National Statistics.

That is despite rising business confidence after manufacturers upgrading their forecast for UK output growth this year to 1.2pc, up 0.8pc.

But researchers said that although expectations appeared to be on the rise, this has not translated into job growth.

They said that factories are trying to do more with less as they battle growing cost pressures and red tape. Hiring has also been harmed by Labour’s Employment Rights Act, which has significantly strengthened workers’ rights.

Fhaheen Khan, a senior economist at Make UK, said: “The sharp slowdown in recruitment shows that high employment, energy and regulatory costs are forcing firms to think twice before taking on new people.”

Mr Khan added that the Budget will determine whether manufacturers will be able to “grow and invest”.

“Manufacturing makes up 10pc of the UK economy and could be vital to delivering the Prime Minister’s priorities,” he said.

Consumer confidence up

Separate findings from PwC also show an uptick in confidence among consumers, although economists warn that it could be short-lived, as rising food and energy prices put renewed pressure on household budgets.

The research shows consumer confidence reached its highest level in five years in August, with its sentiment index climbing from -13 in April to +1.

Almost two in five consumers described their finances as “healthy”, while fewer households expect to cut spending over the next three months.

But this growth in confidence risks being dampened by concerns about the cost of living, with 85pc of households citing this as one of their top worries, along with the state of the UK economy.

Sam Waller, the leader of industry for consumer markets at PwC UK, said: “As we head into autumn, the pressure on household finances will increase as energy and food prices rise.

“This will impact consumer facing businesses – along with wider macroeconomic headwinds that could spell higher interest rates and possible tax rises.

“Businesses should incentivise customers to start Christmas shopping now, and at the same, they must prepare themselves for a slowdown in consumer demand, look for ways to optimise operating costs, and to get their back-of-house in order.”

data.title: The West is hooked on Chinese drugs but they could save your life
data.description:
Sir Keir Starmer’s decision to invite Sir Pascal Soriot, AstraZeneca’s chief executive, to Beijing at the beginning of the year was a textbook piece of modern diplomacy.

The then-prime minister’s attempt to revive economic cooperation rested on a knockout deal that went beyond the usual warm words. Sir Pascal, a sworn Sinophile and one of the biggest cheerleaders of Chinese innovation, was only too happy to oblige.

Within hours of Sir Keir’s arrival, AstraZeneca had unveiled a plan to invest $15bn (£11bn) in China, building on its existing medical manufacturing and research capabilities in Beijing, Shanghai, Wuxi, Taizhou and Qingdao.

AstraZeneca’s pledge was the marquee announcement of Sir Keir’s trip. Sir Pascal said the “landmark investment” marked the next chapter for the company in China. For the politburo, it was further proof that their plan to turn China into a global pharmaceuticals leader has worked.

In the West, China has long been dismissed as little more than a dealer in cheap copycat medicines – both legal and illegal – and increasingly knockoffs too, such as unlicensed GLP-1 weight loss medication.

This portrayal no longer bears scrutiny, however. In recent years, the Chinese pharmaceutical industry has undergone a remarkable reinvention. Western industry leaders view it as a bona fide drug superpower at the forefront of discovery.

China controls an exciting pipeline of groundbreaking medicines and occupies a growing role as a globally important venue for clinical trials.

But for now, cooperation between East and West suits both sides. European and American drugmakers have rushed to embrace Chinese research, forging multi-billion licensing deals. Those with the appetite have opened their own labs and even set up manufacturing outposts.

Chinese science is now “the best in the world” and ignoring it is not an option, says one European pharmaceuticals chairman.

Few have led the charge as enthusiastically as Sir Pascal, AstraZeneca’s swashbuckling French boss. China is now its second-biggest market. Meanwhile GSK, the UK’s other national drug champion, has struck a series of partnerships with Chinese labs to licence promising drugs outside the country.

These relationships are critical for China’s pharmaceuticals industry, providing access to the lucrative markets that fund innovation. At home, their only customer is Xi Jinping, and he sets the price.

Yet this partnership is fragile. Amid growing concern in the US about the threat China’s new scientific prowess poses to drug supplies, innovation and even national security, industry executives fear an iron curtain will be drawn.

Drugs may be the next front in the superpower trade war that has already drawn in telecoms equipment, semiconductors, electric vehicles, rare earth minerals and solar panels.

For Europe, including Britain’s pharmaceutical giants AstraZeneca and GSK, the looming nightmare is that an American administration will sooner or later use its economic muscle to effectively outlaw their cooperation with China.

One senior figure says the possibility of a sweeping American crackdown is “probably the one question that keeps me awake at night”.

China’s rapid scientific progress

Dr Zhao Hong, a renowned Chinese cancer specialist, shocked thousands of Communist Party delegates in March last year: a Guangzhou-based biotech firm had developed a cancer drug that had outperformed the world’s bestselling equivalent in clinical trials.

The work of China’s Akeso Biopharma, lung cancer drug ivonescimab had shown that it could delay non-small-cell lung cancer progression for five months longer than US giant Merck’s Keytruda treatment – the world’s bestselling prescription drug in 2025.

The success of ivonescimab was hailed as a breakthrough moment for China’s pharmaceutical industry.

“China is at the best time of its biopharmaceutical sector’s development,” Hong told state media at the annual Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference.

The speed with which China is catching up in pharmaceuticals and biotech is astonishing.

By 2024, China had 1,255 drugs at the research stage, a nearly eight-fold jump in less than a decade. America had 1,441 – a 15pc rise – while the total in Europe had shrunk slightly to 400.

Experts attribute the leap to a fundamental shift in how the industry was perceived by the Chinese regime.

One veteran UK executive recalls how when he first used to visit China in the late 1990s, it was to complain about “counterfeits and pharmaceuticals that were really dangerous”. Today, China is seen as “a golden opportunity”, he says.

“They have moved deliberately to be at the leading edge of science,” he adds.

Beijing has provided vast support in the form of scores of state-financed biotechnology parks equipped with advanced laboratories and heavily subsidised hardware, together with a sweeping overhaul of the regulatory system beginning in 2015.

A study by Prof Yimin Cui, of Peking University, and colleagues found that the time taken to approve a drug for human trials fell to 87 days after the reforms, from 501 days previously.

Chinese researchers are helped by the sheer size of the country’s population – last counted at more than 1.4 billion – says Freddy Yip, a corporate lawyer at Cooley.

“In the US, it may take a long time to recruit sufficient patients, but in China, you have access to lots of different patients with different kinds of diseases, including many rare diseases,” Yip says.

Sir Pascal has said this combination of scientific capability and rapid execution – “China speed”, as he has called it – can help to dramatically accelerate drug development.

One of China’s leading biotech venture capitalists estimates clinical trials are “two thirds cheaper and half as quick in China”.

Progress has been spurred by a massive increase in spending on research and development – leaping from $35m in 2015 to $15bn in 2023 – and a “reverse brain drain” in which thousands of foreign-educated Chinese scientists and entrepreneurs have returned home, according to Porsche Consulting.

Chinese scientists are now at the vanguard of treatment for cardiovascular diseases and cancer, as well as spearheading drug development for metabolic conditions and neurological disorders, such as Parkinson’s, among many others.

Alarm bells in Washington

Mere months before Sir Pascal was lending heft to Sir Keir’s Beijing bridge-building mission, the Frenchman was being warmly welcomed at the Oval Office by Donald Trump.

Thanking the US president for welcoming him “in this beautiful office”, Sir Pascal was armed with another crowd-pleasing announcement: a pledge to cut drug prescription prices in the US, after Trump had accused other countries of “freeloading” at the expense of Americans.

Sir Pascal went further as well, unveiling a $50bn plan to expand the company’s existing operations in the US. In return, AstraZeneca received a three-year exemption from tariffs.

Privately, AstraZeneca executives acknowledge it was also an attempt to ward off growing concern in the White House about the deepening of ties with China.

“We are cognisant of some of the more hawkish commentary [from US politicians]. It is a delicate balancing act, and we are treading a fine line by recognising what the US is trying to achieve,” an insider says.

Yet, for all Washington’s alarm, dependency has become more pronounced, not less. Western companies have piled into the country, hoovering up clinical trial data and striking licensing deals to develop Chinese medicines outside the mainland, which they hope can then be used to treat patients across the developed world.

“This is the golden age of science and China is white-hot right now,” an industry source says.

Deal activity is being driven by anxiety among European and US companies as their pipeline of drugs peters out.

America’s biotech industry faces the alarming prospect of an estimated $350bn worth of medicines – equivalent to roughly one fifth of projected global prescription-drug revenue – losing patent protection by the end of the decade.

When patents run out, generic rivals are allowed to gatecrash the market, jeopardising sales.

Few have led the way with the verve that AstraZeneca has demonstrated.

Sir Pascal’s Beijing announcement was accompanied by a boast that it had signed 16 global licensing agreements with 15 Chinese partners since 2023 alone – thought to be the most of any overseas pharmaceuticals multi-national.

GSK hasn’t been far behind. Last year, the company struck an alliance with local giant Hengrui Pharma to develop a dozen new medicines outside the mainland. The value of the deal could eventually total $12bn.

The agreements are part of an industry-wide surge in deals totalling $138bn last year – a nearly tenfold jump since 2021 – according to data provider PharmCube. 2026 is expected to be another record.

Deal flow shows little sign of slowing.

A fortnight ago, GSK unveiled a $1.3bn pact with Hutchmed, a Hong Kong-based biopharmaceuticals company with research facilities in Shanghai, for the bulk of the licensing rights to what it called “first in-class” cancer treatments.

Brewing geopolitical storm

Amid the feeding frenzy, concern in Washington has turned to outright hostility in some quarters.

In December last year, Trump signed into law the Biosecure Act, a move widely seen as a sharp escalation in tensions and the moment the longstanding strategic rivalry between the US and China spilt into the biotechnology arena.

The act prevents US companies reliant on federal contracts and funding from working with Chinese biotech firms with ties to the Chinese military and any deemed to pose a national security risk. It also bars Chinese companies from accessing US government funding themselves.

US biotechnology companies with federal contracts are now engaged in a mad dash to purge their supply chains of equipment obtained from any Chinese biotechnology firms on the banned list.

Next up is the Biotech Investment National Security Act. Though not yet signed into law, it will subject licensing deals involving Chinese companies to national security reviews.

Though technically a screening mechanism rather than a ban on licensing Chinese drugs, it will effectively function as one, says Craig Garthwaite, a professor at Northwestern University’s Kellogg School of Management.

There is also pressure to bar the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) from accepting Chinese trial data, amid concerns about their reliability. The FDA has repeatedly rejected one of Hengrui’s cancer drugs, citing questions about quality control at its manufacturing sites.

As one senior City figure puts it: the White House has conjured up other reasons to “erect a wall around China”.

AstraZeneca’s attempt to navigate this geopolitical storm by investing in both China and the US divides opinion. Some see it as an inspired way to keep both Washington and Beijing happy at the same time.

“I think Pascal has been very smart in not allowing anybody to question his US credentials. He’s playing his cards very wisely,” the boss of a rival company says.

Others see it as a high-stakes gamble from a company that is more exposed than most of its competitors and has learnt the hard way the risks that come from operating in China.

Leon Wang, the former head of its Chinese operations, is awaiting trial on charges of illegal trading, unlawful collection of personal information and medical insurance fraud, alongside another former employee, having been arrested in 2024.

If the saga made Sir Pascal reconsider his appetite for doing business in China, there is little sign of it.

Alongside licensing deals potentially worth tens of billions of dollars, it has around 17,000 employees in China, two “global strategic” research and development centres in Beijing and Shanghai, and four advanced manufacturing sites in Wuxi, Taizhou, Qingdao and Beijing.

China is now AstraZeneca’s second-largest market after the US, accounting for roughly 12pc of the company’s global turnover, and its Chinese facilities supply more than 70 markets worldwide.

In a written submission to the Commons business and trade select committee in July, AstraZeneca described co-operation with China as a “win-win”.

But as one investor with extensive interests in China points out: “If you’re a big pharma company with a significant proportion of your licensing spend coming from China and the tap suddenly gets turned off, that’s obviously a problem.”

Europe’s wary response

Despite sharply rising tensions, there are concerns that European policymakers are still a long way off from having a coherent industrial strategy that addresses the China question.

Having been slow to react to the threat that cheap Chinese manufacturing poses to the continent’s steelmakers, solar panel producers and its car industry, the risk is that the pendulum swings too far the other way and Brussels takes a similarly antagonistic approach in trying to shut China out of other sectors, such as pharmaceuticals.

Calls by Oliver Blume, the chief executive of Volkswagen, for tougher trade measures against Beijing have been interpreted in some circles as a signal that EU-China relations are close to a tipping point after years of resistance to anti-Chinese duties from the continent’s car giants.

Yet, a senior industrialist says Europe lacks the “economic counterweight to be able to exclude China”.

“I don’t necessarily think it’s good in the long term for the US to do so, but I think it’s very dangerous for Europe,” he adds.

“We need a more nuanced industrial strategy that seeks Chinese expertise and cost effectiveness, and to somehow bring some of the economic benefit of that into Europe,” he says.

Such sentiment echoes a growing willingness among car manufacturers to partner with Chinese counterparts amid an onslaught of imports. Nissan’s decision to share its Sunderland plant with Chery, one of China’s largest car exporters, is expected to be among the first of many similar tie-ups.

Some believe the growing divide between Washington and Beijing because of pharmaceuticals may even present an opportunity for Europe.

“I’m sure Europe would be more than happy to take Chinese-developed products that are sold to them at a lower price than what they might otherwise get from the United States,” Garthwaite says.

As Brussels bureaucrats try to agree on a co-ordinated approach, the rhetoric, particularly among some influential Republicans, continues to harden.

Chris Klomp, a top lieutenant of Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US health secretary, has likened the situation to “a war”.

Anxiety has been heightened by a so-called “hot mic” incident at a Beijing military parade late last year, in which Vladimir Putin and Xi were overheard discussing the possibility that humans could live to 150 years old, thanks to advances in biotechnology.

Some China hawks saw it as further evidence that the US risked falling behind in the global race for domination in advanced science.

The Council on Foreign Relations, an influential American think tank, has called for reliance on China’s biotech know-how to be treated as a strategic vulnerability akin to critical minerals.

“The US (and just about every other nation) faces a growing risk that China will deliberately withhold essential pharmaceutical inputs as a tool of economic or political coercion … as China has done with rare-earth critical minerals,” it warned in June.

The Atlantic Council, another US think tank with a history of shaping American foreign policy, points out that the US is reliant on China for three quarters of some imported drugs and as much as 99pc of some raw materials that are critical to the production of certain key medicines.

What’s more, China’s 2020 export control law and 2021 biosecurity law “grant broad authority to weaponise pharmaceutical exports”, it said recently.

‘All in or all out’

AstraZeneca declined to comment on its position, but there are signs it is more nervous than it is willing to acknowledge.

It emerged in August that the company had held detailed discussions with American rival Bristol Myers Squibb about a potential £300bn mega-merger.

In seeking to substantially deepen its US footprint, AstraZeneca may have concluded that the best chance it has of escaping any crackdown is if the company can demonstrate it is willing to take action to address Trump’s demands for the “reshoring” of pharmaceutical manufacturing.

Radical corporate restructuring plans have also been explored in China. AstraZeneca previously looked at the possibility of carving out its Chinese business into a separate legal entity and listing it on the Shanghai stock exchange. Though nothing came of those plans, they were seen as an attempt to insulate it from mounting geopolitical tensions.

GSK, meanwhile, sees no reason for such drastic action. Publicly, all a spokesman is willing to say is that it has “a longstanding presence in China, to make sure patients can access our medicines and vaccines”.

“China is also increasingly a source of cutting-edge biopharma innovation, and we have established several important collaborations for potential new treatments in oncology, respiratory, immunology and inflammation,” the spokesman adds.

However, like AstraZeneca, it too has fallen foul of Beijing after the company was engulfed in a bribery scandal in 2014.

GSK was found guilty of bribing Chinese doctors and hospitals to prescribe its medical products and was forced to pay a record $490m fine.

That ordeal prompted GSK bosses to take a much more cautious approach in which its activities were limited to strict licensing deals rather than the asset-heavy approach of others, such as AstraZeneca.

“It [GSK] went through a very difficult time in China. The experience damaged the company immeasurably in terms of its willingness to take risks,” a City source says.

By focusing on developing local collaborations, GSK believes it can still capitalise on the opportunities in China while being “less vulnerable” than rivals who are more “asset-exposed”, an insider explains.

Yet, the same person admits it ultimately boils down to one question: “Are they [China] helping us long-term or are they harming us? And I can’t answer that, which is why we can’t afford to be all in or all out.”

Industry figures hope common sense prevails between the two superpowers.

Garthwaite acknowledges deals that come with potential national security risk should be scrutinised, while attempts to reduce American over-dependence on Chinese antibiotics are also to be applauded.

However, he says the White House needs to distinguish between drug production and drug development, which “shouldn’t be too hard”.

Another investor says patients don’t really care where the drugs come from, “as long as they’re subjected to the same trials”.

In response to a recent US ban on imports of humanoid robots, China’s foreign ministry said: “Protectionism does not make the US more competitive … it will only hurt the interests of US companies and consumers.”﻿

Yet, nor is it in China’s interests to actively undermine American science. Chinese drugmakers simply cannot afford to be shut out of Western markets, particularly the US, experts say.

“China is really vulnerable too. It has to rely on its export machine because it doesn’t have sufficient levels of internal consumption,” one analyst says.

Ultimately, industry sources admit they are at the mercy of an unpredictable Trump administration whose appetite for trade wars shows little sign of waning.

As one boardroom veteran puts it: “It’s akin to walking a tightrope – we’ll continue trying to walk it and hope we stay on.”

data.title: CrossCountry cancels almost all trains after power cut
data.description:
CrossCountry has cancelled almost all its trains after a power cut at its Birmingham headquarters.

The long-distance rail operator warned of “significant disruption” on Sunday and said that services “across almost all routes will be withdrawn until further notice”.

The Birmingham city centre power cut has disrupted operations at CrossCountry’s main control centre, meaning systems used to manage its trains are unavailable.

The only CrossCountry route still running is between Peterborough and Stansted airport, calling at March, Ely and Cambridge.

CrossCountry tickets are being accepted via any reasonable route on all other train companies’ services, according to National Rail Enquiries. A normal service is expected to run on Monday.

A spokesman for CrossCountry said: “A power cut in Birmingham city centre has affected the building where our control centre is located. As a result, many of the systems our control teams use to manage the railway are currently unavailable.

“Although colleagues are working hard to safely operate services using alternative processes, CrossCountry services will be significantly disrupted on Sunday Aug 23.

“While we will run as many trains as possible, passengers should expect significant reductions to services and cancellations across almost all routes throughout the day. We are sorry to passengers affected by this significant and unforeseen disruption.

The National Grid operates the electricity distribution network serving Birmingham city centre.

On Aug 7, a similar power cut in Manchester caused a power cut at a Network Rail signalling control centre, leading to chaos across the north-west of England as all trains came to a standstill as a safety precaution.

The incident was triggered by a fault at a transformer in Ardwick, which provides energy for Network Rail’s Manchester Rail Operating Centre.

Heidi Alexander, the Transport Secretary, said: “I am concerned to hear about a power outage affecting CrossCountry rail services, which I know will be very frustrating to passengers.

“I’ve asked publicly owned operators to lay on extra services where possible. We’ve also sent Network Rail power teams who are on-site and working to restore power and systems as soon as possible.”

A National Grid electricity distribution spokesman said on Sunday afternoon: “Our engineers are on site working to repair a fault affecting CrossCountry’s Birmingham control centre.

“We’re working closely with CrossCountry to restore power safely as soon as possible. We understand the frustration caused by disrupted journeys and are sorry for the inconvenience to passengers.”

Travellers delayed by more than half an hour are eligible to claim Delay Repay compensation from the train company via its website.

data.title: Royal Mail backs down in NHS letter overcharging row
data.description:
Royal Mail is watering down planned price rises for NHS hospital letters and bank statements following a backlash.

The postal service previously said it would increase the amount it charges third-party logistics companies that collect and sort bulk mail by 25pc.

The price rise was due to come into effect next month and would have followed an increase of around 9pc in January.

But Royal Mail will now implement a reduced price rise of 18pc instead after logistics companies protested over the plans.

The climbdown comes after Ofcom intervened to resolve the dispute. The regulator said it would rule on whether the price rises were “fair and reasonable” within the next four months.

Postal bosses have decided to water down the proposals over concerns about the financial impact of a lengthy Ofcom review.

The move ends the dispute and means the revised price increases will come into force in December.

However, it is unclear whether the Mail Competition Forum, which represents logistics firms such as Whistl and UK Mail, will choose to challenge the 18pc price rise after objecting to the 25pc increase.

Doing so could trigger a fresh Ofcom review.

It has previously described Royal Mail’s price rises as “excessive” and criticised the postal service’s “abysmal” quality of service.

The wrangling is centred on wholesale mail, which covers some NHS letters, energy bills and bank statements, rather than the amount consumers pay for a stamp.

Bulk mail costs have remained significantly lower than stamp prices, which have risen sharply in recent years.

The price the public pays for a first-class stamp hit £1.80 in April – almost double what it cost in 2022.

‘Institution in meltdown’

But Royal Mail has been under scrutiny for its quality of service, with customers complaining of hospital letters turning up after appointment dates and delayed bills triggering late-payment charges.

The postal service has been hit with repeated fines for missing its delivery targets, including a record £21m penalty last year.

Liam Byrne, chairman of the Commons business and trade committee, branded the company an “institution in meltdown”.

Royal Mail, which was acquired by Czech billionaire Daniel Křetínský in a £3.6bn deal last year, argues that price rises are needed to put the struggling business on a sustainable footing amid a sharp decline in letter-sending.

The company, which has racked up almost £800m in losses over the last four years, has secured approval to overhaul its universal service obligations, which require it to deliver letters across the country six days a week.

The reforms, which include scrapping second-class letter deliveries on Saturday and watering down Royal Mail’s quality of service targets, are currently being rolled out.

A Royal Mail spokesman said: “Delaying price increases for access business customers is negatively impacting on the financial sustainability of the universal service and as a result we have notified customers of increases that will take effect in December.

“Royal Mail made losses of almost £800m over the last four years and the company’s profitability remains below the level Ofcom considers financially sustainable for the provision of a universal service.

“It is vital that our business prices reflect the true costs of delivering a service to the UK’s 32 million addresses, when letter volumes continue to fall and the costs of maintaining a nationwide service and 130,000 jobs continue to rise.”
