data.title: ‘Maverick’ tycoon Dale Vince bamboozles his climate comrades
data.description:
Explaining why he donated more than £340,000 to Just Stop Oil, Dale Vince said he backed the activists’ simple demand: no new drilling for oil in the North Sea.

The controversial climate group had been waging a campaign of disruptive protests, enraging motorists by blocking traffic and throwing soup at famous artworks.

“It’s a campaign I’m completely behind,” Vince said in 2022. “We’ve got to stop the exploration and production of oil.”

Fast forward to now, however, and the green energy tycoon and Labour Party donor has executed a screeching about-turn that is leaving some of his erstwhile net zero allies scratching their heads.

He has thrown his weight behind the Rosebank and Jackdaw projects, two controversial oil and gas fields that could unlock hundreds of millions of barrels of fossil fuels off the coast of Scotland.

Speaking to BBC Newsnight, he said: “We are using fossil fuels for the next couple of decades. That’s a reality. If we approach things differently, we can actually make sense of drilling the North Sea.”

Friends in the climate movement are loath to criticise the tycoon and put his recent comments down to his eccentric character and occasionally light grip on detail.

They argue Vince’s idea to give oil and gas producers fixed-price contracts will never work and therefore shouldn’t be taken seriously.

“Dale says some very interesting stuff, a lot of which we agree with and some of which we don’t; let’s put it like that,” one veteran activist says. “If you look at the conditions he attached to it, they’re never going to happen.

“So yes, the optics are not altogether helpful from our point of view. But that’s Dale. He’s a bit of a maverick.”

Another activist says: “He’s got some views that are quite out-there. But with the North Sea, this isn’t actually his argument.

“These are lines the oil and gas industry has been pushing for years; they’re not his.

“We’d argue he’s mistaken and that he doesn’t know an awful lot about it. I mean, it’s Dale Vince, isn’t it?”

A spokesman for Vince said: “Maverick is the one word of truth in this lame attempt at a character assassination.

“All of Dale’s positions are logical, and in the national interest – he pursues them with the utmost consistency, being dogged but not dogmatic.”

After speaking to activists, energy industry figures and politicians, The Telegraph found that most of Vince’s opponents were unwilling to go on the record when discussing the tycoon.

His robust approach to criticism has helped create space for a remarkable volte-face for a man who previously lamented that opening up new oil and gas fields would be a “betrayal of millions of us”.

In a sign that Vince’s influence extends beyond energy, Labour is now considering a £14bn raid on capital gains tax outlined in a Budget submission by one of its biggest donors.

The former New Age traveller, who made his fortune through renewable energy supplier Ecotricity, can appear stridently dogmatic, but is capable of unusual elasticity.

He announced he was withdrawing support for Just Stop Oil in 2023, arguing that its use of disruptive protests had become “counter-productive” and that the war would be better waged at the ballot box.

Writing in The Guardian, he said: “In order to ‘just stop oil’, first we need to just stop the Tories; to me that is simple, unarguable logic.”

Vince donated more than £6m to Labour in pursuit of this goal. Yet last year he declared that political donations should be banned, suggesting that parties should instead be publicly funded. “We should take out donor influence and clean up politics,” he said.

A spokesman denied any contradiction in this approach, saying: “[Vince] operates within the rules we have while calling for better ones.”

On energy – home turf – examining Vince’s record induces a similar feeling of whiplash. He called on the Government in September 2015 to effectively scrap the oil and gas windfall tax by controlling wholesale prices to help support domestic producers that had licences already.

“It’s time for Labour to put its arms around the North Sea and support operators with existing licences,” he told The Guardian. “Putting fossil fuels on an equal footing with renewables by giving them a stable price is the key to a just transition.”

By April this year, however, as a US war with Iran sent oil and gas prices surging higher, his position had hardened again.

“What kind of eejit calls for the scrapping of the windfall tax on runaway oil profits – in the middle of an energy crisis with oil prices running away again … seems pretty illogical to me,” he wrote on social media platform X.

It can make for a muddled message from a man who not only makes regular public declarations on energy policy, but has also been accused of holding sway over Labour’s energy policy.

This shifting picture has, however, provided plenty of fuel for Vince’s prolific emissions on social media platforms, such as LinkedIn and X.

The tycoon frequently weighs in on political issues and offers critiques of media coverage, and has enlisted the help of professionals, including flamboyant PR guru Mark Borkowski, to help fine-tune his message.

The Borkowski agency says it worked with Vince after his decision to stop supporting Just Stop Oil, adding that it sought to “place responsibility for the pivot squarely on the intransigence and divisiveness of the Conservative government”.

Vince has reportedly lined up a rescue package for the publisher behind three London newspapers – the Camden New Journal, Islington Tribune and Westminster Extra – in a move that could further boost his influence.

Vince was among a select group of supporters lined up in Downing Street to welcome Andy Burnham on his first day in office. He denies having discussed North Sea drilling with the Prime Minister.

The Telegraph understands Burnham is currently minded to approve Jackdaw, but the fate of Rosebank is still uncertain, and a decision may not come until the autumn.

Vince was also an important backer of Sir Keir Starmer, the former prime minister, before and after he swept into power in 2024 – and similarly showed he was willing to flex his beliefs then.

He insisted he was “relaxed” about Labour watering down commitments to its so-called green prosperity plan – its landmark green energy strategy – from £28bn a year to less than £5bn. The initial pledge was an “arbitrary number”, he insisted, adding that the party was simply “being practical”.

Vince’s seeming caprice nevertheless extends to Labour. Earlier this year, he told The Telegraph that Ed Miliband was “the right man in the right place at the right time”.

Three months later, he blamed the former energy secretary for the “toxification of net zero” and said he was unfit to be chancellor. John Healey, Miliband’s Cabinet colleague, was ultimately appointed to the role.

Vince went further in June by urging ministers to ditch the term “net zero”, break up the “bloated” Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) and abandon major policies, including carbon capture and heat pump subsidies.

That is despite his previous criticisms of both Sir Tony Blair and Greg Jackson, the Octopus Energy boss, for suggesting that some of the more wasteful net zero schemes should be reconsidered.

A spokesman said: “Dale is critical of billions of pounds of taxpayers’ money being spent on heat pumps, nuclear and carbon capture. That is why he has been critical of many of the spending decisions at DESNZ and most recently of the man in charge at the time, Ed Miliband.”

Vince’s position on the North Sea came with a caveat. The entrepreneur said new drilling should be approved only if the oil and gas produced is subject to price controls to make them cheaper than imported energy.

Similar to the contracts for difference provided to wind farms, this would guarantee producers a stable price but also ensure they cannot profit from short-term crises.

A spokesman for Vince argued that his approach to the North Sea had been consistent.

He said: “What he has recently done is to propose something new, something radical – price control of our own oil and gas – in the national interest.

“He has pointed out that if we did this, then the economic argument for new production in the North Sea would exist – where currently it does not.”

It’s a position that commands some support.

“If Dale Vince’s intervention helps move the debate away from ideology and towards this practical reality, then it should be welcomed,” says Russell Borthwick, the chief executive of the Aberdeen and Grampian Chamber of Commerce.

Yet it puts Vince at loggerheads with the green campaigners who are holding fast to their opposition against new drilling.

“Exploiting new North Sea oil and gas will do nothing to reduce our bills and only put us on a course to more of the extreme weather currently causing deadly heatwaves and devastating wildfires,” says Mike Childs, the head of policy at Friends of the Earth.

“It’s the nation’s continuing dependence on fossil fuels that has caused household energy bills to rocket.”

Tessa Khan, the executive director of Uplift, adds: “You only need to scratch the surface of some of the claims being made to justify new drilling to realise that they don’t stack up.

“Rosebank, like most of what’s left in the North Sea, is overwhelmingly oil for export. It will make no meaningful difference to UK energy supply and nothing to lower fuel costs.

“When the impacts of climate change are escalating – whether that’s our farmers struggling to grow food or the devastating floods in Nepal – it would be irresponsible in the extreme for this Government to cave into the demands of the oil industry and allow Rosebank.”

But as Burnham prepares to give a verdict on the future of North Sea drilling, the support of an avowed climate campaigner such as Vince may lend any reversal credibility in the eyes of Labour voters.

“If even a man who used to fund Just Stop Oil has seen the light and now backs us using our own resources in the North Sea, it is extraordinary that the Labour Party are still banning all new licences and dragging their feet on approving Rosebank and Jackdaw,” says Claire Coutinho, shadow energy secretary.

“Burnham should listen to his friend, give the go-ahead to Rosebank and Jackdaw, end the mad ban on new licences and back the North Sea.”

That is assuming, of course, that Vince doesn’t change his mind again.

data.title: Housebuilders face Iran chaos as construction costs surge
data.description:
Housebuilders are facing chaos as soaring energy prices from the Iran war drive up the cost of construction, economists have warned.

Inflation for the construction sector could soon surpass 10pc if oil prices remain above $100 per barrel, said Noble Francis, the economics director at the Construction Products Association.

Oil is used as an input in the manufacturing of plastics, which are used heavily in housing construction, leaving the sector vulnerable to further price spikes if the conflict continues.

Mr Francis said: “We have only just started to see the impacts of the initial Middle East conflict on construction product price inflation, which was 6pc in the year to July.

“If oil prices remain above $100 per barrel for the rest of this year and industrial energy prices remain at their highest levels since those energy and commodity price spikes in 2022, then we would expect that construction products price inflation peaks at double-digit percentages.”

These effects are delayed as manufacturers typically operate on long-term contracts, and are therefore only just starting to come through.

Crude oil prices have soared more than 40pc since the Iran conflict began in February, with Brent crude trading at $103 a barrel on Friday.

Construction cost inflation above 10pc would still be far below the 25pc annual rise recorded during the worst of the 2022 energy crisis.

But it would follow years of cumulative price rises that have heaped pressure on the stretched sector.

‘Big increases in taxes’

Construction product price levels in July 2026 were already 50pc above those in January 2020, before the pandemic, Mr Francis said.

The Home Builders Federation (HBF) calculated earlier this year that price inflation means the cost of building a house has already risen by £76,000 in the last five years, while the cost of building a high-rise flat has jumped by £98,000.

Steve Turner, of the HBF, warned that developers had little leeway to absorb higher costs and any increase would hit the supply of Britain’s future homes.

Mr Turner said: “Any flexibility within the system has been removed by the big increases in taxes and all of the additional policy costs that have been added on over recent years.

“We’re already seeing a huge number of sites that five years ago could have been used for housebuilding, but are now simply not viable any more.”

The warning comes as the developer behind the transformation of Wembley Park faces pressure to sell assets and refinance debt because of the costs spiral.

Quintain said in public filings it needed to sell “one or more” buildings to repay £100m to its shareholders by next June, while the indebted developer was also in talks to refinance one of three loans due before the end of this year.

The two other loans, representing 28pc of its overall £1.3bn debt pile, have already been refinanced.

The developer has built thousands of flats on the industrial land around Wembley Stadium in west London, along with bars and shops. Around £2.8bn has been invested in the scheme since it bought the land in 2002.

When the project is finished, more than 6,000 of its 8,500 homes will consist of flats for rent.

Quintain said it had also been stung by an industry-wide bottleneck in building safety checks, which delayed its ability to lease out newly completed homes until this year.

This included affordable homes that were finished in September 2025, but were forced to stay empty while the regulator dealt with a backlog of design checks.

Around 1,934 people moved into Wembley Park during the period, 15pc down on the previous year when it secured 2,267 new residents.

Quintain did not respond to requests for comment.

data.title: Elon Musk’s X sales rebound in UK despite ad boycott
data.description:
Elon Musk’s X has posted a rebound in UK sales even after brands pulled millions in advertising spending because of safety fears.

The social media site, formerly known as Twitter, reported UK revenues of £46.4m in 2025, an increase of more than 60pc on the previous year. Pre-tax profit doubled to almost £1.6m, according to newly filed accounts at Companies House.

The figures suggest X’s UK business has proved resilient in the face of an advertising boycott that has seen scores of major brands pull campaigns from the site.

The company suffered a collapse in ad revenues following Mr Musk’s $44bn (£33bn) takeover, which saw the billionaire tear up content moderation policies.

Advertiser concerns heightened earlier this year after it emerged that X’s Grok chatbot was being used to undress women in photographs and generate child sexual abuse images.

Ofcom has opened a formal investigation into the issue, marking the first of its kind under new online safety laws, while the data watchdog is also carrying out its own review.

Mr Musk has fuelled tensions with brands after telling companies who withdrew from the site to “go f--- yourself”, while he also filed a lawsuit against brands including Mars and Unilever over claims that they illegally conspired to withhold advertising revenues. A US judge dismissed the lawsuit earlier this year.

The latest accounts show X’s UK advertising revenues were broadly flat compared to the year before, at £22.9m, as brands continued to hold back spending.

X also suffered a $4.5m hit to ad revenue in the first quarter linked to the outbreak of the Iran war.

But overall sales rebounded thanks to a sharp increase in the amount of revenue generated from providing research and development and support services to its parent company. This rose to £23.6m, from £6.9m the previous year.

The figures highlight how X’s UK operations play a crucial role in providing expertise in areas such as software development, coding and advertising technology.

However, the increase in inter-company sales still failed to offset the impact of the ad boycott. X’s revenues remain less than a quarter of the £200m it posted in 2021 before Mr Musk’s takeover.

X recorded a sharp increase in staff costs, which more than tripled to £47m last year. This was driven by a jump in share-based payments to almost £29m from £1m previously.

data.title: Ignore rising factory costs at your peril, Ford boss warns Labour
data.description:
Labour ignores rising energy, tax and regulatory costs “at our peril”, Ford’s UK chief has warned, amid fears of a fresh raid on business.

Lisa Brankin said the car giant’s British operations were already under heavy pressure, forcing the company to work “really hard to make sure that we keep what we’ve got”.

Speaking to The Telegraph during a tour of Ford’s Dagenham plant, she said: “I think we neglect the cost issue at our peril, if we think that new jobs will stay here irrespective of cost.”

Her comments represent the latest warning from Britain’s beleaguered automotive industry after the decision by Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) to cut 4,000 jobs and come as John Healey, the Chancellor, is reportedly mulling more tax rises to plug a hole in the public finances.

Ms Brankin pointed to recent increases to National Insurance contributions and business rates, high industrial electricity prices and the Government’s electric vehicle (EV) targets as examples of costs that were squeezing companies.

She said: “There’s a point where that comes back to bite you and I think we’re seeing the cost – the cost of energy in particular in the UK – becoming really, really challenging.

“I don’t think we’re alone in that, in terms of industry that would say.”

Ms Brankin said Ford’s UK operations would be difficult to replicate elsewhere and that its workforce was highly skilled and efficient but admitted “there are certainly cheaper places to operate”.

Ford builds some 600,000 diesel engines per year at its Dagenham plant, including for the Ranger Super Duty pickup truck and its popular Transit vans, although this represents just half of the historic site’s capacity.

It also makes crankshafts, engine blocks and cylinder heads there.

As part of an effort to secure a £900m contract from the Ministry of Defence to replace the Army’s fleet of Land Rovers, Ford has said the Dagenham plant could also supply engines for a militarised version of the Ranger.

The base chassis would be made in Thailand with final assembly and modifications taking place in Britain.

Ms Brankin suggested on Monday that the Ranger was an “off-the-peg” candidate that was cost-effective and required minimal modifications.

She added: “There’s no development required on these vehicles. They’re already in production.

“We sell Rangers around the world. We build over 300,000 every year, so it’s there and it’s ready.”

Other carmakers bidding for the contract include JLR, General Motors, Babcock, Ineos and the start-up Fering.

Ford is separately investing £380m in an upgrade of its factory in Halewood, Merseyside, where it is transitioning from making gearboxes to drive units for EVs.

‘Hoping to see change’

However, the company is lobbying the Government to relax the requirements of the zero emission vehicle (ZEV) mandate, which sets targets that carmakers must meet for sales of electric cars and vans.

Ford and other carmakers have argued that the targets are too far ahead of consumer demand. If they fail to meet them, they face the prospect of hefty fines.

Asked about the effect on future investment of the mandate and rising costs, Ms Brankin replied: “Everything has an effect on how you look at the UK, which is one of the reasons we’ve been so vociferous in calling for a review of the ZEV mandate.

“Fortunately, the Government just launched its consultation, so we’re hoping to see some change there.

“We’re not looking at it in terms of our business case here, but just thinking about the viability of the business overall.”

The chief executive added: “The transition to EVs is something that we’ve bought into, that we’ve invested really heavily in.

“All we’re concerned about is the pace of change that’s being forced, and that it’s so out of kilter with customer demand, and that’s putting a lot of pressure on our business.”

The Government was approached for comment.

data.title: Jim Ratcliffe lashes out at Labour as he mothballs factories
data.description:
Sir Jim Ratcliffe has accused Labour of “economic vandalism” after his petrochemicals business was forced to close three plants over soaring energy costs.

The facilities in Hull – which employ some 4,000 workers – normally produce raw materials for drugs, clothing, cosmetics, detergents, construction and explosives.

But Ineos, founded by Sir Jim, said they will now be temporarily shut down until further notice because of what he called “ridiculously high” energy prices.

Two have already ceased production, with the third due to come offline in a matter of days.

Sir Jim said the sites “just cannot compete”, pointing to soaring UK gas prices, despite claiming that its facilities are among the most energy-efficient and low-carbon of their kind in Europe.

The Ineos chief also blamed the Government’s energy policies for causing “economic vandalism on an industrial scale”.

He said: “I’m sure people will find it hard to believe that we are being forced to mothball some of the most efficient plants in Europe but with gas prices now 12 times the level in the US and eight times that of China, we just cannot compete.

“Not only is the ridiculously high gas price in the UK destroying our manufacturing base and the jobs of hard-working people on Humberside, it is also massively increasing the environmental burden, with replacement products supplied from the USA at double the carbon emissions and from China at eight times the emission level.”

He added: “The UK Government’s energy policy is leading to economic vandalism on an industrial scale, exporting jobs to China and the United States and driving up global CO2 emissions at a stroke.”

It was not immediately clear whether Ineos was considering closing the three Hull plants permanently, but the company warned that such a closure would have a “dramatic” impact on the Humberside area.

Sir Jim, who has a personal fortune of around £15bn, said last weekend that he did not have “any confidence in Britain” and had no plans to return from his home in Monaco.

The Manchester United co-owner also urged ministers to address problems of immigration and the country’s soaring benefits bill, “otherwise the country ends up in a bad place and goes broke”.

Figures from the Institute for Fiscal Studies published on Tuesday show that British households and industry have to pay the highest electricity costs in Europe.

Electricity for industrial use cost 19.1p per kwh in Britain in 2025, far higher than Ireland, which was in second place at 17.7p.

The analysis showed that this was because British manufacturers have to pay the highest combined charges for network upgrades, taxes and levies, which made up 8.1p, or nearly half, of the total costs.

Industrial energy costs in Great Britain saw the third largest rise in Europe between 2017 and 2025, behind only Ireland and Poland.

Domestic electricity in Great Britain in 2025 cost 33.2p per kwh, after accounting for supply costs, network costs, taxes, levies and VAT, the IFS found. This was the highest level in Europe, above Germany at 33p per kwh.

Household electricity costs have also surged at the highest pace in Europe, climbing by 12.7p per kwh between 2017 and 2025.

UK and European gas prices have surged this summer as the prolonged US-Iran conflict continues to squeeze supplies of oil and gas coming out of the Strait of Hormuz.

There are also fears about European gas storage levels, which are below average for this time of year.

In the UK, the gas price last week hit its highest level for nearly four years at about 198p per therm. It traded at 173p per therm on Tuesday, amid reports that Washington and Tehran could broker a ceasefire.

But Ashley Kelty, an analyst at Panmure Liberum, said markets were “ignoring history” by going “all in on the prospect of a diplomatic solution”.

He added: “We see the intervention by China in asking Iran to try and rein the Houthi rebels in as being a more significant factor as China has stayed on the sidelines during the conflict.”

A government spokesman said: “While this is a commercial decision from Ineos, we know this will be a concerning time for workers in Saltend and their families.

“We’ve taken bold action to support our chemicals industry including £350m for strategically important chemicals producers, which will be available on a co-investment basis.

“We’ve also put trade measures in place on foreign chemicals imports and are tackling high electricity costs via our supercharger and British industrial competitiveness scheme to keep our chemicals sector competitive.”

data.title: Khan accused of ‘mad vanity project’ with London bus power grab
data.description:
Lord Khan has been accused of a “mad vanity project” after revealing plans for a publicly-owned bus company in London.

The plan would see a new company, Buses for London, created with an initial fleet of 100 vehicles and a depot in the west of the city.

Lord Khan, the Mayor of London, said the move provided an opportunity to “reimagine” the network to provide better value for money and support Labour’s climate goals.

However, an industry source said the proposals were “mad” and “a Sadiq Khan vanity project” that would heap costs on Transport for London (TfL), which is already £14bn in debt.

The source said TfL already controlled London’s buses, with eight private operators running individual routes through a franchising system built around competitive tendering that had worked well for more than 40 years.

They said: “The only reason for this is that the unions are putting pressure on Sadiq Khan because they see pound signs in their eyes. They’ll be wanting TfL pension rates rather than what they’re on at Go-Ahead, Arriva or Stagecoach.

“The current system works and has for a long time. TfL already has full control over the buses and operators only get paid if they run them efficiently, so they are massively incentivised to hit performance standards.”

The move will be linked to Andy Burnham’s push to get more bus routes into public ownership. He pioneered the approach as mayor of Manchester, while Richard Parker, the Mayor of the West Midlands, has also unveiled plans to take on routes in his region.

However the Confederation of Passenger Transport (CPT), which represents bus firms, said passengers needed faster, more reliable journeys rather than a new public bus operator.

Graham Vidler, the CPT chief executive, said: “Buses typically travel at just 9mph in London – slower than the average cyclist. Nothing in the announcement will tackle this chronic issue and get Londoners to their destinations more quickly.

“Tackling unplanned, uncoordinated streetworks and giving buses priority at junctions is essential for improving passenger journeys.”

He said private bus operators had invested in new vehicles while being hit by soaring diesel prices and £36m in costs from the increase in employers’ National Insurance contributions.

If Lord Khan’s plan comes to fruition, Mr Vidler said, the costs “would increasingly fall on London’s taxpayers”.

TfL said Buses for London will be based at Park Royal Depot in west London and will initially take over the number 6 route between nearby Willesden and Victoria station from 2027, with a further four launch services to be announced over the coming year.

Some 700 routes are currently contracted to the eight private firms, which typically serve routes around a collection of depots that each owns outright.

TfL said it will have greater control over how services are run, enabling it to boost reliability and safety while crucially reinvesting profits in the network.

The industry source said the reality of the change would be that the “big systemic issues will be kicked into the long grass” while TfL is left “marking its own homework.”

Buses on the number 6 route, operated by Metroline, travelled at an average of 8mph in the morning peak in the first five months of this year, 5pc slower than last year, the source said.

They added: “Utilities digging up the streets every five minutes, all these systemic issues. Nothing in this announcement is going to fix that. It’s just a side show, it’s pointless.”

Another source close to a London bus operator said the Mayor was “jumping on the Burnham bandwagon” and exploiting the Prime Minister’s support for localising bus services to deepen his control over a network that was already devolved.
